The algorithm is based on a novel, artificial neural network, called a "Siamese" neural network. This network consists of two identical sub-networks joined at their out(cid:173) puts. During training the two sub-networks extract features from two signatures, while the joining neuron measures the distance be(cid:173) tween the two feature vectors. Verification consists of comparing an extracted feature vector ~ith a stored feature vector for the signer. Signatures closer to this stored representation than a chosen thresh(cid:173) old are accepted, all other signatures are rejected as forgeries.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for verifying signatures captured on a pen-input tablet. Its central component is a Siamese neural network made of two identical subnetworks joined at their outputs. The architecture processes two signatures so that the system can compare their learned representations, making similarity the basis of verification.

During training, each subnetwork extracts a feature vector from one signature. A joining neuron measures the distance between the two vectors. This arrangement puts feature extraction and comparison into the same network design. The representation matters because the final decision depends on distance in the extracted feature space, rather than on a direct comparison described only at the input level.

At verification time, the system extracts features from a submitted signature and compares them with a stored feature vector for the claimed signer. A chosen distance threshold determines acceptance: sufficiently close signatures pass, and the others are rejected as forgeries. The paper's stated contribution is this paired-network algorithm and the resulting reference-and-threshold decision process.
summary.tldr: A Siamese network verifies tablet-written signatures by comparing learned feature vectors against a stored reference and distance threshold.

title: Signature Verification using a "Siamese" Time Delay Neural Network

abstract: The localization and orientation to various novel or interesting events in the environment is a critical sensorimotor ability in all animals, predator or prey. In mammals, the superior colliculus (SC) plays a major role in this behavior, the deeper layers ex(cid:173) hibiting topographically mapped responses to visual, auditory, and somatosensory stimuli. Sensory information arriving from differ(cid:173) ent modalities should then be represented in the same coordinate frame. Auditory cues, in particular, are thought to be computed in head-based coordinates which must then be transformed to reti(cid:173) nal coordinates. In this paper, an analog VLSI implementation for auditory localization in the azimuthal plane is described which ex(cid:173) tends the architecture proposed for the barn owl to a primate eye movement system where further transformation is required. This transformation is intended to model the projection in primates from auditory cortical areas to the deeper layers of the primate superior colliculus. This system is interfaced with an analog VLSI-based saccadic eye movement system also being constructed in our labo(cid:173) ratory.

paragraphs: The paper describes an analog chip for locating sounds and translating their positions into coordinates suitable for eye movements. This addresses a sensorimotor problem: information from hearing and vision must be expressed in a compatible frame to guide orientation toward an event. The superior colliculus motivates the design because its deeper layers contain spatially organized responses to multiple senses.

The proposed hardware localizes sound in the azimuthal plane, corresponding to direction around the listener. It extends an architecture associated with barn owl auditory localization to a primate eye movement system. That extension requires an additional transformation because auditory position is treated as head-based, whereas the visual representation is tied to the retina.

The coordinate transformation is intended to model the pathway from auditory cortical areas to deeper layers of the primate superior colliculus. The chip is interfaced with an analog hardware system for rapid eye movements being developed in the same laboratory. Its contribution is a concrete implementation connecting sound localization, coordinate conversion, and an eye movement interface.
summary.tldr: An analog chip combines sound localization with the coordinate transformation needed to guide a primate-inspired eye movement system.

title: An Auditory Localization and Coordinate Transform Chip

abstract: An application of reinforcement learning to a linear-quadratic, differential game is presented. The reinforcement learning system uses a recently developed algorithm, the residual gradient form of advantage updating. The game is a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with continuous time, states, and actions, linear dynamics, and a quadratic cost function. The game consists of two players, a missile and a plane; the missile pursues the plane and the plane evades the missile. The reinforcement learning algorithm for optimal control is modified for differential games in order to find the minimax point, rather than the maximum. Simulation results are compared to the optimal solution, demonstrating that the simulated reinforcement learning system converges to the optimal answer. The performance of both the residual gradient and non-residual gradient forms of advantage updating and Q-learning are compared. The results show that advantage updating converges faster than Q-learning in all simulations. The results also show advantage updating converges regardless of the time step duration; Q-learning is unable to converge as the time step duration ~rows small. U.S .A.F. For each state x and action u, the advantage, A(x,u), is stored, representing an estimate of the degree to which the expected total discounted reinforcement is increased by performing action u rather than the action currently considered best. paragraphs: The paper applies reinforcement learning to a pursuit-and-evasion game between a missile and a plane. Time, states, and actions are continuous, while the dynamics are linear and the cost is quadratic. These assumptions define the particular control problem and provide an optimal solution against which the learned behavior can be compared.

The method uses the residual gradient form of advantage updating. It keeps separate estimates of a state's value and the relative benefit of taking an action there. The authors modify the control algorithm to seek a minimax solution, reflecting the opposing objectives of the two players rather than optimizing for a single decision maker.

In simulations, the learned solution converges to the optimal answer. Comparisons include residual gradient and non-residual gradient versions of advantage updating and Q-learning. Advantage updating converges faster in every reported simulation and continues to converge across time-step durations, while Q-learning fails as the steps become small. The findings connect the choice of learning representation to performance when a continuous-time problem is implemented through discrete updates.
summary.tldr: Advantage updating reaches the optimal simulated pursuit-and-evasion solution faster than Q-learning and remains effective as time steps shrink.

title: Advantage Updating Applied to a Differential Game

abstract: A new learning algorithm is developed for the design of statistical classifiers minimizing the rate of misclassification. The method, which is based on ideas from information theory and analogies to statistical physics, assigns data to classes in probability. The dis(cid:173) tributions are chosen to minimize the expected classification error while simultaneously enforcing the classifier's structure and a level of "randomness" measured by Shannon's entropy. Achievement of the classifier structure is quantified by an associated cost. The con(cid:173) strained optimization problem is equivalent to the minimization of a Helmholtz free energy, and the resulting optimization method is a basic extension of the deterministic annealing algorithm that explicitly enforces structural constraints on assignments while re(cid:173) ducing the entropy and expected cost with temperature. In the limit of low temperature, the error rate is minimized directly and a hard classifier with the requisite structure is obtained. This learn(cid:173) ing algorithm can be used to design a variety of classifier structures. The approach is compared with standard methods for radial basis function design and is demonstrated to substantially outperform other design methods on several benchmark examples, while of(cid:173) ten retaining design complexity comparable to, or only moderately greater than that of strict descent-based methods. 592 D. paragraphs: The paper develops a classifier training method aimed directly at reducing misclassification. During learning, examples receive probabilistic class assignments. These distributions must balance expected classification error, the required structure of the classifier, and a controlled amount of randomness measured by Shannon entropy.

The authors express this constrained problem through a free-energy objective and extend deterministic annealing to enforce structural requirements. A temperature parameter governs the progression of learning: as temperature falls, assignment entropy and expected cost are reduced. At low temperature, assignments become hard class decisions, and the procedure directly targets error while producing the required classifier structure.

This formulation matters because it connects the classification objective with constraints on how the classifier can be built. The framework accommodates multiple structures, and the reported comparisons concern radial basis function design. Across several benchmarks, it substantially outperforms other design methods, often with computational design complexity comparable to, or only moderately above, methods based strictly on descent. The reported benefit therefore combines improved classification with a manageable optimization burden.
summary.tldr: A constrained annealing algorithm turns probabilistic assignments into structured classifiers while directly targeting classification error.

title: An Information-theoretic Learning Algorithm for Neural Network Classification

abstract: We study the number of hidden layers required by a multilayer neu(cid:173) ral network with threshold units to compute a function f from n d to {O, I}. In dimension d = 2, Gibson characterized the functions computable with just one hidden layer, under the assumption that there is no "multiple intersection point" and that f is only defined on a compact set. We consider the restriction of f to the neighbor(cid:173) hood of a multiple intersection point or of infinity, and give neces(cid:173) sary and sufficient conditions for it to be locally computable with one hidden layer. We show that adding these conditions to Gib(cid:173) son's assumptions is not sufficient to ensure global computability with one hidden layer, by exhibiting a new non-local configuration, the "critical cycle", which implies that f is not computable with one hidden layer.

paragraphs: How many hidden layers are needed to represent a function depends on more than parameter count. This paper studies threshold-unit networks for binary functions, concentrating on the geometry of two-dimensional decision regions. It extends an earlier characterization that excluded multiple boundary intersections and restricted attention to compact domains.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for one-hidden-layer representation near multiple intersection points and near infinity. These local results fill gaps in the earlier setting. They then ask whether satisfying all such local requirements is enough to guarantee a single hidden layer can represent the whole function.

It is not: a nonlocal configuration called a critical cycle prevents global representation despite the added local conditions. The contribution identifies a genuinely global obstacle to shallow-network expressivity. This shows why checking neighborhoods separately can miss dependencies among decision boundaries that determine whether an additional hidden layer is required.
summary.tldr: A critical-cycle obstruction shows that locally compatible threshold decision regions can still require more than one hidden layer globally.

title: Multilayer Neural Networks: One or Two Hidden Layers?

abstract: There is strong evidence that face processing is localized in the brain. The double dissociation between prosopagnosia, a face recognition deficit occurring after brain damage, and visual object agnosia, difficulty recognizing otber kinds of complex objects, indicates tbat face and non(cid:173) face object recognition may be served by partially independent mecha(cid:173) nisms in the brain. Is neural specialization innate or learned? We sug(cid:173) gest that this specialization could be tbe result of a competitive learn(cid:173) ing mechanism that, during development, devotes neural resources to the tasks they are best at performing. Furtber, we suggest that the specializa(cid:173) tion arises as an interaction between task requirements and developmen(cid:173) tal constraints. In this paper, we present a feed-forward computational model of visual processing, in which two modules compete to classify input stimuli. When one module receives low spatial frequency infor(cid:173) mation and the other receives high spatial frequency information, and the task is to identify the faces while simply classifying the objects, the low frequency network shows a strong specialization for faces. No otber combination of tasks and inputs shows this strong specialization. We take these results as support for the idea that an innately-specified face processing module is unnecessary.

paragraphs: Evidence that face recognition and other object recognition can be impaired separately suggests partially independent processing mechanisms. This paper asks whether such specialization must be innately specified. It proposes that competition during learning can allocate neural resources according to the interaction between available visual information and the task being learned.

The authors build a feed-forward model with two modules competing to classify stimuli. In the critical condition, one module receives low spatial frequencies, which convey coarser image structure, while the other receives high spatial frequencies, which convey finer detail. The task requires identifying individual faces while only classifying the other objects.

Under that combination, the low-frequency module develops strong specialization for faces. No other tested combination of tasks and inputs produces the same strong specialization. The finding therefore ties specialization to both the information supplied and the distinctions demanded by the task. The authors interpret this as support for a learned route to face specialization, showing how a dedicated face-processing module need not be specified in advance.
summary.tldr: A competitive model develops face specialization through a specific interaction between spatial-frequency inputs and identification demands.

title: Task and Spatial Frequency Effects on Face Specialization

abstract: The psychophysical evidence for "selective attention" originates mainly from visual search experiments. In this work, we formulate a hierarchi(cid:173) cal system of interconnected modules consisting in populations of neu(cid:173) rons for modeling the underlying mechanisms involved in selective visual attention. We demonstrate that our neural system for visual search works across the visual field in parallel but due to the different intrinsic dynamics can show the two experimentally observed modes of visual attention, namely: the serial and the parallel search mode. In other words, neither explicit model of a focus of attention nor saliencies maps are used. The focus of attention appears as an emergent property of the dynamic behavior of the system. The neural population dynamics are handled in the framework of the mean-field approximation. Conse(cid:173) quently, the whole process can be expressed as a system of coupled dif(cid:173) ferential equations.

paragraphs: Visual search experiments reveal behavior that can look parallel, with information considered together, or serial, with attention apparently proceeding through successive locations. This paper models the neural mechanisms behind those two patterns using a hierarchy of interconnected modules. Each module represents a population of neurons whose activity changes through interactions with other populations.

The system operates across the visual field in parallel, yet differences in its internal dynamics allow it to display both observed search modes. This distinction matters because apparently serial behavior need not imply that the model explicitly moves a designated attentional focus from place to place. The authors demonstrate that such behavior can arise from the evolving activity of the network.

The model uses neither an explicit focus-of-attention mechanism nor saliency maps. Instead, attentional focus emerges from the system's dynamics. A mean-field approximation describes the neural populations collectively, allowing the process to be written as coupled differential equations. The work thus offers a dynamical account connecting distributed neural processing with different patterns of visual search.
summary.tldr: A parallel neural population model produces both serial and parallel visual search through its internal dynamics.

title: A Neurodynamical Approach to Visual Attention

abstract: Attractor networks, which map an input space to a discrete out(cid:173) put space, are useful for pattern completion. However, designing a net to have a given set of attractors is notoriously tricky; training procedures are CPU intensive and often produce spurious afuac(cid:173) tors and ill-conditioned attractor basins. These difficulties occur because each connection in the network participates in the encod(cid:173) ing of multiple attractors. We describe an alternative formulation of attractor networks in which the encoding of knowledge is local, not distributed. Although localist attractor networks have similar dynamics to their distributed counterparts, they are much easier to work with and interpret. We propose a statistical formulation of localist attract or net dynamics, which yields a convergence proof and a mathematical interpretation of model parameters. Attractor networks map an input space, usually continuous, to a sparse output space composed of a discrete set of alternatives. Attractor networks have a long history in neural network research. Attractor networks are often used for pattern completion, which involves filling in missing, noisy, or incorrect features in an input pattern. The initial state of the attractor net is typically determined by the input pattern. Over time, the state is drawn to one of a predefined set of states-the attractors. Attractor net dynam(cid:173) ics can be described by a state trajectory (Figure 1a). An attractor net is generally implemented by a set of visible units whose activity represents the instantaneous state, and optionally, a set of hidden units that assist in the computation. Attractor dynamics arise from interactions among the units. In most formulations of afuac(cid:173) tor nets,2,3 the dynamics can be characterized by gradient descent in an energy landscape, allowing one to partition the output space into attractor basins. Instead of homogeneous attractor basins, it is often desirable to sculpt basins that depend on the recent history of the network and the arrangement of attractors in the space. In psychological models of human cognition, for example, priming is fundamental: after the model visits an attractor, it should be faster to fall into the same attractor in the near future, i.e., the attractor basin should be broadened. 1 ,6 Another property of attractor nets is key to explaining behavioral data in psycho(cid:173) logical and neurobiological models: the gang effect, in which the strength of an attractor is influenced by other attractors in its neighborhood. Figure 1b illustrates the gang effect: the proximity of the two rightmost afuactors creates a deeper at(cid:173) tractor basin, so that if the input starts at the origin it will get pulled to the right. paragraphs: Attractor networks complete patterns by letting an initial, possibly corrupted input evolve toward one of several stored states. Designing those destinations and the regions that lead to them can be difficult. In distributed formulations, individual connections help encode several attractors, so changing the network to improve one stored pattern can affect others.

The paper proposes a localist formulation in which knowledge is encoded locally. Its dynamics resemble those of distributed attractor networks, but the authors describe the resulting networks as easier to manipulate and interpret. A statistical account of these dynamics supplies both a convergence proof and a mathematical meaning for the model parameters.

The supplied text also explains why the shape of an attractor's surrounding region matters. Recent visits can make a state easier to reach again, while nearby attractors can collectively strengthen attraction toward their neighborhood. These considerations connect network dynamics to behavioral phenomena. The contribution is a formulation that makes attractor behavior more mathematically interpretable while retaining dynamics similar to familiar distributed networks.
summary.tldr: A localist statistical formulation makes attractor networks easier to interpret and provides a convergence proof.

title: A Generative Model for Attractor Dynamics

abstract: Reaching movements require the brain to generate motor com- mands that rely on an internal model of the task's dynamics. Here we consider the errors that subjects make early in their reaching trajectories to various targets as they learn an internal model. Us- ing a framework from function approximation, we argue that the sequence of errors should reflect the process of gradient descent. If so, then the sequence of errors should obey hidden state transitions of a simple dynamical system. Fitting the system to human data, we find a surprisingly good fit accounting for 98% of the variance. This allows us to draw tentative conclusions about the basis ele- ments used by the brain in transforming sensory space to motor commands. To test the robustness of the results, we estimate the shape of the basis elements under two conditions: in a traditional learning paradigm with a consistent force field, and in a random sequence of force fields where learning is not possible. Remarkably, we find that the basis remains invariant. 1 Introduction It appears that in constructing the motor commands to guide the arm toward a target, the brain relies on an internal model (IM) of the dynamics of the task that it learns through practice [1]. The IM is presumably a system that transforms a desired limb trajectory in sensory coordinates to motor commands. The motor commands in turn create the complex activation of muscles necessary to cause action. A major issue in motor control is to infer characteristics of the IM from the actions of subjects. Recently, we took a first step toward mathematically characterizing the IM's rep- resentation in the brain [2]. We analyzed the sequence of errors made by subjects on successive movements as they reached to targets while holding a robotic arm. The robot produced a force field and subjects learned to compensate for the field (presumably by constructing an IM) and eventually produced straight movements within the field. Our analysis sought to draw conclusions about the structure of the IM from the sequence of errors generated by the subjects. For instance, in a velocity-dependent force field (such as the fields we use), the IM must be able to encode velocity in order to anticipate the upcoming force. We hoped that the e#ect of errors in one direction on subsequent movements in other directions would give information about the width of the elements which the IM used in encoding velocity. For example, if the basis elements were narrow, then movements in a given direction would result in little or no change in performance in neighboring directions. Wide basis elements would mean appropriately larger e#ects. We hypothesized that an estimate of the width of the basis elements could be cal- culated by fitting the time sequence of errors to a set of equations representing a dynamical system. The dynamical system assumed that error in a movement resulted from a di#erence between the IM's approximation and the actual environ- ment, an assumption that has recently been corroborated [3]. Recently, we took a first step toward mathematically characterizing the IM's rep- resentation in the brain [2]. We analyzed the sequence of errors made by subjects on successive movements as they reached to targets while holding a robotic arm. The robot produced a force field and subjects learned to compensate for the field (presumably by constructing an IM) and eventually produced straight movements within the field. Our analysis sought to draw conclusions about the structure of the IM from the sequence of errors generated by the subjects. For instance, in a velocity-dependent force field (such as the fields we use), the IM must be able to encode velocity in order to anticipate the upcoming force. We hoped that the e#ect of errors in one direction on subsequent movements in other directions would give information about the width of the elements which the IM used in encoding velocity. For example, if the basis elements were narrow, then movements in a given direction would result in little or no change in performance in neighboring directions. Wide basis elements would mean appropriately larger e#ects. We hypothesized that an estimate of the width of the basis elements could be cal- culated by fitting the time sequence of errors to a set of equations representing a dynamical system. The dynamical system assumed that error in a movement resulted from a di#erence between the IM's approximation and the actual environ- ment, an assumption that has recently been corroborated [3]. The error in turn changed the IM, a#ecting subsequent movements:
title: Linking Motor Learning to Function Approximation: Learning in an Unlearnable Force Field

abstract: The problem of computing a resample estimate for the reconstruction error in PCA is reformulated as an inference problem with the help of the replica method. Using the expectation consistent (EC) approximation, the intractable inference problem can be solved efficiently using only two variational parameters. A perturbative correction to the result is computed and an alternative simplified derivation is also presented.
originalAbstract: The problem of computing a resample estimate for the reconstruction error in PCA is reformulated as an inference problem with the help of the replica method. Using the expectation consistent (EC) approximation, the intractable inference problem can be solved efficiently using only two variational parameters. A perturbative correction to the result is computed and an alternative simplified derivation is also presented.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to compute a resampling-based estimate of reconstruction error for principal component analysis, or PCA. Reconstruction error measures how much information is lost when data are represented through PCA and then reconstructed. The target here is an estimate based on resampling, rather than simply the error of a single fitted reconstruction.

The authors use the replica method to turn this estimation task into an inference problem. That change of formulation creates a route to approximation, although the resulting inference problem is itself intractable. They then apply the expectation consistent approximation, which makes the calculation efficient while requiring only two variational parameters.

The paper also computes a perturbative correction and gives an alternative, simplified derivation. These contributions address both the approximation and how it can be understood mathematically. The main significance is a compact computational formulation: an otherwise difficult resample-error calculation can be approached through a small approximate inference problem. The stated result concerns this efficient approximation, rather than an exact replacement for the underlying inference task.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates PCA resample-error estimation as approximate inference that can be computed efficiently using two variational parameters.

title: An Approximate Inference Approach for the PCA Reconstruction Error

abstract: Markov networks are commonly used in a wide variety of applications, ranging from computer vision, to natural language, to computational biology. In most current applications, even those that rely heavily on learned models, the structure of the Markov network is constructed by hand, due to the lack of effective algorithms for learning Markov network structure from data. In this paper, we provide a computationally efficient method for learning Markov network structure from data. Our method is based on the use of L1 regularization on the weights of the log-linear model, which has the effect of biasing the model towards solutions where many of the parameters are zero. This formulation converts the Markov network learning problem into a convex optimization problem in a continuous space, which can be solved using efficient gradient methods. A key issue in this setting is the (unavoidable) use of approximate inference, which can lead to errors in the gradient computation when the network structure is dense. Thus, we explore the use of different feature introduction schemes and compare their performance. We provide results for our method on synthetic data, and on two real world data sets: pixel values in the MNIST data, and genetic sequence variations in the human HapMap data. We show that our L1 -based method achieves considerably higher generalization performance than the more standard L2 -based method (a Gaussian parameter prior) or pure maximum-likelihood learning. We also show that we can learn MRF network structure at a computational cost that is not much greater than learning parameters alone, demonstrating the existence of a feasible method for this important problem. Undirected graphical models, such as Markov networks or log-linear models, have been used in an ever-growing variety of applications, including computer vision, natural language, computational biology, and more. However, as this modeling framework is used in increasingly more complex and less well-understood domains, the problem of selecting from the exponentially large space of possible network structures becomes of great importance. Including all of the possibly relevant interactions in the model generally leads to overfitting, and can also lead to difficulties in running inference over the network. Moreover, learning a "good" structure can be an important task in its own right, as it can provide insight about the underlying structure in the domain. Unfortunately, the problem of learning Markov networks remains a challenge. The key difficulty is that the maximum likelihood (ML) parameters of these networks have no analytic closed form; finding these parameters requires an iterative procedure (such as conjugate gradient [15] or BFGS [5]), where each iteration runs inference over the current model. This type of procedure is computationally expensive even for models where inference is tractable. The problem of structure learning is considerably harder. The dominant type of solution to this problem uses greedy local heuristic search, which incrementally modifies the model by adding and possibly deleting features.

abstract: We consider the problem of learning classifiers for structurally incomplete data, where some ob jects have a subset of features inherently absent due to complex relationships between the features. The common approach for handling missing features is to begin with a preprocessing phase that completes the missing features, and then use a standard classification procedure. In this paper we show how incomplete data can be classified directly without any completion of the missing features using a max-margin learning framework. We formulate this task using a geometrically-inspired ob jective function, and discuss two optimization approaches: The linearly separable case is written as a set of convex feasibility problems, and the non-separable case has a non-convex ob jective that we optimize iteratively. By avoiding the pre-processing phase in which the data is completed, these approaches offer considerable computational savings. More importantly, we show that by elegantly handling complex patterns of missing values, our approach is both competitive with other methods when the values are missing at random and outperforms them when the missing values have non-trivial structure. We demonstrate our results on two real-world problems: edge prediction in metabolic pathways, and automobile detection in natural images.

paragraphs: The paper addresses structurally incomplete data, where some features are inherently absent because of relationships among the features. Filling in missing entries before classification is a common approach. The authors instead develop a max-margin framework that works directly with incomplete observations, avoiding that completion stage.

Their objective is motivated by geometry, and the optimization treatment depends on whether the data are linearly separable. For the separable case, they formulate a collection of convex feasibility problems. For the nonseparable case, the objective is nonconvex and is optimized iteratively. This distinction is part of the method's formulation, rather than treating both settings as one convex problem.

Avoiding completion provides considerable computational savings. The authors also report competitive performance when entries are missing at random and better performance than comparison methods when missingness has nontrivial structure. They demonstrate the approach on edge prediction in metabolic pathways and automobile detection in natural images. These findings emphasize the predictive value of handling structured absence directly within the classifier.
summary.tldr: A max-margin framework classifies incomplete data directly and performs particularly well when missing features follow structured patterns.

title: Max-margin classification of incomplete data

abstract: We derive a cost functional for estimating the relationship between highdimensional observations and the low-dimensional process that generated them with no input-output examples. Limiting our search to invertible observation functions confers numerous benefits, including a compact representation and no suboptimal local minima. Our approximation algorithms for optimizing this cost functional are fast and give diagnostic bounds on the quality of their solution. Our method can be viewed as a manifold learning algorithm that utilizes a prior on the low-dimensional manifold coordinates. The benefits of taking advantage of such priors in manifold learning and searching for the inverse observation functions in system identification are demonstrated empirically by learning to track moving targets from raw measurements in a sensor network setting and in an RFID tracking experiment.

paragraphs: High-dimensional measurements can arise from a process described by relatively few variables. This paper seeks to recover the relationship between those measurements and the underlying process without paired input-output examples. The authors derive a cost functional for this unsupervised regression problem, with applications to identifying nonlinear systems.

They restrict the search to invertible observation functions. Under that restriction, the formulation has a compact representation and no suboptimal local minima. Approximation algorithms optimize the objective quickly and provide diagnostic bounds on solution quality. The method can also be interpreted as manifold learning that incorporates a prior on the low-dimensional coordinates.

This prior provides information about the underlying coordinates while the method searches for inverse observation functions linking measurements back to the process. Experiments demonstrate benefits in learning to track moving targets from raw sensor-network measurements and in an RFID tracking setting. The results support using coordinate priors and inverse-function estimation together, with the stated optimization advantages tied to the invertibility restriction.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised regression uses invertible observation functions and coordinate priors to recover low-dimensional processes from raw measurements.

title: Unsupervised Regression with Applications to Nonlinear System Identification

abstract: We study the rates of growth of the regret in online convex optimization. First, we show that a simple extension of the algorithm of Hazan et al eliminates the need for a priori knowledge of the lower bound on the second derivatives of the observed functions. We then provide an algorithm, Adaptive Online Gradient Descent, which interpolates between the results of Zinkevich for linear functions and of Hazan et al for strongly convex functions, achieving intermediate rates T and log T . Furthermore, we show strong optimality of the algorithm. between Finally, we provide an extension of our results to general norms.

We then provide an algorithm, Adaptive Online Gradient Descent, which interpolates between the results of Zinkevich for linear functions and of Hazan et al for strongly convex functions, achieving intermediate rates T and log T . Furthermore, we show strong optimality of the algorithm. between Finally, we provide an extension of our results to general norms.

paragraphs: The paper studies regret in online convex optimization: how a learner’s accumulated performance compares with an appropriate retrospective choice as functions arrive over time. Its focus is the rate at which regret grows, and how that rate depends on the curvature of the functions being observed.

The first contribution extends an existing algorithm so that it no longer requires advance knowledge of a lower bound on second derivatives. This removes a particular piece of information that would otherwise need to be supplied before learning begins. The authors then introduce Adaptive Online Gradient Descent, which connects previously established results for linear functions and strongly convex functions.

The adaptive algorithm achieves intermediate regret rates between those endpoint settings, allowing the analysis to reflect a broader range of curvature behavior. The paper also establishes a strong optimality result and extends its conclusions to general norms. Together, these contributions make the regret analysis less dependent on knowing a curvature bound in advance and less restricted to a single geometric setting.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Online Gradient Descent obtains curvature-sensitive regret rates without requiring advance knowledge of a lower curvature bound.

title: Adaptive Online Gradient Descent

abstract: We propose a novel hierarchical, nonlinear model that predicts brain activity in area V1 evoked by natural images. In the study reported here brain activity was measured by means of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a noninvasive technique that provides an indirect measure of neural activity pooled over a small volume (~ 2mm cube) of brain tissue. Our model, which we call the SpAM V1 model, is based on the reasonable assumption that fMRI measurements reflect the (possibly nonlinearly) pooled, rectified output of a large population of simple and complex cells in V1. It has a hierarchical filtering stage that consists of three layers: model simple cells, model complex cells, and a third layer in which the complex cells are linearly pooled (called âpooled-complexâ cells). The pooling stage then obtains the measured fMRI signals as a sparse additive model (SpAM) in which a sparse nonparametric (nonlinear) combination of model complex cell and model pooled-complex cell outputs are summed. Our results show that the SpAM V1 model predicts fMRI responses evoked by natural images better than a benchmark model that only provides linear pooling of model complex cells. Furthermore, the spatial receptive fields, frequency tuning and orientation tuning curves of the SpAM V1 model estimated for each voxel appears to be consistent with the known properties of V1, and with previous analyses of this data set. A visualization procedure applied to the SpAM V1 model shows that most of the nonlinear pooling consists of simple compressive or saturating nonlinearities.

paragraphs: This paper predicts fMRI responses in visual area V1 when people view natural images. The measurements indirectly summarize neural activity within a small volume of tissue. The proposed SpAM V1 model assumes these signals reflect pooled, rectified responses from many simple and complex cells, with pooling that may be nonlinear.

The model first processes images through a hierarchy representing simple cells, complex cells, and pooled-complex cells. The third layer linearly combines complex-cell outputs. A subsequent sparse additive stage sums nonparametric nonlinear contributions from complex and pooled-complex outputs to predict the measured signal. This separates the construction of visual responses from the way those responses contribute to an fMRI measurement.

The model predicts the reported responses better than a benchmark restricted to linear pooling of complex-cell outputs. Its estimated spatial receptive fields and frequency and orientation tuning appear consistent with known V1 properties and earlier analyses of the data. Visualizations suggest that most learned pooling nonlinearities compress or saturate responses, providing an interpretable account of the nonlinear combinations used for prediction.
summary.tldr: A sparse hierarchical model with nonlinear pooling predicts natural-image V1 fMRI responses better than a linear-pooling benchmark.

title: Nonparametric sparse hierarchical models describe V1 fMRI responses to natural images

abstract: We explore a recently proposed mixture model approach to understand- ing interactions between conﬂicting sensory cues. Alternative model for- mulations, differing in their sensory noise models and inference methods, are compared based on their ﬁt to experimental data. Heavy-tailed sen- sory likelihoods yield a better description of the subjects’ response behavior than standard Gaussian noise models. We study the underlying cause for this result, and then present several testable predictions of these models.
originalAbstract: We explore a recently proposed mixture model approach to understand- ing interactions between conﬂicting sensory cues. Alternative model for- mulations, differing in their sensory noise models and inference methods, are compared based on their ﬁt to experimental data. Heavy-tailed sen- sory likelihoods yield a better description of the subjects’ response behavior than standard Gaussian noise models. We study the underlying cause for this result, and then present several testable predictions of these models.

paragraphs: The paper examines how people respond when sensory cues disagree. It builds on a mixture-model approach to describing interactions between conflicting cues. The goal is to understand which versions of that approach best account for observed responses, making the assumptions about sensory uncertainty an explicit part of the investigation.

The authors compare formulations that differ in two respects: how they model sensory noise and how they perform inference. They assess these alternatives by their fit to experimental data. Heavy-tailed sensory likelihoods describe the subjects’ behavior better than standard Gaussian noise models. Such likelihoods allow more probability for large deviations, so this comparison concerns how the model represents unusual sensory observations.

The study also investigates why the heavy-tailed formulations provide the better fit and develops several testable predictions. This moves the contribution beyond choosing a model solely by its agreement with existing responses. The predictions provide ways to examine the models further, while the reported empirical conclusion remains specifically about their description of behavior in the data studied.
summary.tldr: Mixture models with heavy-tailed sensory noise better describe observed responses to conflicting cues than Gaussian alternatives.

title: Characterizing response behavior in multisensory perception with conflicting cues

abstract: We present a mixture model whose components are Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). This possibility has not been considered before because computing the partition function of an RBM is intractable, which appears to make learning a mixture of RBMs intractable as well. Surprisingly, when formulated as a third-order Boltzmann machine, such a mixture model can be learned tractably using contrastive divergence. The energy function of the model captures three-way interactions among visible units, hidden units, and a single hidden multinomial unit that represents the cluster labels. The distinguishing feature of this model is that, unlike other mixture models, the mixing proportions are not explicitly parameterized. Instead, they are defined implicitly via the energy function and depend on all the parameters in the model. We present results for the MNIST and NORB datasets showing that the implicit mixture of RBMs learns clusters that reflect the class structure in the data.

paragraphs: This paper builds a mixture model whose components are restricted Boltzmann machines, or RBMs. The apparent obstacle is that an RBM's partition function is intractable to compute, making a mixture of such components seem intractable to learn as well. The authors address this obstacle by changing how the mixture is represented.

They formulate it as a third-order Boltzmann machine, with an energy function describing three-way interactions among visible units, hidden units, and a hidden multinomial unit representing cluster labels. In this formulation, contrastive divergence provides a tractable learning approach. The mixture proportions are unusual: they are determined implicitly by the energy function and depend on all model parameters, rather than appearing as separate explicit parameters.

Results on MNIST and NORB show learned clusters that reflect the datasets' class structure. This supports the model's ability to discover meaningful groupings in those experiments. The contribution combines a tractable training formulation with a different way of expressing mixture membership, where component prevalence emerges from the same energy-based system that represents the data.
summary.tldr: An energy-based formulation enables contrastive-divergence training of RBM mixtures whose mixing proportions arise implicitly from the model parameters.

title: Implicit Mixtures of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: As the availability and importance of relational data -- such as the friendships summarized on a social networking website -- increases, it becomes increasingly important to have good models for such data. The kinds of latent structure that have been considered for use in predicting links in such networks have been relatively limited. In particular, the machine learning community has focused on latent class models, adapting nonparametric Bayesian methods to jointly infer how many latent classes there are while learning which entities belong to each class. We pursue a similar approach with a richer kind of latent variable -- latent features -- using a nonparametric Bayesian technique to simultaneously infer the number of features at the same time we learn which entities have each feature. The greater expressiveness of this approach allows us to improve link prediction on three datasets.

paragraphs: Relational data records connections between entities, such as friendships in a social network. Predicting those connections requires a model of the hidden structure underlying them. This paper moves beyond latent class models, which describe entities through class membership, toward latent features that provide a richer representation of each entity.

The approach uses nonparametric Bayesian modeling to infer how many hidden features are needed while also learning which entities possess each feature. These are parts of the same inference problem. The representation can describe entities through combinations of features, expanding the kinds of latent structure available for predicting links.

The authors report improved link prediction on three datasets and attribute the improvement to the approach's greater expressiveness. The result supports the usefulness of the feature-based representation in those evaluations. The contribution combines a richer account of entities with inference over the number of features, extending the nonparametric approach previously used to learn both class counts and class assignments.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian model jointly learns latent features and their number, improving link prediction on three datasets.

title: Nonparametric Latent Feature Models for Link Prediction

abstract: Object detection and multi-class image segmentation are two closely related tasks that can be greatly improved when solved jointly by feeding information from one task to the other. However, current state-of-the-art models use a separate representation for each task making joint inference clumsy and leaving classification of many parts of the scene ambiguous. In this work, we propose a hierarchical region-based approach to joint object detection and image segmentation. Our approach reasons about pixels, regions and objects in a coherent probabilistic model. Importantly, our model gives a single unified description of the scene. We explain every pixel in the image and enforce global consistency between all variables in our model. We run experiments on challenging vision datasets and show significant improvement over state-of-the-art object detection accuracy.

However, current state-of-the-art models use a separate representation for each task making joint inference clumsy and leaving classification of many parts of the scene ambiguous. Our approach reasons about pixels, regions and objects in a coherent probabilistic model. Importantly, our model gives a single unified description of the scene. We run experiments on challenging vision datasets and show significant improvement over state-of-the-art object detection accuracy.

paragraphs: Object detection and image segmentation describe related aspects of a scene: which objects are present and how the image is divided into labeled parts. The paper argues that the tasks can benefit from exchanging information. Separate representations, however, make joint reasoning awkward and can leave the interpretation of scene parts ambiguous.

The authors propose a hierarchical, region-based probabilistic model that reasons jointly about pixels, regions, and objects. These levels form one description of the scene. Every pixel is accounted for, and global consistency is enforced among the model's variables. This provides a shared structure through which object-level and region-level information can influence the interpretation of the image.

Experiments on challenging vision datasets show a significant improvement over state-of-the-art object detection accuracy. The stated finding supports the value of combining the tasks within a coherent scene model. The approach matters because information sharing is built into the representation itself: decisions about objects and image regions are required to fit together as parts of a single explanation.
summary.tldr: A unified probabilistic model of pixels, regions, and objects jointly handles segmentation and detection and improves object detection accuracy.

title: Region-based Segmentation and Object Detection

abstract: Many clustering techniques aim at optimizing empirical criteria that are of the form of a U-statistic of degree two. Given a measure of dissimilarity between pairs of observations, the goal is to minimize the within cluster point scatter over a class of partitions of the feature space. It is the purpose of this paper to define a general statistical framework, relying on the theory of U-processes, for studying the performance of such clustering methods. In this setup, under adequate assumptions on the complexity of the subsets forming the partition candidates, the excess of clustering risk is proved to be of the order O(1/\sqrt{n}). Based on recent results related to the tail behavior of degenerate U-processes, it is also shown how to establish tighter rate bounds. Model selection issues, related to the number of clusters forming the data partition in particular, are also considered.

Given a measure of dissimilarity between pairs of observations, the goal is to minimize the within cluster point scatter over a class of partitions of the feature space. It is the purpose of this paper to define a general statistical framework, relying on the theory of U-processes, for studying the performance of such clustering methods. In this setup, under adequate assumptions on the complexity of the subsets forming the partition candidates, the excess of clustering risk is proved to be of the order O(1/\sqrt{n}). Model selection issues, related to the number of clusters forming the data partition in particular, are also considered.

paragraphs: The paper provides a statistical framework for clustering methods that minimize pairwise dissimilarity within groups. Their empirical objectives have the form of degree-two U-statistics: they aggregate quantities calculated from pairs of observations. This pairwise structure makes U-process theory a natural tool for studying how clustering performance changes with sample size.

The analysis compares the clustering risk of a learned partition with the best risk available in the candidate class. Under suitable assumptions on the complexity of the sets defining those partitions, the excess risk is of order 1/sqrt(n). The guarantee therefore connects the amount of data and the richness of the partition class to the quality of the resulting clustering.

The authors also explain how results on the tail behavior of degenerate U-processes can yield tighter rate bounds. They consider model selection as well, including the choice of the number of clusters. The contribution is a general way to analyze pairwise clustering objectives and their statistical performance, with stronger rates available through more refined analysis.
summary.tldr: U-process theory yields conditional clustering-risk guarantees for pairwise objectives and supports tighter bounds and cluster-number selection analysis.

title: On U-processes and clustering performance

abstract: An increasing number of experimental studies indicate that perception encodes a posterior probability distribution over possible causes of sensory stimuli, which is used to act close to optimally in the environment. One outstanding difficulty with this hypothesis is that the exact posterior will in general be too complex to be represented directly, and thus neurons will have to represent an approximation of this distribution. Two influential proposals of efficient posterior representation by neural populations are: 1) neural activity represents samples of the underlying distribution, or 2) they represent a parametric representation of a variational approximation of the posterior. We show that these approaches can be combined for an inference scheme that retains the advantages of both: it is able to represent multiple modes and arbitrary correlations, a feature of sampling methods, and it reduces the represented space to regions of high probability mass, a strength of variational approximations. Neurally, the combined method can be interpreted as a feed-forward preselection of the relevant state space, followed by a neural dynamics implementation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to approximate the posterior over the relevant states. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this approach on a sparse coding model. In numerical experiments on artificial data and image patches, we compare the performance of the algorithms to that of exact EM, variational state space selection alone, MCMC alone, and the combined select and sample approach. The select and sample approach integrates the advantages of the sampling and variational approximations, and forms a robust, neurally plausible, and very efficient model of processing and learning in cortical networks. For sparse coding we show applications easily exceeding a thousand observed and a thousand hidden dimensions.
originalAbstract: An increasing number of experimental studies indicate that perception encodes a posterior probability distribution over possible causes of sensory stimuli, which is used to act close to optimally in the environment. One outstanding difficulty with this hypothesis is that the exact posterior will in general be too complex to be represented directly, and thus neurons will have to represent an approximation of this distribution. Two influential proposals of efficient posterior representation by neural populations are: 1) neural activity represents samples of the underlying distribution, or 2) they represent a parametric representation of a variational approximation of the posterior. We show that these approaches can be combined for an inference scheme that retains the advantages of both: it is able to represent multiple modes and arbitrary correlations, a feature of sampling methods, and it reduces the represented space to regions of high probability mass, a strength of variational approximations. Neurally, the combined method can be interpreted as a feed-forward preselection of the relevant state space, followed by a neural dynamics implementation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to approximate the posterior over the relevant states. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this approach on a sparse coding model. In numerical experiments on artificial data and image patches, we compare the performance of the algorithms to that of exact EM, variational state space selection alone, MCMC alone, and the combined select and sample approach. The select and sample approach integrates the advantages of the sampling and variational approximations, and forms a robust, neurally plausible, and very efficient model of processing and learning in cortical networks. For sparse coding we show applications easily exceeding a thousand observed and a thousand hidden dimensions.

paragraphs: The paper combines two proposals for how neural populations might approximate uncertainty about the causes of sensory input. Sampling represents a posterior through draws from it, while variational approximation uses a more compact representation. The challenge is to preserve complex uncertainty without explicitly representing an intractably large posterior distribution.

The proposed method first selects a relevant region of the state space and then samples within it. Selection concentrates computation in regions containing substantial probability mass. Sampling retains the ability to represent multiple modes and arbitrary correlations. The neural interpretation pairs a feed-forward selection stage with dynamics implementing Markov chain Monte Carlo over the selected states.

Experiments use a sparse coding model with artificial data and image patches. The comparisons include exact expectation-maximization, selection alone, sampling alone, and the combined approach. The authors report effective and efficient inference and learning, including sparse coding applications exceeding a thousand observed and a thousand hidden dimensions. These demonstrations support the combined scheme as a robust, neurally plausible computational model.
summary.tldr: Selecting high-probability states before sampling combines efficient posterior approximation with the ability to represent complex uncertainty.

title: Select and Sample - A Model of Efficient Neural Inference and Learning

abstract: POMDP planning faces two major computational challenges: large state spaces and long planning horizons. The recently introduced Monte Carlo Value Iteration (MCVI) can tackle POMDPs with very large discrete state spaces or continuous state spaces, but its performance degrades when faced with long planning horizons. This paper presents Macro-MCVI, which extends MCVI by exploiting macro-actions for temporal abstraction. We provide sufficient conditions for Macro-MCVI to inherit the good theoretical properties of MCVI. Macro-MCVI does not require explicit construction of probabilistic models for macro-actions and is thus easy to apply in practice. Experiments show that Macro-MCVI substantially improves the performance of MCVI with suitable macro-actions.

paragraphs: Planning with partially observed states becomes difficult when the state space is large or decisions must extend far into the future. Monte Carlo Value Iteration already handles very large discrete state spaces and continuous ones, but its performance deteriorates with long planning horizons. This paper addresses that remaining challenge through temporal abstraction.

The proposed extension, Macro-MCVI, incorporates macro-actions so planning can operate over temporally extended actions. The authors provide sufficient conditions under which the extension inherits MCVI's favorable theoretical properties. These conditions establish when the guarantees carry over; the claim does not make them necessary conditions for successful use.

Macro-MCVI also avoids requiring explicit construction of probabilistic models for the macro-actions, which the authors identify as a practical advantage. Experiments show substantial improvement over MCVI when suitable macro-actions are available. The result connects the benefit of temporal abstraction with the choice of those actions: the reported gains depend on their suitability, rather than implying that any collection of macro-actions will improve planning.
summary.tldr: Macro-MCVI uses temporally extended actions to improve long-horizon planning, with conditional guarantees and gains from suitable macro-actions.

title: Monte Carlo Value Iteration with Macro-Actions

abstract: In many applications classification systems often require in the loop human intervention. In such cases the decision process must be transparent and comprehensible simultaneously requiring minimal assumptions on the underlying data distribution. To tackle this problem, we formulate it as an axis-alligned subspacefinding task under the assumption that query specific information dictates the complementary use of the subspaces. We develop a regression-based approach called RECIP that efficiently solves this problem by finding projections that minimize a nonparametric conditional entropy estimator. Experiments show that the method is accurate in identifying the informative projections of the dataset, picking the correct ones to classify query points and facilitates visual evaluation by users.

paragraphs: Classification systems involving human intervention need decisions that people can inspect and understand. The paper approaches this through informative projections of the data, while seeking to make few assumptions about the underlying distribution. It formulates the task as finding axis-aligned subspaces, so the projections correspond to selections of existing feature dimensions.

The approach assumes that information specific to each query determines how different subspaces should complement one another. The proposed regression-based method, RECIP, finds projections by minimizing a nonparametric estimate of conditional entropy. This criterion directs the search toward projections that reduce uncertainty relevant to classification.

Experiments report that RECIP accurately identifies informative projections and selects suitable ones for classifying query points. The projections also facilitate visual evaluation by users. These findings connect predictive usefulness with inspectability: the selected views serve both the classification procedure and the person evaluating it. The query-specific assumption is central, because the method’s formulation allows different points to call for different informative views of the same dataset.
summary.tldr: RECIP retrieves query-relevant feature projections that support accurate classification and visual inspection by users.

title: Projection Retrieval for Classification

abstract: We informally call a stochastic process learnable if it admits a generalization error approaching zero in probability for any concept class with finite VC-dimension (IID processes are the simplest example). A mixture of learnable processes need not be learnable itself, and certainly its generalization error need not decay at the same rate. In this paper, we argue that it is natural in predictive PAC to condition not on the past observations but on the mixture component of the sample path. This definition not only matches what a realistic learner might demand, but also allows us to sidestep several otherwise grave problems in learning from dependent data. In particular, we give a novel PAC generalization bound for mixtures of learnable processes with a generalization error that is not worse than that of each mixture component. We also provide a characterization of mixtures of absolutely regular ($\beta$-mixing) processes, of independent interest.

paragraphs: Combining individually learnable stochastic processes can produce a mixture that is harder to learn, or fails to remain learnable under the same definition. The paper studies this difficulty for dependent data, using a notion of learnability in which generalization error approaches zero in probability for concept classes of finite VC dimension.

The authors propose defining predictive PAC guarantees by conditioning on the mixture component responsible for the sample path, rather than on past observations. This changes the reference point for evaluating prediction. Their argument is that component-conditioned guarantees better reflect a realistic learner's demands and avoid several serious difficulties arising from dependence.

Under this definition, they establish a PAC generalization bound for mixtures whose error is no worse than that of each component. The guarantee is tied to the proposed conditioning choice; it does not erase the initial difficulty for arbitrary definitions of mixture learning. The paper also characterizes mixtures of absolutely regular, or β-mixing, processes, adding a structural result about dependent processes.
summary.tldr: Conditioning predictive PAC guarantees on a process's mixture component yields bounds that preserve component-level generalization performance.

title: Predictive PAC Learning and Process Decompositions

abstract: In a closed-loop brain-computer interface (BCI), adaptive decoders are used to learn parameters suited to decoding the user's neural response. Feedback to the user provides information which permits the neural tuning to also adapt. We present an approach to model this process of co-adaptation between the encoding model of the neural signal and the decoding algorithm as a multi-agent formulation of the linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control problem. In simulation we characterize how decoding performance improves as the neural encoding and adaptive decoder optimize, qualitatively resembling experimentally demonstrated closed-loop improvement. We then propose a novel, modified decoder update rule which is aware of the fact that the encoder is also changing and show it can improve simulated co-adaptation dynamics. Our modeling approach offers promise for gaining insights into co-adaptation as well as improving user learning of BCI control in practical settings.

paragraphs: A brain-computer interface can change on both sides of its feedback loop. Its decoder learns how to interpret the user's neural signals, while feedback lets the user adapt the neural activity producing those signals. The paper models these coupled changes rather than treating decoder learning as an isolated process.

The authors express this interaction as a multi-agent version of linear quadratic Gaussian control. In this formulation, neural encoding and decoding are both participants in an optimization process. Simulations characterize how decoding improves as the two adapt, producing patterns that qualitatively resemble previously demonstrated improvements in closed-loop experiments.

The framework also motivates a modified decoder update that accounts for the encoder changing at the same time. This update improves simulated co-adaptation dynamics. The contribution is therefore both an explanatory model and a proposed adjustment to learning: recognizing that the user is adapting can change how the decoder should update. Its benefits for practical user learning remain a promising application of the modeling results.
summary.tldr: Modeling users and decoders as jointly adapting agents suggests a decoder update that improves simulated brain-computer interface learning.

title: A multi-agent control framework for co-adaptation in brain-computer interfaces

abstract: People can learn a new visual class from just one example, yet machine learning algorithms typically require hundreds or thousands of examples to tackle the same problems. Here we present a Hierarchical Bayesian model based on compositionality and causality that can learn a wide range of natural (although simple) visual concepts, generalizing in human-like ways from just one image. We evaluated performance on a challenging one-shot classification task, where our model achieved a human-level error rate while substantially outperforming two deep learning models. We also used a visual Turing test" to show that our model produces human-like performance on other conceptual tasks, including generating new examples and parsing."

We evaluated performance on a challenging one-shot classification task, where our model achieved a human-level error rate while substantially outperforming two deep learning models. paragraphs: The paper addresses learning a new visual category from a single image. Its hierarchical Bayesian model combines compositionality, which represents concepts through parts, with causality, which concerns how an image is produced. Learning is framed around recovering that structured process from the observed example.

This approach allows the model to generalize across a range of natural but simple visual concepts. The emphasis on a process behind the image supports more than assigning a class label: the same conceptual representation can also be assessed through generating examples and parsing visual structure.

On a challenging one-shot classification task, the model achieves an error rate comparable to humans and substantially outperforms two deep learning models. A visual Turing test also finds human-like performance on generation and parsing tasks. These are results for the evaluated tasks and the paper's relatively simple visual concepts. Together, they show that a compositional, causal Bayesian representation can support several forms of generalization from one observation, rather than requiring separate evidence for each conceptual task.
summary.tldr: A compositional causal Bayesian model learns simple visual concepts from one image and achieves human-level error on the evaluated classification task.

title: One-shot learning by inverting a compositional causal process

abstract: Robust PCA methods are typically based on batch optimization and have to load all the samples into memory. This prevents them from efficiently processing big data. In this paper, we develop an Online Robust Principal Component Analysis (OR-PCA) that processes one sample per time instance and hence its memory cost is independent of the data size, significantly enhancing the computation and storage efficiency. The proposed method is based on stochastic optimization of an equivalent reformulation of the batch RPCA method. Indeed, we show that OR-PCA provides a sequence of subspace estimations converging to the optimum of its batch counterpart and hence is provably robust to sparse corruption. Moreover, OR-PCA can naturally be applied for tracking dynamic subspace. Comprehensive simulations on subspace recovering and tracking demonstrate the robustness and efficiency advantages of the OR-PCA over online PCA and batch RPCA methods.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks an underlying subspace while accounting for sparse corruption in the observations. Typical batch methods require loading all samples into memory, which hinders their use on large datasets. This paper develops an online method that handles one sample at a time, so memory cost does not grow with the number of samples.

The proposed OR-PCA algorithm uses stochastic optimization of a reformulation equivalent to the batch robust PCA problem. The authors show that its sequence of subspace estimates converges to the optimum of its batch counterpart. This connection supplies a theoretical basis for robustness to sparse corruption, linking the online computation to the batch objective.

The method can also be used to track a subspace that changes over time. Simulations examine both subspace recovery and tracking, demonstrating robustness and efficiency advantages over online PCA and batch robust PCA methods. The contribution combines reduced storage requirements with a convergence result and evidence that the online formulation is useful for evolving data.
summary.tldr: OR-PCA processes samples individually, converges to its batch counterpart's optimum, and supports robust subspace recovery and tracking.

title: Online Robust PCA via Stochastic Optimization

abstract: In the last decade, policy gradient methods have significantly grown in popularity in the reinforcement--learning field. In particular, they have been largely employed in motor control and robotic applications, thanks to their ability to cope with continuous state and action domains and partial observable problems. Policy gradient researches have been mainly focused on the identification of effective gradient directions and the proposal of efficient estimation algorithms. Nonetheless, the performance of policy gradient methods is determined not only by the gradient direction, since convergence properties are strongly influenced by the choice of the step size: small values imply slow convergence rate, while large values may lead to oscillations or even divergence of the policy parameters. Step--size value is usually chosen by hand tuning and still little attention has been paid to its automatic selection. In this paper, we propose to determine the learning rate by maximizing a lower bound to the expected performance gain. Focusing on Gaussian policies, we derive a lower bound that is second--order polynomial of the step size, and we show how a simplified version of such lower bound can be maximized when the gradient is estimated from trajectory samples. The properties of the proposed approach are empirically evaluated in a linear--quadratic regulator problem.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a decision-making policy by moving its parameters along an estimated gradient. The direction is only part of the choice: the distance moved also affects learning. Very small steps can make progress slow, while large steps can cause oscillation or divergence. This paper addresses automatic selection of that step size.

The proposed approach chooses the learning rate by maximizing a lower bound on the expected improvement in performance. For Gaussian policies, the authors derive a bound that is a second-order polynomial in the step size. This turns the step-size decision into an optimization problem tied to predicted performance gain, rather than leaving it entirely to manual tuning.

The authors also show how to maximize a simplified version of the bound when the gradient comes from sampled trajectories. This connects the analytical proposal to the way gradients are estimated in practice. They empirically study the method in a linear-quadratic regulator problem. The stated evidence concerns that evaluation and the Gaussian-policy derivation, rather than a universal convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper selects policy-gradient step sizes by maximizing a lower bound on expected performance improvement, with a derivation for Gaussian policies.

title: Adaptive Step-Size for Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: An important goal in visual recognition is to devise image representations that are invariant to particular transformations. In this paper, we address this goal with a new type of convolutional neural network (CNN) whose invariance is encoded by a reproducing kernel. Unlike traditional approaches where neural networks are learned either to represent data or for solving a classification task, our network learns to approximate the kernel feature map on training data. Such an approach enjoys several benefits over classical ones. First, by teaching CNNs to be invariant, we obtain simple network architectures that achieve a similar accuracy to more complex ones, while being easy to train and robust to overfitting. Second, we bridge a gap between the neural network literature and kernels, which are natural tools to model invariance. We evaluate our methodology on visual recognition tasks where CNNs have proven to perform well, e.g., digit recognition with the MNIST dataset, and the more challenging CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets, where our accuracy is competitive with the state of the art.
