paragraphs: Visual recognition benefits from image representations that remain stable under particular transformations. This paper builds that goal into a convolutional network through a reproducing kernel. The kernel encodes the desired invariance, and the network learns to approximate its feature map using training data.

This changes the role of network training: the representation is guided by the feature map of a kernel with specified invariance properties. The approach connects convolutional neural networks with kernel methods, giving the architecture a mathematical target for what its representation should preserve. The authors report that this produces simple architectures with accuracy similar to more complex networks, while being easy to train and robust to overfitting.

The evaluation covers digit recognition on MNIST and visual recognition on CIFAR-10 and STL-10. Reported accuracy is competitive with the state of the art on these tasks. The findings support kernel feature approximation as a useful way to construct convolutional representations, combining an explicit treatment of invariance with competitive empirical recognition performance.
summary.tldr: Convolutional kernel networks learn kernel feature maps that encode invariance, achieving competitive visual recognition with simple architectures.

title: Convolutional Kernel Networks

abstract: Kernel machines such as kernel SVM and kernel ridge regression usually construct high quality models; however, their use in real-world applications remains limited due to the high prediction cost. In this paper, we present two novel insights for improving the prediction efficiency of kernel machines. First, we show that by adding “pseudo landmark points” to the classical Nystr¨om kernel approximation in an elegant way, we can significantly reduce the prediction error without much additional prediction cost. Second, we provide a new theoretical analysis on bounding the error of the solution computed by using Nystr¨om kernel approximation method, and show that the error is related to the weighted kmeans objective function where the weights are given by the model computed from the original kernel. This theoretical insight suggests a new landmark point selection technique for the situation where we have knowledge of the original model. Based on these two insights, we provide a divide-and-conquer framework for improving the prediction speed. First, we divide the whole problem into smaller local subproblems to reduce the problem size. In the second phase, we develop a kernel approximation based fast prediction approach within each subproblem. We apply our algorithm to real world large-scale classification and regression datasets, and show that the proposed algorithm is consistently and significantly better than other competitors. For example, on the Covertype classification problem, in terms of prediction time, our algorithm achieves more than 10000 times speedup over the full kernel SVM, and a two-fold speedup over the state-of-the-art LDKL approach, while obtaining much higher prediction accuracy than LDKL (95.2% vs. 89.53%).

summary.tldr: Improved Nyström landmarks and local problem decomposition deliver faster kernel prediction with strong reported accuracy.

title: Fast Prediction for Large-Scale Kernel Machines

abstract: Since being analyzed by Rokhlin, Szlam, and Tygert and popularized by Halko, Martinsson, and Tropp, randomized Simultaneous Power Iteration has become the method of choice for approximate singular value decomposition. It is more accurate than simpler sketching algorithms, yet still converges quickly for any matrix, independently of singular value gaps. After ~O(1/epsilon) iterations, it gives a low-rank approximation within (1+epsilon) of optimal for spectral norm error.We give the first provable runtime improvement on Simultaneous Iteration: a randomized block Krylov method, closely related to the classic Block Lanczos algorithm, gives the same guarantees in just ~O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) iterations and performs substantially better experimentally. Our analysis is the first of a Krylov subspace method that does not depend on singular value gaps, which are unreliable in practice.Furthermore, while it is a simple accuracy benchmark, even (1+epsilon) error for spectral norm low-rank approximation does not imply that an algorithm returns high quality principal components, a major issue for data applications. We address this problem for the first time by showing that both Block Krylov Iteration and Simultaneous Iteration give nearly optimal PCA for any matrix. This result further justifies their strength over non-iterative sketching methods.

paragraphs: Approximate singular value decomposition seeks a compact, low-rank representation of a matrix. Randomized simultaneous power iteration provides strong approximation accuracy without relying on gaps between singular values. This paper improves its iteration requirement while retaining that independence from singular-value gaps, which the authors describe as unreliable in practice.

The proposed randomized block Krylov method is closely related to Block Lanczos. It reaches a low-rank approximation within a factor of 1 + ε of optimal spectral-norm error in roughly O(1/√ε) iterations, compared with roughly O(1/ε) for simultaneous iteration. The paper proves the improvement and reports substantially better experimental performance.

A strong spectral-norm error guarantee alone does not establish that the returned principal components are good. They prove that both block Krylov iteration and simultaneous iteration provide nearly optimal PCA for any matrix. This additional result addresses a distinct requirement of data analysis and strengthens the justification for using these iterative methods over non-iterative sketching approaches.
summary.tldr: Randomized block Krylov iteration accelerates approximate SVD guarantees without singular-value-gap assumptions and also provides nearly optimal PCA.

title: Randomized Block Krylov Methods for Stronger and Faster Approximate Singular Value Decomposition

abstract: We study the stochastic optimization of canonical correlation analysis (CCA), whose objective is nonconvex and does not decouple over training samples. Although several stochastic gradient based optimization algorithms have been recently proposed to solve this problem, no global convergence guarantee was provided by any of them. Inspired by the alternating least squares/power iterations formulation of CCA, and the shift-and-invert preconditioning method for PCA, we propose two globally convergent meta-algorithms for CCA, both of which transform the original problem into sequences of least squares problems that need only be solved approximately. We instantiate the meta-algorithms with state-of-the-art SGD methods and obtain time complexities that significantly improve upon that of previous work. Experimental results demonstrate their superior performance.

Although several stochastic gradient based optimization algorithms have been recently proposed to solve this problem, no global convergence guarantee was provided by any of them. Inspired by the alternating least squares/power iterations formulation of CCA, and the shift-and-invert preconditioning method for PCA, we propose two globally convergent meta-algorithms for CCA, both of which transform the original problem into sequences of least squares problems that need only be solved approximately. paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis presents a difficult stochastic optimization problem because its objective is nonconvex and does not separate into independent contributions from individual training samples. The paper addresses a gap in earlier stochastic gradient approaches: they offered methods for solving the problem without providing a global convergence guarantee.

The authors propose two general algorithmic frameworks that convert CCA into a sequence of least-squares problems. These subproblems only need approximate solutions, making the conversion compatible with efficient stochastic solvers. The designs draw on alternating least squares and power iterations for CCA, together with shift-and-invert preconditioning developed for principal component analysis.

Both frameworks have global convergence guarantees. When instantiated with established stochastic gradient methods, they yield time-complexity bounds that significantly improve on previous work, and experiments demonstrate superior performance. The key contribution is a way to organize approximate computations so that the overall nonconvex optimization retains a global guarantee. This links practical stochastic solution methods with a stronger theoretical account of where the optimization converges.
summary.tldr: Two CCA optimization frameworks use approximate least-squares solves to obtain global convergence and improved computational complexity.

title: Efficient Globally Convergent Stochastic Optimization for Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: Clustering, in particular $k$-means clustering, is a central topic in data analysis. Clustering with Bregman divergences is a recently proposed generalization of $k$-means clustering which has already been widely used in applications. In this paper we analyze theoretical properties of Bregman clustering when the number of the clusters $k$ is large. We establish quantization rates and describe the limiting distribution of the centers as $k\to \infty$, extending well-known results for $k$-means clustering.

paragraphs: This paper studies the mathematical behavior of clustering when the number of clusters becomes large. Its focus is Bregman clustering, a generalization of k-means that uses Bregman divergences to measure how well cluster centers represent data. The question is how this broader family behaves as more and more centers become available.

The analysis establishes quantization rates. These describe how the error from representing data through a collection of centers changes as the number of centers increases. It also characterizes the limiting distribution of the centers: the pattern of their allocation as the cluster count tends to infinity. Together, these results address both representation quality and the arrangement of the representatives.

The contribution extends established k-means theory to Bregman clustering, connecting an already-used generalization with corresponding asymptotic foundations. The large-cluster setting is central to the findings: the results concern rates and limiting behavior as the number of clusters grows. They provide a theoretical description of that regime, rather than a reported comparison of clustering algorithms on datasets.
summary.tldr: The paper extends k-means asymptotic theory to Bregman clustering by characterizing error rates and center distributions as the cluster count grows.

title: Clustering with Bregman Divergences: an Asymptotic Analysis

abstract: We consider the linear contextual bandit problem with resource consumption, in addition to reward generation. In each round, the outcome of pulling an arm is a reward as well as a vector of resource consumptions. The expected values of these outcomes depend linearly on the context of that arm. The budget/capacity constraints require that the sum of these vectors doesn't exceed the budget in each dimension. The objective is once again to maximize the total reward. This problem turns out to be a common generalization of classic linear contextual bandits (linContextual), bandits with knapsacks (BwK), and the online stochastic packing problem (OSPP). We present algorithms with near-optimal regret bounds for this problem. Our bounds compare favorably to results on the unstructured version of the problem, where the relation between the contexts and the outcomes could be arbitrary, but the algorithm only competes against a fixed set of policies accessible through an optimization oracle. We combine techniques from the work on linContextual, BwK and OSPP in a nontrivial manner while also tackling new difficulties that are not present in any of these special cases.

paragraphs: Many sequential decisions produce both a reward and a cost in limited resources. This paper studies a contextual bandit problem in which choosing an option yields a reward and a vector of resource consumptions. The learner seeks the largest total reward while keeping cumulative consumption within every resource budget.

The key modeling assumption is that expected rewards and expected resource use depend linearly on an option's context. This links information about available choices to both their benefits and their demands on the remaining budget. The formulation brings together linear contextual bandits, bandits with resource budgets, and online stochastic packing within one problem.

The authors develop algorithms with near-optimal regret bounds, combining techniques from those three settings while addressing difficulties introduced by their interaction. Their bounds compare favorably with results for an unstructured formulation that permits arbitrary context-outcome relationships but competes against a fixed policy set accessed through an optimization oracle. The contribution shows how linear structure can support strong learning guarantees when exploration and reward seeking must also respect multiple resource constraints.
summary.tldr: The paper gives near-optimal regret guarantees for contextual decisions whose rewards and resource use are linear in context and subject to multiple budgets.

title: Linear Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks

abstract: Decentralized (PO)MDPs provide an expressive framework for sequential decision making in a multiagent system. Given their computational complexity, recent research has focused on tractable yet practical subclasses of Dec-POMDPs. We address such a subclass called CDec-POMDP where the collective behavior of a population of agents affects the joint-reward and environment dynamics. Our main contribution is an actor-critic (AC) reinforcement learning method for optimizing CDec-POMDP policies. Vanilla AC has slow convergence for larger problems. To address this, we show how a particular decomposition of the approximate action-value function over agents leads to effective updates, and also derive a new way to train the critic based on local reward signals. Comparisons on a synthetic benchmark and a real world taxi fleet optimization problem show that our new AC approach provides better quality solutions than previous best approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies planning for populations of agents whose collective behavior affects both shared rewards and how the environment evolves. It focuses on CDec-POMDPs, a particular subclass of decentralized partially observable decision problems. The narrower setting is motivated by the computational difficulty of solving general decentralized multiagent problems.

The authors develop an actor-critic reinforcement-learning method for optimizing policies in this setting. Standard actor-critic learning converges slowly on larger problems, so they change how the approximate action-value function is represented. A particular decomposition across agents leads to more effective policy updates. They also derive a new procedure for training the critic from local reward signals.

These changes connect population-level planning with learning signals organized around individual agents. Comparisons on a synthetic benchmark and a real-world taxi fleet optimization problem produce higher-quality solutions than previous leading approaches. The findings support this decomposition and critic-training strategy for collective multiagent planning, with the problem structure providing the basis for the method rather than an unrestricted solution to every decentralized planning problem.
summary.tldr: An agent-wise value decomposition and locally trained critic improve reported solutions for collective multiagent planning.

title: Policy Gradient With Value Function Approximation For Collective Multiagent Planning

abstract: Training models that generalize to new domains at test time is a problem of fundamental importance in machine learning. In this work, we encode this notion of domain generalization using a novel regularization function. We pose the problem of finding such a regularization function in a Learning to Learn (or) meta-learning framework. The objective of domain generalization is explicitly modeled by learning a regularizer that makes the model trained on one domain to perform well on another domain. Experimental validations on computer vision and natural language datasets indicate that our method can learn regularizers that achieve good cross-domain generalization.
originalAbstract: Training models that generalize to new domains at test time is a problem of fundamental importance in machine learning. In this work, we encode this notion of domain generalization using a novel regularization function. We pose the problem of finding such a regularization function in a Learning to Learn (or) meta-learning framework. The objective of domain generalization is explicitly modeled by learning a regularizer that makes the model trained on one domain to perform well on another domain. Experimental validations on computer vision and natural language datasets indicate that our method can learn regularizers that achieve good cross-domain generalization.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained on available domains can work well in new domains at test time. Success within a training domain does not directly establish this ability. MetaReg addresses the problem by making cross-domain performance the target of a learned regularization function.

The method places the search for that regularizer inside a meta-learning framework. It learns a regularizer that encourages a model trained on one domain to perform well on another. This connects the training preference imposed by regularization to the particular behavior sought at deployment: carrying useful knowledge across changes in domain. The regularizer itself is therefore an object of learning.

Experiments on computer vision and natural language datasets indicate that the method can learn regularizers with good cross-domain generalization. The evidence supports the proposed way of encoding transfer into training, rather than guaranteeing success on every unseen domain. The paper's main contribution is a concrete learning-to-learn formulation in which performance across domains determines what kind of regularization should guide the underlying model.
summary.tldr: MetaReg learns a regularizer by training it to promote good performance across different domains.

title: MetaReg: Towards Domain Generalization using Meta-Regularization

abstract: This paper focusses on the formulation of numerical integration as an inferential task. To date, research effort has largely focussed on the development of Bayesian cubature, whose distributional output provides uncertainty quantification for the integral. However, the point estimators associated to Bayesian cubature can be inaccurate and acutely sensitive to the prior when the domain is high-dimensional. To address these drawbacks we introduce Bayes-Sard cubature, a probabilistic framework that combines the flexibility of Bayesian cubature with the robustness of classical cubatures which are well-established. This is achieved by considering a Gaussian process model for the integrand whose mean is a parametric regression model, with an improper prior on each regression coefficient. The features in the regression model consist of test functions which are guaranteed to be exactly integrated, with remaining degrees of freedom afforded to the non-parametric part. The asymptotic convergence of the Bayes-Sard cubature method is established and the theoretical results are numerically verified. In particular, we report two orders of magnitude reduction in error compared to Bayesian cubature in the context of a high-dimensional financial integral.

paragraphs: Numerical integration estimates an integral from evaluations of a function. Bayesian cubature treats this as inference, producing uncertainty about the integral as well as an estimate. The paper addresses a weakness of that approach: its estimates can be inaccurate and highly sensitive to the prior in high-dimensional domains.

Bayes-Sard cubature combines a Gaussian process model with a parametric regression model for its mean. The regression features are selected test functions, and each coefficient receives an improper prior. This construction guarantees exact integration of those test functions while leaving the nonparametric component flexibility to represent other behavior. It brings a concrete property of classical integration rules into a probabilistic framework.

The authors establish asymptotic convergence and numerically verify their theoretical results. For one high-dimensional financial integral, they report an error reduction of two orders of magnitude relative to Bayesian cubature. That result demonstrates the potential value of combining exactness for chosen functions with uncertainty-aware integration; it is a finding for the reported application rather than a universal improvement factor.
summary.tldr: Bayes-Sard cubature combines probabilistic integration with exact integration of selected test functions to improve robustness.

title: A Bayes-Sard Cubature Method

abstract: We study the problem of finding clusters in random bipartite graphs. We present a simple two-step algorithm which provably finds even tiny clusters of size $O(n^\epsilon)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph and $\epsilon > 0$. Previous algorithms were only able to identify clusters of size $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We evaluate the algorithm on synthetic and on real-world data; the experiments show that the algorithm can find extremely small clusters even in presence of high destructive noise.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of finding clusters in random bipartite graphs. We present a simple two-step algorithm which provably finds even tiny clusters of size $O(n^\epsilon)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph and $\epsilon > 0$. Previous algorithms were only able to identify clusters of size $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We evaluate the algorithm on synthetic and on real-world data; the experiments show that the algorithm can find extremely small clusters even in presence of high destructive noise.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover clusters in random bipartite graphs. Its focus is cluster size: small groups can be difficult to identify, and the previous algorithms described in the abstract could only recover clusters at least on the order of the square root of the number of vertices. The authors seek to reach substantially smaller groups.

They propose a simple algorithm with two steps and prove that it can find tiny clusters of size O(n^ε), where n is the graph's number of vertices and ε is positive. For small positive exponents, this reaches sizes below the square-root scale. The guarantee concerns the random bipartite graph setting studied in the paper.

Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data show recovery of extremely small clusters even with substantial destructive noise. These observations complement the theoretical size result by examining noisy data. The contribution is therefore both a stronger provable reach for small clusters in the stated setting and empirical evidence that the algorithm can recover small groups under noise.
summary.tldr: A two-step algorithm provably recovers tiny clusters in random bipartite graphs and finds very small noisy clusters in experiments.

title: Bipartite Stochastic Block Models with Tiny Clusters

abstract: In many machine learning applications, one needs to interactively select a sequence of items (e.g., recommending movies based on a user's feedback) or make sequential decisions in a certain order (e.g., guiding an agent through a series of states). Not only do sequences already pose a dauntingly large search space, but we must also take into account past observations, as well as the uncertainty of future outcomes. Without further structure, finding an optimal sequence is notoriously challenging, if not completely intractable. In this paper, we view the problem of adaptive and sequential decision making through the lens of submodularity and propose an adaptive greedy policy with strong theoretical guarantees. Additionally, to demonstrate the practical utility of our results, we run experiments on Amazon product recommendation and Wikipedia link prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Many decisions involve building an ordered sequence while learning from feedback along the way. Movie recommendations, for example, can depend on a user's reactions to earlier suggestions. Such problems combine three difficulties: the number of possible sequences is enormous, order matters, and future outcomes remain uncertain. An effective decision rule must account for observations already collected.

This paper approaches that combination through submodularity, using mathematical structure to make adaptive sequence selection more manageable. The authors propose an adaptive greedy policy: a procedure that builds its decisions progressively and responds to the information available at each stage. They establish strong theoretical guarantees for the policy within their framework, giving a principled basis for using a comparatively direct selection strategy.

The authors also run experiments on Amazon product recommendation and Wikipedia link prediction to demonstrate practical utility. The contribution connects ordered, feedback-driven decisions with a tractable policy supported by theory. Its guarantees arise from the proposed structure; the abstract does not claim that arbitrary sequential decision problems become easy.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a submodularity framework and a theoretically supported greedy policy for selecting ordered sequences while adapting to feedback.

title: Adaptive Sequence Submodularity

abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings achieve excellent performance when embedding hierarchical data structures like synonym or type hierarchies, but they can be limited by numerical error when ordinary floating-point numbers are used to represent points in hyperbolic space. Standard models such as the Poincar{\'e} disk and the Lorentz model have unbounded numerical error as points get far from the origin. To address this, we propose a new model which uses an integer-based tiling to represent \emph{any} point in hyperbolic space with provably bounded numerical error. This allows us to learn high-precision embeddings without using BigFloats, and enables us to store the resulting embeddings with fewer bits. We evaluate our tiling-based model empirically, and show that it can both compress hyperbolic embeddings (down to $2\%$ of a Poincar{\'e} embedding on WordNet Nouns) and learn more accurate embeddings on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic embeddings represent hierarchical relationships, such as synonym or type hierarchies, using points in hyperbolic space. Their numerical representation can become problematic: with ordinary floating-point arithmetic, standard Poincaré disk and Lorentz models have unbounded numerical error as points move far from the origin. This can limit the usefulness of an otherwise suitable geometry.

The paper proposes a representation based on an integer tiling of hyperbolic space. It proves a bound on numerical error for representing any point. The resulting model allows high-precision embedding learning without BigFloats and supports storing learned embeddings using fewer bits. Thus, the representation addresses both numerical accuracy and storage requirements.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate compression and improved embedding accuracy on real-world datasets. On WordNet Nouns, the reported compressed representation uses as little as 2% of the storage of a Poincaré embedding. That specific result illustrates the potential storage benefit, while the theoretical contribution concerns bounded numerical error throughout hyperbolic space.
summary.tldr: An integer-tiling representation bounds hyperbolic embedding error and enables high precision and substantial storage compression.

title: Numerically Accurate Hyperbolic Embeddings Using Tiling-Based Models

abstract: While artificial intelligence (AI) holds promise for addressing societal challenges, issues of exactly which tasks to automate and to what extent to do so remain understudied. We approach this problem of task delegability from a human-centered perspective by developing a framework on human perception of task delegation to AI. We consider four high-level factors that can contribute to a delegation decision: motivation, difficulty, risk, and trust. To obtain an empirical understanding of human preferences in different tasks, we build a dataset of 100 tasks from academic papers, popular media portrayal of AI, and everyday life, and administer a survey based on our proposed framework. We find little preference for full AI control and a strong preference for machine-in-the-loop designs, in which humans play the leading role. Among the four factors, trust is the most correlated with human preferences of optimal human-machine delegation. This framework represents a first step towards characterizing human preferences of AI automation across tasks. We hope this work encourages future efforts towards understanding such individual attitudes; our goal is to inform the public and the AI research community rather than dictating any direction in technology development.

paragraphs: This paper examines how people think tasks should be shared between humans and AI. Technical capability alone does not answer how much control people want to delegate. The authors develop a human-centered framework around four factors that may shape these decisions: motivation, difficulty, risk, and trust.

To study preferences empirically, they assemble 100 tasks drawn from academic papers, portrayals of AI in popular media, and everyday life. They then conduct a survey using the framework. This connects the abstract question of delegation to judgments about concrete tasks, allowing the authors to examine how preferences relate to the four proposed factors.

Survey responses show little preference for complete AI control and a strong preference for arrangements in which humans lead with machine assistance. Trust has the strongest correlation with delegation preferences among the four factors; this finding does not establish that trust causes those preferences. The authors present the framework as an initial characterization of human attitudes intended to inform discussion and research, rather than prescribe a direction for technology development.
summary.tldr: A survey-based delegation framework finds a preference for human-led AI assistance, with trust most strongly correlated with delegation preferences.

title: Ask not what AI can do, but what AI should do: Towards a framework of task delegability

abstract: Pre-training is a dominant paradigm in computer vision. For example, supervised ImageNet pre-training is commonly used to initialize the backbones of object detection and segmentation models. He et al., however, show a striking result that ImageNet pre-training has limited impact on COCO object detection. Here we investigate self-training as another method to utilize additional data on the same setup and contrast it against ImageNet pre-training. Our study reveals the generality and flexibility of self-training with three additional insights: 1) stronger data augmentation and more labeled data further diminish the value of pre-training, 2) unlike pre-training, self-training is always helpful when using stronger data augmentation, in both low-data and high-data regimes, and 3) in the case that pre-training is helpful, self-training improves upon pre-training. For example, on the COCO object detection dataset, pre-training benefits when we use one fifth of the labeled data, and hurts accuracy when we use all labeled data. Self-training, on the other hand, shows positive improvements from +1.3 to +3.4AP across all dataset sizes. In other words, self-training works well exactly on the same setup that pre-training does not work (using ImageNet to help COCO). On the PASCAL segmentation dataset, which is a much smaller dataset than COCO, though pre-training does help significantly, self-training improves upon the pre-trained model. On COCO object detection, we achieve 53.8AP, an improvement of +1.7AP over the strongest SpineNet model. On PASCAL segmentation, we achieve 90.5mIOU, an improvement of +1.5mIOU over the previous state-of-the-art result by DeepLabv3+.

paragraphs: This paper compares pretraining and self-training as ways to use additional data for visual recognition. It examines a setting where ImageNet pretraining has limited value for COCO object detection and asks whether self-training can still help. The comparison focuses on how the amount of labeled data and the strength of data augmentation affect the two approaches.

In the experiments, stronger augmentation and more labeled data further reduce the value of pretraining. On COCO, pretraining helps with one fifth of the labels but hurts accuracy when all labels are used. Self-training improves performance across the evaluated dataset sizes, with gains ranging from 1.3 to 3.4 AP, and remains useful with stronger augmentation.

Self-training also adds value when pretraining is beneficial, as shown on the smaller PASCAL segmentation dataset. The reported final results reach 53.8 AP on COCO and 90.5 mIOU on PASCAL. These findings show that the usefulness of additional data depends on how it enters training, and that weak gains from pretraining do not imply weak gains from self-training in the same evaluated setup.
summary.tldr: Self-training improves the evaluated detection and segmentation systems even in settings where pretraining offers little benefit or hurts accuracy.

title: Rethinking Pre-training and Self-training

abstract: We present a series of new PAC-Bayes learning guarantees for randomized algorithms with sample-dependent priors. Our most general bounds make no assumption on the priors and are given in terms of certain covering numbers under the infinite-Renyi divergence and the L1 distance. We show how to use these general bounds to derive leaning bounds in the setting where the sample-dependent priors obey an infinite-Renyi divergence or L1-distance sensitivity condition. We also provide a flexible framework for computing PAC-Bayes bounds, under certain stability assumptions on the sample-dependent priors, and show how to use this framework to give more refined bounds when the priors satisfy an infinite-Renyi divergence sensitivity condition.
originalAbstract: We present a series of new PAC-Bayes learning guarantees for randomized algorithms with sample-dependent priors. Our most general bounds make no assumption on the priors and are given in terms of certain covering numbers under the infinite-Renyi divergence and the L1 distance. We show how to use these general bounds to derive leaning bounds in the setting where the sample-dependent priors obey an infinite-Renyi divergence or L1-distance sensitivity condition. We also provide a flexible framework for computing PAC-Bayes bounds, under certain stability assumptions on the sample-dependent priors, and show how to use this framework to give more refined bounds when the priors satisfy an infinite-Renyi divergence sensitivity condition.

paragraphs: This paper develops PAC-Bayes learning guarantees for randomized algorithms whose priors depend on the observed sample. Such dependence must be accounted for when relating learning from the sample to predictive performance. The contribution is a series of bounds that accommodate this dependence at different levels of generality.

The most general results place no assumptions on the priors themselves. Their bounds instead involve covering numbers measured using infinite-Renyi divergence and L1 distance. These quantities provide a way to express the complexity of the priors under the chosen measures. The authors then derive specialized bounds when sample-dependent priors satisfy sensitivity conditions expressed through either measure.

A further framework supports computing PAC-Bayes bounds under stability assumptions on the priors. Within that framework, infinite-Renyi sensitivity leads to more refined guarantees. The paper thus connects broad bounds with more structured, assumption-dependent results. Its significance lies in giving multiple routes for reasoning about sample-dependent priors while making clear which additional guarantees rely on sensitivity or stability.
summary.tldr: New PAC-Bayes bounds accommodate sample-dependent priors, with refined guarantees available under sensitivity and stability conditions.

title: PAC-Bayes Learning Bounds for Sample-Dependent Priors

abstract: We study how to learn a policy with compositional generalizability. We propose a two-stage framework, which refactorizes a high-reward teacher policy into a generalizable student policy with strong inductive bias. Particularly, we implement an object-centric GNN-based student policy, whose input objects are learned from images through self-supervised learning. Empirically, we evaluate our approach on four difficult tasks that require compositional generalizability, and achieve superior performance compared to baselines.
originalAbstract: We study how to learn a policy with compositional generalizability. We propose a two-stage framework, which refactorizes a high-reward teacher policy into a generalizable student policy with strong inductive bias. Particularly, we implement an object-centric GNN-based student policy, whose input objects are learned from images through self-supervised learning. Empirically, we evaluate our approach on four difficult tasks that require compositional generalizability, and achieve superior performance compared to baselines.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to learn policies that generalize compositionally: using learned components effectively when they appear in different combinations. Its approach begins with a teacher policy that already earns high reward. A second stage refactors that policy into a student whose architecture supplies a strong bias toward the desired kind of generalization.

The student is object-centered and uses a graph neural network. Its input objects are learned from images through self-supervised learning. This puts objects and their organization at the center of the student's decision process. The two-stage framework combines the teacher's successful behavior with a student representation designed to support composition.

The authors evaluate the approach on four difficult tasks that require compositional generalization and report better performance than the comparison methods. These empirical findings support transferring a successful policy into an architecture structured around objects. The contribution brings together policy refactoring, self-supervised object discovery, and graph-based decision-making as a way to improve generalization beyond the combinations encountered during learning.
summary.tldr: A two-stage framework refactors a high-reward teacher into an object-centered graph-network student that improves compositional generalization on four tasks.

title: Refactoring Policy for Compositional Generalizability using Self-Supervised Object Proposals

abstract: We develop a novel generative model for zero-shot learning to recognize fine-grained unseen classes without training samples. Our observation is that generating holistic features of unseen classes fails to capture every attribute needed to distinguish small differences among classes. We propose a feature composition framework that learns to extract attribute-based features from training samples and combines them to construct fine-grained features for unseen classes. Feature composition allows us to not only selectively compose features of unseen classes from only relevant training samples, but also obtain diversity among composed features via changing samples used for composition. In addition, instead of building a global feature of an unseen class, we use all attribute-based features to form a dense representation consisting of fine-grained attribute details. To recognize unseen classes, we propose a novel training scheme that uses a discriminative model to construct features that are subsequently used to train itself. Therefore, we directly train the discriminative model on composed features without learning separate generative models. We conduct experiments on four popular datasets of DeepFashion, AWA2, CUB, and SUN, showing that our method significantly improves the state of the art.
originalAbstract: We develop a novel generative model for zero-shot learning to recognize fine-grained unseen classes without training samples. Our observation is that generating holistic features of unseen classes fails to capture every attribute needed to distinguish small differences among classes. We propose a feature composition framework that learns to extract attribute-based features from training samples and combines them to construct fine-grained features for unseen classes. Feature composition allows us to not only selectively compose features of unseen classes from only relevant training samples, but also obtain diversity among composed features via changing samples used for composition. In addition, instead of building a global feature of an unseen class, we use all attribute-based features to form a dense representation consisting of fine-grained attribute details. To recognize unseen classes, we propose a novel training scheme that uses a discriminative model to construct features that are subsequently used to train itself. Therefore, we directly train the discriminative model on composed features without learning separate generative models. We conduct experiments on four popular datasets of DeepFashion, AWA2, CUB, and SUN, showing that our method significantly improves the state of the art.

paragraphs: Recognizing a class without training examples is especially difficult when classes differ only in small visual details. This paper argues that generating one overall feature representation for an unseen class can overlook the individual attributes needed to distinguish it. The proposed approach instead constructs unseen-class representations from attribute-based features extracted from available training samples.

Composition serves two purposes. It selects features from samples relevant to the attributes being assembled, and it creates diversity by changing which samples supply those features. Rather than compressing the result into a single global summary, the method keeps a dense representation containing fine-grained attribute information. This preserves the details that motivate the approach.

The training scheme uses a discriminative model to construct features that subsequently train that same model, avoiding the need to learn a separate generator. Experiments on DeepFashion, AWA2, CUB, and SUN report significant improvements over the state of the art. The findings support attribute-level composition as a useful way to supply training representations for classes lacking their own examples.
summary.tldr: The method recognizes unseen classes by composing diverse, detailed attribute features from relevant training samples and using them to train its classifier.

title: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning via Fine-Grained Dense Feature Composition

abstract: Humans easily interpret expressions that describe unfamiliar situations composed from familiar parts ("greet the pink brontosaurus by the ferris wheel"). Modern neural networks, by contrast, struggle to interpret novel compositions. In this paper, we introduce a new benchmark, gSCAN, for evaluating compositional generalization in situated language understanding. Going beyond a related benchmark that focused on syntactic aspects of generalization, gSCAN defines a language grounded in the states of a grid world, facilitating novel evaluations of acquiring linguistically motivated rules. For example, agents must understand how adjectives such as 'small' are interpreted relative to the current world state or how adverbs such as 'cautiously' combine with new verbs. We test a strong multi-modal baseline model and a state-of-the-art compositional method finding that, in most cases, they fail dramatically when generalization requires systematic compositional rules.

paragraphs: Understanding a familiar word in an unfamiliar combination requires more than recognizing patterns seen during training. This paper introduces gSCAN, a benchmark for testing whether language models can apply learned meanings and rules systematically. Its language refers to situations in a grid world, so interpreting an instruction depends on both the words and the surrounding environment.

That grounding makes it possible to test abilities beyond rearranging sentence structures. An adjective such as small must be understood relative to the objects currently present. An adverb such as cautiously must retain its meaning when combined with a new verb. These tasks examine whether a model can reuse familiar linguistic components under changed circumstances.

The authors evaluate a strong multimodal baseline and an existing compositional method. Both fail dramatically in most cases requiring systematic compositional rules. The finding identifies a substantial weakness in the tested methods and makes gSCAN a way to examine precisely where learned language understanding stops transferring to new combinations.
summary.tldr: gSCAN tests language understanding in a grid world and exposes major failures when tested models must generalize familiar meanings to unfamiliar combinations.

title: A Benchmark for Systematic Generalization in Grounded Language Understanding

abstract: Parsing sentences into syntax trees can benefit downstream applications in NLP. Transition-based parsers build trees by executing actions in a state transition system. They are computationally efficient, and can leverage machine learning to predict actions based on partial trees. However, existing transition-based parsers are predominantly based on the shift-reduce transition system, which does not align with how humans are known to parse sentences. Psycholinguistic research suggests that human parsing is strongly incremental—humans grow a single parse tree by adding exactly one token at each step. In this paper, we propose a novel transition system called attach-juxtapose. It is strongly incremental; it represents a partial sentence using a single tree; each action adds exactly one token into the partial tree. Based on our transition system, we develop a strongly incremental parser. At each step, it encodes the partial tree using a graph neural network and predicts an action. We evaluate our parser on Penn Treebank (PTB) and Chinese Treebank (CTB). On PTB, it outperforms existing parsers trained with only constituency trees; and it performs on par with state-of-the-art parsers that use dependency trees as additional training data. On CTB, our parser establishes a new state of the art. Code is available at https://github.com/princeton-vl/attach-juxtapose-parser.

paragraphs: Constituency parsing organizes a sentence into a syntax tree. Transition-based parsers build that structure through a sequence of actions, but the commonly used shift-reduce system differs from the strongly incremental behavior suggested by psycholinguistic research. This paper develops a parser that maintains one growing tree and incorporates exactly one token at each step.

Its attach-juxtapose transition system defines how each new token enters the existing partial tree. A graph neural network encodes that tree, and the parser uses the encoding to predict its next action. The design therefore makes the currently assembled syntax structure directly available when deciding how to extend the parse.

On Penn Treebank, the parser outperforms existing parsers trained only with constituency trees and matches leading parsers that additionally use dependency-tree training data. On Chinese Treebank, it establishes a new state of the art. These results show that the proposed incremental constraint is compatible with strong parsing accuracy, while providing a tree-building process motivated by evidence about human sentence processing.
summary.tldr: An attach-juxtapose parser uses graph neural networks to grow one syntax tree token by token while achieving strong benchmark accuracy.

title: Strongly Incremental Constituency Parsing with Graph Neural Networks

abstract: DBSCAN is a popular density-based clustering algorithm. It computes the $\epsilon$-neighborhood graph of a dataset and uses the connected components of the high-degree nodes to decide the clusters. However, the full neighborhood graph may be too costly to compute with a worst-case complexity of $O(n^2)$. In this paper, we propose a simple variant called SNG-DBSCAN, which clusters based on a subsampled $\epsilon$-neighborhood graph, only requires access to similarity queries for pairs of points and in particular avoids any complex data structures which need the embeddings of the data points themselves. The runtime of the procedure is $O(sn^2)$, where $s$ is the sampling rate. We show under some natural theoretical assumptions that $s \approx \log n/n$ is sufficient for statistical cluster recovery guarantees leading to an $O(n\log n)$ complexity. We provide an extensive experimental analysis showing that on large datasets, one can subsample as little as $0.1\%$ of the neighborhood graph, leading to as much as over 200x speedup and 250x reduction in RAM consumption compared to scikit-learn's implementation of DBSCAN, while still maintaining competitive clustering performance.

paragraphs: DBSCAN finds clusters using a graph that connects points within a chosen neighborhood distance, then examines connected regions of high-degree points. Constructing the complete neighborhood graph can require quadratic work in the number of data points. SNG-DBSCAN reduces that expense by clustering from a subsampled version of the graph.

The method needs only similarity queries between pairs of points. It avoids complex data structures requiring access to the points' underlying embeddings. Its runtime is proportional to the sampling rate times the square of the dataset size. Under the paper's theoretical assumptions, a sampling rate around log(n)/n is sufficient for statistical cluster recovery guarantees, giving an n log(n) runtime.

Experiments on large datasets show that sampling as little as 0.1% of the neighborhood graph can retain competitive clustering performance. Reported gains reach over 200-fold faster execution and a 250-fold reduction in RAM consumption relative to scikit-learn's DBSCAN implementation. These are reported experimental outcomes, while the stronger cluster-recovery statement depends on the theoretical assumptions. Together, they support subsampling as a simple way to make density-based clustering less expensive.
summary.tldr: SNG-DBSCAN clusters using a sampled neighborhood graph, offering conditional recovery guarantees and large observed savings in runtime and memory.

title: Faster DBSCAN via subsampled similarity queries

abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) has proven to be a successful framework for leveraging experience from prior tasks to rapidly learn new related tasks, however, current meta-RL approaches struggle to learn in sparse reward environments. Although existing meta-RL algorithms can learn strategies for adapting to new sparse reward tasks, the actual adaptation strategies are learned using hand-shaped reward functions, or require simple environments where random exploration is sufficient to encounter sparse reward. In this paper we present a formulation of hindsight relabelling for meta-RL, which relabels experience during meta-training to enable learning to learn entirely using sparse reward. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a suite of challenging sparse reward environments that previously required dense reward during meta-training to solve. Our approach solves these environments using the true sparse reward function, with performance comparable to training with a proxy dense reward function.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning uses experience across tasks to learn how to adapt quickly to related new tasks. Sparse rewards make this difficult because useful feedback is rarely encountered. Existing methods may adapt to sparse-reward tasks while still depending on hand-designed dense rewards during meta-training, or on environments simple enough for random exploration to find rewards.

This paper introduces hindsight task relabelling for meta-reinforcement learning. It relabels experience during meta-training so that learning an adaptation strategy can itself proceed entirely with sparse rewards. The key contribution concerns the training of the learning strategy, addressing the stage where earlier approaches often required a richer reward signal than the actual task provides.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging sparse-reward environments that previously needed dense rewards during meta-training to solve. Their approach solves these environments with the true sparse reward function and achieves performance comparable to training with a proxy dense reward. The results demonstrate that experience relabelling can reduce dependence on manually shaped feedback in the tested meta-learning problems.
summary.tldr: Hindsight task relabelling enables meta-reinforcement learning with sparse rewards throughout training, matching dense-reward training performance on the tested environments.

title: Hindsight Task Relabelling: Experience Replay for Sparse Reward Meta-RL

abstract: Recently, deep multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has shown the promise to solve complex cooperative tasks. Its success is partly because of parameter sharing among agents. However, such sharing may lead agents to behave similarly and limit their coordination capacity. In this paper, we aim to introduce diversity in both optimization and representation of shared multi-agent reinforcement learning. Specifically, we propose an information-theoretical regularization to maximize the mutual information between agents' identities and their trajectories, encouraging extensive exploration and diverse individualized behaviors. In representation, we incorporate agent-specific modules in the shared neural network architecture, which are regularized by L1-norm to promote learning sharing among agents while keeping necessary diversity. Empirical results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on Google Research Football and super hard StarCraft II micromanagement tasks.

In representation, we incorporate agent-specific modules in the shared neural network architecture, which are regularized by L1-norm to promote learning sharing among agents while keeping necessary diversity. paragraphs: Sharing neural-network parameters helps cooperative reinforcement-learning agents learn together, but it can also encourage them to behave alike. That similarity may restrict coordination when different agents need different behaviors. This paper addresses the tension by introducing diversity into both the training objective and the network representation while retaining shared learning.

For the objective, the authors use an information-theoretic regularizer that increases mutual information between agent identities and their trajectories. In plain language, an agent's sequence of behavior should carry information about which agent produced it. This encourages individualized behavior and broader exploration. For the representation, the shared network includes agent-specific modules, with L1 regularization encouraging sharing while preserving necessary differences.

These mechanisms address complementary parts of the problem: the objective rewards behavioral distinctions, and the architecture gives agents a way to represent them. The authors report state-of-the-art empirical performance on Google Research Football and super hard StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. The findings support the usefulness of explicitly balancing common learning with individual specialization in these cooperative settings.
summary.tldr: Identity-based regularization and agent-specific network modules improve shared multi-agent learning by encouraging useful behavioral diversity.

title: Celebrating Diversity in Shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recognizing fine-grained categories remains a challenging task, due to the subtle distinctions among different subordinate categories, which results in the need of abundant annotated samples. To alleviate the data-hungry problem, we consider the problem of learning novel categories from web data with the support of a clean set of base categories, which is referred to as weak-shot learning. In this setting, we propose a method called SimTrans to transfer pairwise semantic similarity from base categories to novel categories. Specifically, we firstly train a similarity net on clean data, and then leverage the transferred similarity to denoise web training data using two simple yet effective strategies. In addition, we apply adversarial loss on similarity net to enhance the transferability of similarity. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our weak-shot setting and our SimTrans method.

paragraphs: Fine-grained classification distinguishes closely related categories whose visual differences can be subtle. Learning those distinctions usually demands many annotated examples. This paper studies weak-shot learning, where clean examples of base categories support learning new categories from web data. The challenge is to benefit from the web examples while reducing the effect of their noise.

The proposed SimTrans method transfers pairwise semantic similarity from the clean base categories to the new categories. It first trains a similarity network on clean data, then uses the transferred similarity in two strategies for denoising the web training data. An adversarial loss further encourages the similarity network to transfer across the category groups.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of both the weak-shot setting and SimTrans. The approach matters because the transferable resource is a learned notion of similarity between examples, which can help assess web data for categories without the same clean supervision. The reported findings support using clean base-category data to improve learning from noisy examples of new, finely distinguished categories.
summary.tldr: SimTrans transfers semantic similarity from clean base categories to denoise web data for learning new fine-grained categories.

title: Weak-shot Fine-grained Classification via Similarity Transfer

abstract: Matching markets are often organized in a multi-stage and decentralized manner. Moreover, participants in real-world matching markets often have uncertain preferences. This article develops a framework for learning optimal strategies in such settings, based on a nonparametric statistical approach and variational analysis. We propose an efficient algorithm, built upon concepts of "lower uncertainty bound" and "calibrated decentralized matching," for maximizing the participants' expected payoff. We show that there exists a welfare-versus-fairness trade-off that is characterized by the uncertainty level of acceptance. Participants will strategically act in favor of a low uncertainty level to reduce competition and increase expected payoff. We prove that participants can be better off with multi-stage matching compared to single-stage matching. We demonstrate aspects of the theoretical predictions through simulations and an experiment using real data from college admissions.

paragraphs: Matching markets often unfold over several stages without a single central decision maker. Participants also face uncertainty about preferences and acceptance. This paper develops a framework for learning strategies in that setting, where a participant's choices must account for both potential payoff and uncertainty about whether a match will occur.

The approach combines nonparametric statistical methods with variational analysis. Its efficient algorithm uses concepts called a lower uncertainty bound and calibrated decentralized matching to maximize expected payoff. The analysis identifies a trade-off between welfare and fairness whose character depends on uncertainty about acceptance, making that uncertainty central to market behavior.

The authors show that participants strategically favor lower uncertainty to reduce competition and increase expected payoff. They also prove that participants can benefit from having multiple matching stages compared with a single stage; this is a possibility result rather than a claim that everyone always benefits. Simulations and an experiment using college-admissions data demonstrate aspects of the theoretical predictions, connecting the framework to an applied matching setting.
summary.tldr: A learning framework for decentralized matching links acceptance uncertainty to strategic behavior, welfare–fairness trade-offs, and possible benefits from multiple stages.

title: Learning in Multi-Stage Decentralized Matching Markets

abstract: The problem of causal inference with panel data is a central econometric question. The following is a fundamental version of this problem: Let $M^*$ be a low rank matrix and $E$ be a zero-mean noise matrix. For a `treatment' matrix $Z$ with entries in $\{0,1\}$ we observe the matrix $O$ with entries $O_{ij} := M^*_{ij} + E_{ij} + \mathcal{T}_{ij} Z_{ij}$ where $\mathcal{T}_{ij} $ are unknown, heterogenous treatment effects. The problem requires we estimate the average treatment effect $\tau^* := \sum_{ij} \mathcal{T}_{ij} Z_{ij} / \sum_{ij} Z_{ij}$. The synthetic control paradigm provides an approach to estimating $\tau^*$ when $Z$ places support on a single row. This paper extends that framework to allow rate-optimal recovery of $\tau^*$ for general $Z$, thus broadly expanding its applicability. Our guarantees are the first of their type in this general setting. Computational experiments on synthetic and real-world data show a substantial advantage over competing estimators.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an intervention's average effect from panel data when treatment can occur across a general pattern of entries. It models observations as three parts: an underlying low-rank matrix, zero-mean noise, and treatment effects added wherever a binary treatment matrix indicates intervention. Individual treatment effects are allowed to differ across entries.

The target is the average effect among treated entries. This distinction matters because the method is not required to recover every heterogeneous effect separately. The authors extend the synthetic-control framework beyond the setting where all treated entries lie in a single row. Allowing a general treatment matrix broadens the intervention arrangements that the framework can address.

Within the stated modeling setting, the paper provides rate-optimal recovery guarantees for the average treatment effect and describes them as the first guarantees of their kind in this general case. Computational experiments on synthetic and real-world data show a substantial advantage over competing estimators. The contribution combines broader treatment-pattern coverage with theoretical accuracy guarantees, while retaining the low-rank baseline and zero-mean-noise assumptions that define the problem.
summary.tldr: The paper extends synthetic-control-style estimation to general treatment patterns, with rate-optimal average-effect recovery under a low-rank panel model.

title: Learning Treatment Effects in Panels with General Intervention Patterns

abstract: This paper presents an efficient multi-scale vision Transformer, called ResT, that capably served as a general-purpose backbone for image recognition. Unlike existing Transformer methods, which employ standard Transformer blocks to tackle raw images with a fixed resolution, our ResT have several advantages: (1) A memory-efficient multi-head self-attention is built, which compresses the memory by a simple depth-wise convolution, and projects the interaction across the attention-heads dimension while keeping the diversity ability of multi-heads; (2) Positional encoding is constructed as spatial attention, which is more flexible and can tackle with input images of arbitrary size without interpolation or fine-tune; (3) Instead of the straightforward tokenization at the beginning of each stage, we design the patch embedding as a stack of overlapping convolution operation with stride on the token map. We comprehensively validate ResT on image classification and downstream tasks. Experimental results show that the proposed ResT can outperform the recently state-of-the-art backbones by a large margin, demonstrating the potential of ResT as strong backbones. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/wofmanaf/ResT.

paragraphs: ResT is a multiscale vision Transformer designed as a general-purpose backbone for image recognition. The paper modifies attention, positional encoding, and patch embedding to improve efficiency and flexibility. These changes address how the network represents images at different stages as well as how much memory its attention mechanism requires.

Its attention module uses depth-wise convolution to compress memory and introduces interactions across attention heads while preserving their diversity. Positional encoding takes the form of spatial attention, allowing arbitrary image sizes without interpolation or fine-tuning for that purpose. Patch embedding uses stacked, overlapping strided convolutions on the token map instead of straightforward tokenization at each stage.

The authors evaluate ResT on image classification and downstream tasks, reporting substantial improvements over the recent state-of-the-art backbones used for comparison. The findings support the combined architecture as a useful visual feature extractor. Its significance lies in bringing several design decisions together: economical attention, flexible handling of image dimensions, and overlapping image representations within a multiscale Transformer.
summary.tldr: ResT combines efficient attention, flexible positional encoding, and overlapping convolutional embeddings in a strong multiscale vision backbone.

title: ResT: An Efficient Transformer for Visual Recognition

abstract: A challenging aspect of the bandit problem is that a stochastic reward is observed only for the chosen arm and the rewards of other arms remain missing. The dependence of the arm choice on the past context and reward pairs compounds the complexity of regret analysis.We propose a novel multi-armed contextual bandit algorithm called Doubly Robust Thompson Sampling (DRTS) employing the doubly-robust estimator used in missing data literature to Thompson Sampling with contexts (\texttt{LinTS}).Different from previous works relying on missing data techniques (Dimakopoulou et al. [2019], Kim and Paik [2019]), the proposed algorithm is designed to allow a novel additive regret decomposition leading to an improved regret bound with the order of $\tilde{O}(\phi^{-2}\sqrt{T})$, where $\phi^2$ is the minimum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix of contexts.This is the first regret bound of \texttt{LinTS} using $\phi^2$ without $d$, where $d$ is the dimension of the context.Applying the relationship between $\phi^2$ and $d$, the regret bound of the proposed algorithm is $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T})$ in many practical scenarios, improving the bound of \texttt{LinTS} by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$.A benefit of the proposed method is that it uses all the context data, chosen or not chosen, thus allowing to circumvent the technical definition of unsaturated arms used in theoretical analysis of \texttt{LinTS}.Empirical studies show the advantage of the proposed algorithm over \texttt{LinTS}.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit chooses among actions using information about each option, but observes a reward only for the action it takes. The unobserved rewards create a missing-data problem, made harder because previous observations influence later choices. This paper introduces Doubly Robust Thompson Sampling, combining a missing-data estimator with Thompson sampling for linear contextual rewards.

The algorithm uses context information for every available action, including actions that were not selected. Its design enables an additive decomposition of regret, the accumulated shortfall relative to the comparison strategy. The resulting bound scales as approximately φ⁻²√T, ignoring logarithmic factors, where φ² is the smallest eigenvalue of the context covariance matrix and T is the number of rounds.

This expression uses context covariance without explicitly including context dimension d, although covariance can itself depend on dimension. In many practical scenarios, the relationship gives an approximately d√T bound, improving the LinTS bound by a factor of √d. The analysis also avoids a technical category of actions used in earlier LinTS proofs. Empirical studies report an advantage over LinTS.
summary.tldr: Doubly Robust Thompson Sampling uses all available contexts to obtain improved regret guarantees and empirical gains over LinTS.

title: Doubly Robust Thompson Sampling with Linear Payoffs

abstract: Exact multi-label classification is the task of assigning each datapoint a set of class labels such that the assigned set exactly matches the ground truth. Optimizing for exact multi-label classification is important in domains where missing a single label can be especially costly, such as in object detection for autonomous vehicles or symptom classification for disease diagnosis. Recurrent Classifier Chains (RCCs), a recurrent neural network extension of ensemble-based classifier chains, are the state-of-the-art exact multi-label classification method for maximizing subset accuracy. However, RCCs iteratively predict classes with an unprincipled ordering, and therefore indiscriminately condition class probabilities. These disadvantages make RCCs prone to predicting inaccurate label sets. In this work we propose Recurrent Bayesian Classifier Chains (RBCCs), which learn a Bayesian network of class dependencies and leverage this network in order to condition the prediction of child nodes only on their parents. By conditioning predictions in this way, we perform principled and non-noisy class prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our RBCC method on a variety of real-world multi-label datasets, where we routinely outperform the state of the art methods for exact multi-label classification.

Recurrent Classifier Chains (RCCs), a recurrent neural network extension of ensemble-based classifier chains, are the state-of-the-art exact multi-label classification method for maximizing subset accuracy. However, RCCs iteratively predict classes with an unprincipled ordering, and therefore indiscriminately condition class probabilities. These disadvantages make RCCs prone to predicting inaccurate label sets. In this work we propose Recurrent Bayesian Classifier Chains (RBCCs), which learn a Bayesian network of class dependencies and leverage this network in order to condition the prediction of child nodes only on their parents. By conditioning predictions in this way, we perform principled and non-noisy class prediction. paragraphs: Exact multi-label classification requires predicting the entire correct set of labels for each example. Getting most labels right is insufficient under this objective, making dependencies among labels especially consequential. The paper focuses on improving recurrent classifier chains, which predict labels iteratively but can use an unprincipled ordering and condition on unsuitable class information.

The result concerns correctly recovering complete label sets, rather than merely improving isolated label predictions. Its broader significance is that the structure used to connect predictions can matter alongside the predictive network itself, especially when one incorrect label makes the whole output set wrong.
summary.tldr: Recurrent Bayesian Classifier Chains use learned class dependencies to improve prediction of complete, exactly correct label sets.

title: Recurrent Bayesian Classifier Chains for Exact Multi-Label Classification

abstract: Channel pruning is a popular technique for compressing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where various pruning criteria have been proposed to remove the redundant filters. From our comprehensive experiments, we found two blind spots of pruning criteria: (1) Similarity: There are some strong similarities among several primary pruning criteria that are widely cited and compared. According to these criteria, the ranks of filters’ Importance Score are almost identical, resulting in similar pruned structures. (2) Applicability: The filters' Importance Score measured by some pruning criteria are too close to distinguish the network redundancy well. In this paper, we analyze the above blind spots on different types of pruning criteria with layer-wise pruning or global pruning. We also break some stereotypes, such as that the results of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ pruning are not always similar. These analyses are based on the empirical experiments and our assumption (Convolutional Weight Distribution Assumption) that the well-trained convolutional filters in each layer approximately follow a Gaussian-alike distribution. This assumption has been verified through systematic and extensive statistical tests.

paragraphs: Channel pruning compresses a convolutional network by removing filters judged redundant. Many criteria assign each filter an importance score, but this paper asks whether those scores actually lead to meaningfully different or informative decisions. Its experiments identify two weaknesses in widely used criteria.

First, several prominent criteria produce almost the same filter ranking, so comparing their formulas can overstate how different their pruning behavior is. Second, some criteria assign scores that are too similar to distinguish redundancy clearly. The authors analyze these issues for both layer-wise pruning and global pruning, where the scope of the selection differs.

The analysis also challenges the assumption that pruning based on the ℓ1 and ℓ2 norms always produces similar results. Its reasoning combines empirical experiments with an assumption that well-trained filters within a layer have an approximately Gaussian-like distribution, supported by extensive statistical tests. The findings encourage judging a criterion by its actual rankings and ability to separate filters, while retaining the distributional assumption underlying the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that common CNN pruning criteria can produce nearly identical rankings or poorly separated scores, complicating claims about filter importance.

title: Rethinking the Pruning Criteria for Convolutional Neural Network

abstract: A wide variety of machine learning tasks such as knowledge base completion, ontology alignment, and multi-label classification can benefit from incorporating into learning differentiable representations of graphs or taxonomies. While vectors in Euclidean space can theoretically represent any graph, much recent work shows that alternatives such as complex, hyperbolic, order, or box embeddings have geometric properties better suited to modeling real-world graphs. Experimentally these gains are seen only in lower dimensions, however, with performance benefits diminishing in higher dimensions. In this work, we introduce a novel variant of box embeddings that uses a learned smoothing parameter to achieve better representational capacity than vector models in low dimensions, while also avoiding performance saturation common to other geometric models in high dimensions. Further, we present theoretical results that prove box embeddings can represent any DAG. We perform rigorous empirical evaluations of vector, hyperbolic, and region-based geometric representations on several families of synthetic and real-world directed graphs. Analysis of these results exposes correlations between different families of graphs, graph characteristics, model size, and embedding geometry, providing useful insights into the inductive biases of various differentiable graph representations.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn relationships into representations that learning systems can optimize. Although Euclidean vectors can theoretically represent any graph, other geometries may fit particular graph structures more naturally. The paper examines why such alternatives often help at small representation sizes but lose their advantage as the number of dimensions increases.

The authors introduce a box-embedding variant with a learned smoothing parameter. It provides greater representational capacity than vector models in low dimensions while avoiding the performance saturation observed in other geometric models at higher dimensions. They also prove that box embeddings can represent any directed acyclic graph, establishing a broad expressiveness result for graphs without directed cycles.

The empirical study compares vector, hyperbolic, and region-based representations on several families of synthetic and real directed graphs. It identifies correlations among graph characteristics, graph family, model size, and embedding geometry. These results help explain the structural preferences built into different representations: choosing a geometry affects which relationships are convenient to learn, even when multiple representations have substantial theoretical capacity.
summary.tldr: A box-embedding model with learned smoothing improves capacity across dimensions, while theory and experiments clarify how geometry fits directed graphs.

title: Capacity and Bias of Learned Geometric Embeddings for Directed Graphs

abstract: Recent works recognized lidars as an inherently streaming data source and showed that the end-to-end latency of lidar perception models can be reduced significantly by operating on wedge-shaped point cloud sectors rather then the full point cloud. However, due to use of cartesian coordinate systems these methods represent the sectors as rectangular regions, wasting memory and compute. In this work we propose using a polar coordinate system and make two key improvements on this design. First, we increase the spatial context by using multi-scale padding from neighboring sectors: preceding sector from the current scan and/or the following sector from the past scan. Second, we improve the core polar convolutional architecture by introducing feature undistortion and range stratified convolutions. Experimental results on the nuScenes dataset show significant improvements over other streaming based methods. We also achieve comparable results to existing non-streaming methods but with lower latencies.
