paragraphs: Lidar data arrives as a stream, making it possible to process wedge-shaped sectors before a complete scan is available. This can reduce perception latency, but representing those sectors as Cartesian rectangles wastes memory and computation. PolarStream uses polar coordinates to better match the geometry of the arriving data for object detection and segmentation.

The method also addresses the limited spatial context of processing one sector at a time. It adds multi-scale padding using neighboring sectors: the preceding sector from the current scan, the following sector from an earlier scan, or both. Its polar convolutional architecture further incorporates feature undistortion and range-stratified convolutions. These changes refine how the system processes features within the polar representation.

Experiments on nuScenes show significant improvements over other streaming methods. PolarStream also achieves results comparable to existing methods that process full scans, while operating at lower latency. The findings show how matching the representation to the sensor's streaming geometry, together with borrowing neighboring context, can make partial-scan perception more effective without giving up its latency advantage.
summary.tldr: PolarStream combines polar-coordinate lidar sectors with neighboring context to improve streaming perception while maintaining low latency.

title: PolarStream: Streaming Object Detection and Segmentation with Polar Pillars

abstract: With model trustworthiness being crucial for sensitive real-world applications, practitioners are putting more and more focus on improving the uncertainty calibration of deep neural networks.Calibration errors are designed to quantify the reliability of probabilistic predictions but their estimators are usually biased and inconsistent.In this work, we introduce the framework of \textit{proper calibration errors}, which relates every calibration error to a proper score and provides a respective upper bound with optimal estimation properties.This relationship can be used to reliably quantify the model calibration improvement.We theoretically and empirically demonstrate the shortcomings of commonly used estimators compared to our approach.Due to the wide applicability of proper scores, this gives a natural extension of recalibration beyond classification.

paragraphs: Assessing a model's uncertainty requires a reliable way to measure the quality of its probabilistic predictions. This paper focuses on a problem with that measurement step: commonly used calibration-error estimators are often biased and inconsistent. Consequently, evaluating whether a recalibration method improves a model can itself involve an unreliable estimate.

The authors introduce proper calibration errors, a framework connecting calibration errors with proper scores. That relationship supplies a corresponding upper bound with optimal estimation properties. The upper bound matters because it provides a statistically supported route to quantifying calibration improvements, rather than relying entirely on the problematic estimators the paper examines.

The paper supports its argument with both theoretical and empirical comparisons showing shortcomings of commonly used estimators relative to the proposed approach. Because proper scores apply broadly, the framework also provides a natural extension of recalibration beyond classification. Its contribution is therefore both a better foundation for measuring improvement and a route to using that foundation in additional prediction settings.
summary.tldr: Proper calibration errors connect calibration measurement to proper scores, yielding upper bounds that support reliable assessment beyond classification.

title: Better Uncertainty Calibration via Proper Scores for Classification and Beyond

abstract: Many applications of text generation require incorporating different constraints to control the semantics or style of generated text. These constraints can be hard (e.g., ensuring certain keywords are included in the output) and soft (e.g., contextualizing the output with the left- or right-hand context). In this paper, we present Energy-based Constrained Decoding with Langevin Dynamics (COLD), a decoding framework which unifies constrained generation as specifying constraints through an energy function, then performing efficient differentiable reasoning over the constraints through gradient-based sampling. COLD decoding is a flexible framework that can be applied directly to off-the-shelf left-to-right language models without the need for any task-specific fine-tuning, as demonstrated through three challenging text generation applications: lexically-constrained generation, abductive reasoning, and counterfactual reasoning. Our experiments on these constrained generation tasks point to the effectiveness of our approach, both in terms of automatic and human evaluation.

paragraphs: Text generation often needs to satisfy requirements beyond producing fluent sentences. Some requirements are hard constraints, such as including specified keywords. Others are softer preferences, such as fitting surrounding text or expressing a particular style. The paper introduces COLD, a decoding framework that brings these different requirements into a shared mathematical formulation.

COLD represents constraints through an energy function and uses gradient-based sampling with Langevin dynamics to reason over them. This makes the constraints part of the generation procedure. The framework can be applied directly to existing language models that generate from left to right, without training a separate task-specific version of the model.

The authors demonstrate the approach on generation with required words, abductive reasoning, and counterfactual reasoning. Across these applications, both automatic measurements and human assessments support its effectiveness. The contribution is therefore a flexible way to control generation through the decoding process itself. Its unifying formulation matters because the same framework accommodates different kinds of requirements, rather than requiring each application to be handled through its own fine-tuned language model.
summary.tldr: COLD uses energy functions and gradient-based sampling to guide existing language models through text-generation constraints without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: COLD Decoding: Energy-based Constrained Text Generation with Langevin Dynamics

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating states (e.g., position and velocity) and physical parameters (e.g., friction, elasticity) from a sequence of observations when provided a dynamic equation that describes the behavior of the system. The dynamic equation can arise from first principles (e.g., Newton’s laws) and provide useful cues for learning, but its physical parameters are unknown. To address this problem, we propose a model that estimates states and physical parameters of the system using two main components. First, an autoencoder compresses a sequence of observations (e.g., sensor measurements, pixel images) into a sequence for the state representation that is consistent with physics by including a simulation of the dynamic equation. Second, an estimator is coupled with the autoencoder to predict the values of the physical parameters. We also theoretically and empirically show that using Fourier feature mappings improves generalization of the estimator in predicting physical parameters compared to raw state sequences. In our experiments on three visual and one sensor measurement tasks, our model imposes interpretability on latent states and achieves improved generalization performance for long-term prediction of system dynamics over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Observations of a physical system may reveal its behavior without directly exposing states such as position and velocity or parameters such as friction and elasticity. This paper estimates both from observation sequences. Its setting assumes that a governing dynamic equation is supplied, while the physical parameters within that equation remain unknown.

The model couples an autoencoder with a parameter estimator. The autoencoder compresses measurements or images into a sequence of latent states, incorporating simulation of the supplied equation to make those states consistent with physics. The estimator predicts the unknown physical parameters. The authors also study Fourier feature mappings and provide theoretical and empirical evidence that these improve parameter-estimation generalization compared with using raw state sequences.

Experiments cover three visual tasks and one task using sensor measurements. The reported results show interpretable latent states and better generalization for long-term dynamics prediction than state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a way to combine known physical structure with learned states and parameters, so that prediction benefits from the supplied dynamics.
summary.tldr: A physics-constrained autoencoder jointly learns interpretable states and unknown physical parameters, improving long-term prediction in the evaluated tasks.

title: Learning Physics Constrained Dynamics Using Autoencoders

abstract: The stochastic gradient Langevin Dynamics is one of the most fundamental algorithms to solve sampling problems and non-convex optimization appearing in several machine learning applications. Especially, its variance reduced versions have nowadays gained particular attention. In this paper, we study two variants of this kind, namely, the Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient Langevin Dynamics and the Stochastic Recursive Gradient Langevin Dynamics. We prove their convergence to the objective distribution in terms of KL-divergence under the sole assumptions of smoothness and Log-Sobolev inequality which are weaker conditions than those used in prior works for these algorithms. With the batch size and the inner loop length set to $\sqrt{n}$, the gradient complexity to achieve an $\epsilon$-precision is $\tilde{O}((n+dn^{1/2}\epsilon^{-1})\gamma^2 L^2\alpha^{-2})$, which is an improvement from any previous analyses. We also show some essential applications of our result to non-convex optimization.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics is used for sampling and for non-convex optimization. Variance-reduced versions aim to control variability in stochastic gradient estimates. This paper studies two such methods: Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient Langevin Dynamics and Stochastic Recursive Gradient Langevin Dynamics, with the goal of strengthening their convergence analysis.

The authors prove convergence to the target distribution measured by KL-divergence. Their assumptions are smoothness and a Log-Sobolev inequality, which they describe as weaker than those used in earlier analyses of these algorithms. The contribution therefore concerns both the quality of the convergence bound and the conditions under which it holds.

With batch size and inner-loop length both set to the square root of n, the paper gives an improved gradient-complexity bound for reaching a specified precision. Its dependence includes a term proportional to n and another proportional to d times the square root of n divided by the target precision, alongside the stated problem factors and suppressed logarithms. The authors also develop applications of this sampling result to non-convex optimization.
summary.tldr: Two variance-reduced Langevin methods receive improved sampling convergence bounds under smoothness and a Log-Sobolev inequality.

title: Improved Convergence Rate of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics with Variance Reduction and its Application to Optimization

abstract: Modular Reinforcement Learning (RL) decentralizes the control of multi-joint robots by learning policies for each actuator. Previous work on modular RL has proven its ability to control morphologically different agents with a shared actuator policy. However, with the increase in the Degree of Freedom (DoF) of robots, training a morphology-generalizable modular controller becomes exponentially difficult. Motivated by the way the human central nervous system controls numerous muscles, we propose a Synergy-Oriented LeARning (SOLAR) framework that exploits the redundant nature of DoF in robot control. Actuators are grouped into synergies by an unsupervised learning method, and a synergy action is learned to control multiple actuators in synchrony. In this way, we achieve a low-rank control at the synergy level. We extensively evaluate our method on a variety of robot morphologies, and the results show its superior efficiency and generalizability, especially on robots with a large DoF like Humanoids++ and UNIMALs.

paragraphs: Modular reinforcement learning distributes robot control across actuators, allowing a shared actuator policy to operate on different body structures. As robots gain more degrees of freedom, however, learning a controller that generalizes across those structures becomes much harder. This paper uses the coordinated control of human muscles as motivation for reducing that difficulty.

The proposed SOLAR framework groups actuators into synergies through unsupervised learning. It then learns actions at the synergy level, with each action coordinating multiple actuators. This exploits redundancy in the robot's degrees of freedom and produces low-rank control: behavior is organized through a smaller collection of coordinated action patterns.

Evaluations across varied robot morphologies show better efficiency and generalizability, with particularly strong results on robots with many degrees of freedom, including Humanoids++ and UNIMALs. The findings support learning coordinated actuator groups as a useful structure for modular control. Rather than requiring every actuator to be handled as an independent control choice, the framework learns shared patterns that can make high-dimensional robot control more manageable.
summary.tldr: SOLAR learns groups of coordinated actuators to improve modular reinforcement learning efficiency and generalization, especially for robots with many degrees of freedom.

title: Low-Rank Modular Reinforcement Learning via Muscle Synergy

abstract: Machine learning models often generalize poorly to out-of-distribution (OOD) data as a result of relying on features that are spuriously correlated with the label during training. Recently, the technique of Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) was proposed to learn predictors that only use invariant features by conserving the feature-conditioned label expectation $\mathbb{E}_e[y|f(x)]$ across environments. However, more recent studies have demonstrated that IRM-v1, a practical version of IRM, can fail in various settings. Here, we identify a fundamental flaw of IRM formulation that causes the failure. We then introduce a complementary notion of invariance, MRI, based on conserving the label-conditioned feature expectation $\mathbb{E}_e[f(x)|y]$, which is free of this flaw. Further, we introduce a simplified, practical version of the MRI formulation called MRI-v1. We prove that for general linear problems, MRI-v1 guarantees invariant predictors given sufficient number of environments. We also empirically demonstrate that MRI-v1 strongly out-performs IRM-v1 and consistently achieves near-optimal OOD generalization in image-based nonlinear problems.

paragraphs: Models can fail outside their training distribution when they rely on correlations that change across environments. Invariant Risk Minimization aims to avoid this by keeping the expected label, conditioned on learned features, consistent across environments. This paper identifies a fundamental flaw in that formulation that explains failures of its practical version, IRM-v1.

The authors propose a complementary invariance principle called MRI. It reverses the conditioning: the expected features, given a label, should remain consistent across environments. They show that this formulation avoids the identified flaw and introduce MRI-v1 as a simplified practical implementation. The change alters what relationship the method requires to stay stable.

For general linear problems, the paper proves that MRI-v1 yields invariant predictors when sufficiently many environments are available. In nonlinear image-based experiments, MRI-v1 strongly outperforms IRM-v1 and consistently approaches optimal out-of-distribution generalization. The theoretical guarantee depends on the linear setting and environment condition, while the nonlinear findings provide empirical evidence for the value of the complementary principle.
summary.tldr: MRI reverses IRM's conditioning to enforce a complementary invariance, with conditional linear guarantees and strong nonlinear experimental results.

title: The Missing Invariance Principle found -- the Reciprocal Twin of Invariant Risk Minimization

abstract: A core goal in systems neuroscience and neuroethology is to understand how neural circuits generate naturalistic behavior. One foundational idea is that complex naturalistic behavior may be composed of sequences of stereotyped behavioral syllables, which combine to generate rich sequences of actions. To investigate this, a common approach is to use autoregressive hidden Markov models (ARHMMs) to segment video into discrete behavioral syllables. While these approaches have been successful in extracting syllables that are interpretable, they fail to account for other forms of behavioral variability, such as differences in speed, which may be better described as continuous in nature. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a class of warped ARHMMs (WARHMM). As is the case in the ARHMM, behavior is modeled as a mixture of autoregressive dynamics. However, the dynamics under each discrete latent state (i.e. each behavioral syllable) are additionally modulated by a continuous latent ``warping variable.'' We present two versions of warped ARHMM in which the warping variable affects the dynamics of each syllable either linearly or nonlinearly. Using depth-camera recordings of freely moving mice, we demonstrate that the failure of ARHMMs to account for continuous behavioral variability results in duplicate cluster assignments. WARHMM achieves similar performance to the standard ARHMM while using fewer behavioral syllables. Further analysis of behavioral measurements in mice demonstrates that WARHMM identifies structure relating to response vigor.

paragraphs: Natural behavior may consist of recurring action units, or behavioral syllables, whose sequences produce more complex activity. Autoregressive hidden Markov models identify such units by dividing recordings into discrete states with different dynamics. However, a single action can also vary continuously, for example in speed, creating variation that a purely discrete description does not capture.

Warped autoregressive hidden Markov models add a continuous hidden variable that modifies the dynamics within each discrete state. The paper develops versions in which this modification acts linearly or nonlinearly. This lets the model represent both which behavioral syllable is occurring and continuous variation in how that syllable unfolds.

Using depth-camera recordings of freely moving mice, the authors show that standard models can assign duplicate clusters when continuous variability goes unmodeled. Their warped models achieve similar performance with fewer syllables, yielding a more compact behavioral description. Further analysis identifies structure associated with response vigor. The findings support separating action identity from continuous differences in its expression when interpreting behavioral recordings.
summary.tldr: Warped autoregressive models separate discrete mouse behaviors from continuous variation, achieving similar performance with fewer behavioral categories.

title: Distinguishing discrete and continuous behavioral variability using warped autoregressive HMMs

abstract: We initiate the study of active learning polynomial threshold functions (PTFs). While traditional lower bounds imply that even univariate quadratics cannot be non-trivially actively learned, we show that allowing the learner basic access to the derivatives of the underlying classifier circumvents this issue and leads to a computationally efficient algorithm for active learning degree-$d$ univariate PTFs in $\tilde{O}(d^3\log(1/\varepsilon\delta))$ queries. We extend this result to the batch active setting, providing a smooth transition between query complexity and rounds of adaptivity, and also provide near-optimal algorithms for active learning PTFs in several average case settings. Finally, we prove that access to derivatives is insufficient for active learning multivariate PTFs, even those of just two variables.

paragraphs: A polynomial threshold function classifies an input according to the sign of a polynomial. This paper studies how to learn these classifiers actively, choosing queries to reduce the information needed. The starting obstacle is strong: existing lower bounds rule out nontrivial active learning even for quadratic polynomials with a single input variable under traditional access.

The authors change what information the learner can request. With basic access to derivatives of the underlying classifier, they give a computationally efficient method for learning degree-d polynomials in one variable. Its query bound is roughly cubic in d and logarithmic in the inverse accuracy and confidence parameters, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. They also extend the method to batches, trading query complexity against the number of adaptive rounds.

Further algorithms are near optimal in several average-case settings. However, the extra derivative information does not resolve the problem generally: the paper proves that it is insufficient for multivariate polynomial threshold functions, even with only two variables. The contribution therefore identifies both a useful information source and a sharp boundary on its power.
summary.tldr: Derivative access enables efficient active learning of one-variable polynomial threshold functions, but remains insufficient even for two-variable ones.

title: Active Learning Polynomial Threshold Functions

abstract: Neural processes (NPs) formulate exchangeable stochastic processes and are promising models for meta learning that do not require gradient updates during the testing phase. However, most NP variants place a strong emphasis on a global latent variable. This weakens the approximation power and restricts the scope of applications using NP variants, especially when data generative processes are complicated.To resolve these issues, we propose to combine the Mixture of Expert models with Neural Processes to develop more expressive exchangeable stochastic processes, referred to as Mixture of Expert Neural Processes (MoE-NPs). Then we apply MoE-NPs to both few-shot supervised learning and meta reinforcement learning tasks. Empirical results demonstrate MoE-NPs' strong generalization capability to unseen tasks in these benchmarks.

paragraphs: Neural processes are models for learning across tasks that can make predictions at test time without gradient updates. They formulate exchangeable stochastic processes, making them useful for meta learning. This paper identifies a restriction in many existing variants: placing too much representational emphasis on a single global latent variable.

The authors argue that this emphasis weakens approximation power, particularly when the underlying data-generating processes are complicated. Their proposed Mixture of Expert Neural Processes combines neural processes with mixture-of-experts models to construct more expressive exchangeable processes. The change targets the capacity of the learned representation, allowing the model to represent task structure through a mixture of experts.

The resulting models are evaluated on both few-shot supervised learning and meta reinforcement learning. The reported experiments show strong generalization to previously unseen tasks within those benchmarks. This matters because both settings require knowledge acquired across tasks to support a new task with limited task-specific experience. The findings support the proposed mixture as a way to broaden neural-process representations for these applications.
summary.tldr: Mixture of Expert Neural Processes expands neural-process representations and shows strong generalization on few-shot and meta reinforcement learning benchmarks.

title: Learning Expressive Meta-Representations with Mixture of Expert Neural Processes

abstract: Inverse rendering is an ill-posed problem. Previous work has sought to resolve this by focussing on priors for object or scene shape or appearance. In this work, we instead focus on a prior for natural illuminations. Current methods rely on spherical harmonic lighting or other generic representations and, at best, a simplistic prior on the parameters. We propose a conditional neural field representation based on a variational auto-decoder with a SIREN network and, extending Vector Neurons, build equivariance directly into the network. Using this, we develop a rotation-equivariant, high dynamic range (HDR) neural illumination model that is compact and able to express complex, high-frequency features of natural environment maps. Training our model on a curated dataset of 1.6K HDR environment maps of natural scenes, we compare it against traditional representations, demonstrate its applicability for an inverse rendering task and show environment map completion from partial observations.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering tries to infer properties of a scene from its images, but multiple explanations can fit the observations. This paper addresses that ambiguity by learning a prior over natural illumination. The focus is on representing plausible lighting, complementing approaches that emphasize prior knowledge about shape or surface appearance.

The proposed representation combines a variational auto-decoder with a SIREN neural field and extends Vector Neurons to build rotation equivariance into the network. This makes the model respond consistently to rotations. The resulting high dynamic range illumination model is compact while retaining the ability to represent complex, high-frequency structure in natural environment maps.

The authors train the model on a curated collection of 1,600 HDR environment maps of natural scenes and compare it with traditional representations. They demonstrate its use in an inverse-rendering task and in completing environment maps from partial observations. These applications show how a learned illumination prior can support both interpreting images and inferring missing lighting information, while explicitly respecting the rotational structure of the representation.
summary.tldr: A compact, rotation-equivariant neural illumination model learns natural lighting structure for inverse rendering and environment-map completion.

title: Rotation-Equivariant Conditional Spherical Neural Fields for Learning a Natural Illumination Prior

abstract: This work develops a flexible and mathematically sound framework for the design and analysis of graph scattering networks with variable branching ratios and generic functional calculus filters.Spectrally-agnostic stability guarantees for node- and graph-level perturbations are derived; the vertex-set non-preserving case is treated by utilizing recently developed mathematical-physics based tools. Energy propagation through the network layers is investigated and related to truncation stability. New methods of graph-level feature aggregation are introduced and stability of the resulting composite scattering architectures is established. Finally, scattering transforms are extended to edge- and higher order tensorial input. Theoretical results are complemented by numerical investigations: Suitably chosen scattering networks conforming to the developed theory perform better than traditional graph-wavelet based scattering approaches in social network graph classification tasks andsignificantly outperform other graph-based learning approaches to regression of quantum-chemical energies on QM$7$.

paragraphs: This paper broadens the design of graph scattering networks beyond traditional graph-wavelet constructions. Its framework allows different branching ratios and a more general family of filters defined through functional calculus. The aim is to provide flexibility in architecture design together with mathematical tools for understanding how those architectures behave.

The authors establish stability guarantees for changes at both the node and graph levels, including changes that do not preserve the vertex set. They also examine how energy propagates through layers and connect this behavior to stability when the network is truncated. Additional results cover graph-level aggregation and extend the input types to edges and higher-order tensors.

Numerical investigations complement the theory. Suitably chosen networks within the framework outperform traditional graph-wavelet scattering methods on social-network classification tasks and significantly outperform other evaluated graph-based approaches on quantum-chemical energy regression using QM7. These findings show that the added design freedom can be useful in practice while remaining compatible with the framework's stability analysis.
summary.tldr: A broader graph scattering framework combines flexible filters and architectures with stability guarantees and strong results on evaluated graph tasks.

title: Graph Scattering beyond Wavelet Shackles

abstract: The recent advances of deep learning have dramatically changed how machine learning, especially in the domain of natural language processing, can be applied to legal domain. However, this shift to the data-driven approaches calls for larger and more diverse datasets, which are nevertheless still small in number, especially in non-English languages. Here we present the first large-scale benchmark of Korean legal AI datasets, LBOX OPEN, that consists of one legal corpus, two classification tasks, two legal judgement prediction (LJP) tasks, and one summarization task. The legal corpus consists of 147k Korean precedents (259M tokens), of which 63k are sentenced in last 4 years and 96k are from the first and the second level courts in which factual issues are reviewed. The two classification tasks are case names (11.3k) and statutes (2.8k) prediction from the factual description of individual cases. The LJP tasks consist of (1) 10.5k criminal examples where the model is asked to predict fine amount, imprisonment with labor, and imprisonment without labor ranges for the given facts, and (2) 4.7k civil examples where the inputs are facts and claim for relief and outputs are the degrees of claim acceptance. The summarization task consists of the Supreme Court precedents and the corresponding summaries (20k). We also release realistic variants of the datasets by extending the domain (1) to infrequent case categories in case name (31k examples) and statute (17.7k) classification tasks, and (2) to long input sequences in the summarization task (51k). Finally, we release LCUBE, the first Korean legal language model trained on the legal corpus from this study. Given the uniqueness of the Law of South Korea and the diversity of the legal tasks covered in this work, we believe that LBOX OPEN contributes to the multilinguality of global legal research. LBOX OPEN and LCUBE will be publicly available.

paragraphs: LBOX OPEN addresses the shortage of large, varied datasets for studying legal language outside English. It brings together a Korean legal text collection and tasks covering classification, judgment prediction, and summarization. The corpus contains 147,000 precedents and 259 million tokens, including substantial representation from lower courts where factual issues are reviewed.

The tasks test different connections between legal facts and legal outcomes. Classification models predict case names or relevant statutes from case descriptions. Criminal judgment prediction asks for ranges of fines and imprisonment, while civil prediction asks how much of a claim is accepted given the facts and requested relief. Summarization pairs Supreme Court precedents with their summaries.

The benchmark also includes variants with uncommon case categories and longer documents, expanding the situations that models must handle. Alongside the datasets, the authors introduce LCUBE, a Korean legal language model trained on the collected corpus. Together, these resources provide a shared basis for evaluating several kinds of Korean legal language processing and broadening multilingual legal research.
summary.tldr: LBOX OPEN introduces a large Korean legal corpus, multiple evaluation tasks, and a language model trained on that corpus.

title: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Korean Legal Language Understanding and Judgement Prediction

abstract: In risk-averse reinforcement learning (RL), the goal is to optimize some risk measure of the returns. A risk measure often focuses on the worst returns out of the agent's experience. As a result, standard methods for risk-averse RL often ignore high-return strategies. We prove that under certain conditions this inevitably leads to a local-optimum barrier, and propose a mechanism we call soft risk to bypass it. We also devise a novel cross entropy module for sampling, which (1) preserves risk aversion despite the soft risk; (2) independently improves sample efficiency. By separating the risk aversion of the sampler and the optimizer, we can sample episodes with poor conditions, yet optimize with respect to successful strategies. We combine these two concepts in CeSoR - Cross-entropy Soft-Risk optimization algorithm - which can be applied on top of any risk-averse policy gradient (PG) method. We demonstrate improved risk aversion in maze navigation, autonomous driving, and resource allocation benchmarks, including in scenarios where standard risk-averse PG completely fails.

paragraphs: Risk-averse reinforcement learning emphasizes unfavorable returns, but that focus can cause learning algorithms to overlook successful strategies. The authors prove that, under certain conditions, this produces a barrier at a local optimum. Their concern is therefore both what an agent should optimize and whether its learning procedure can discover strategies that improve that objective.

They introduce soft risk to bypass this barrier and pair it with a cross-entropy sampling module. The sampler preserves risk aversion despite the softened optimization and also improves sample efficiency independently. Separating these responsibilities allows training to sample episodes with poor conditions while still learning from strategies that succeed within them.

The combined algorithm, CeSoR, can be added to any risk-averse policy gradient method. Experiments in maze navigation, autonomous driving, and resource allocation show improved risk aversion, including scenarios where standard risk-averse policy gradients fail completely. These findings support separating difficult-condition sampling from the optimizer's treatment of returns, rather than relying on one mechanism to perform both jobs.
summary.tldr: CeSoR separates risk-focused sampling from softened optimization to improve risk-averse policy learning and bypass a conditional local-optimum barrier.

title: Efficient Risk-Averse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: As a successful approach to self-supervised learning, contrastive learning aims to learn invariant information shared among distortions of the input sample. While contrastive learning has yielded continuous advancements in sampling strategy and architecture design, it still remains two persistent defects: the interference of task-irrelevant information and sample inefficiency, which are related to the recurring existence of trivial constant solutions. From the perspective of dimensional analysis, we find out that the dimensional redundancy and dimensional confounder are the intrinsic issues behind the phenomena, and provide experimental evidence to support our viewpoint. We further propose a simple yet effective approach MetaMask, short for the dimensional Mask learned by Meta-learning, to learn representations against dimensional redundancy and confounder. MetaMask adopts the redundancy-reduction technique to tackle the dimensional redundancy issue and innovatively introduces a dimensional mask to reduce the gradient effects of specific dimensions containing the confounder, which is trained by employing a meta-learning paradigm with the objective of improving the performance of masked representations on a typical self-supervised task. We provide solid theoretical analyses to prove MetaMask can obtain tighter risk bounds for downstream classification compared to typical contrastive methods. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning seeks representations that preserve information shared across distorted versions of an input. This paper examines interference from irrelevant information and inefficient use of training examples. It connects these problems to redundancy across representation dimensions and to dimensions containing confounding information, providing experimental evidence for that interpretation.

MetaMask combines redundancy reduction with a learned mask over representation dimensions. The redundancy-reduction component addresses duplicated information, while the mask reduces the gradient effects of particular dimensions containing confounders. A meta-learning procedure trains the mask with the objective of improving the masked representation’s performance on a self-supervised task.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that MetaMask can obtain tighter downstream classification risk bounds than typical contrastive methods. They also report state-of-the-art results across various benchmarks. The approach matters because it changes how individual dimensions influence learning, alongside efforts to make dimensions less redundant. Its stated theoretical and empirical findings support treating the internal organization of a representation as a meaningful target for improving self-supervised learning.
summary.tldr: MetaMask uses redundancy reduction and a meta-learned dimensional mask to improve self-supervised representations and downstream classification risk bounds.

title: MetaMask: Revisiting Dimensional Confounder for Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Transfer learning and ensembling are two popular techniques for improving the performance and robustness of neural networks. Due to the high cost of pre-training, ensembles of models fine-tuned from a single pre-trained checkpoint are often used in practice. Such models end up in the same basin of the loss landscape, which we call the pre-train basin, and thus have limited diversity. In this work, we show that ensembles trained from a single pre-trained checkpoint may be improved by better exploring the pre-train basin, however, leaving the basin results in losing the benefits of transfer learning and in degradation of the ensemble quality. Based on the analysis of existing exploration methods, we propose a more effective modification of the Snapshot Ensembles (SSE) for transfer learning setup, StarSSE, which results in stronger ensembles and uniform model soups.

paragraphs: An economical way to build an ensemble is to fine-tune several models from one pretrained checkpoint. These models tend to remain in the same region, or basin, of the loss landscape, which limits their diversity. This paper examines how to increase useful diversity while retaining the benefits inherited from pretraining.

The authors show that ensembles from a shared checkpoint may improve when training explores the pretrained basin more effectively. However, leaving that basin loses transfer-learning benefits and degrades ensemble quality in their analysis. The relevant distinction is therefore between broader exploration within the basin and movement outside the region that preserves useful pretrained behavior.

Building on an analysis of existing exploration methods, the authors propose StarSSE, a modification of Snapshot Ensembles for transfer learning. It produces stronger ensembles and uniform model soups, which combine model parameters through uniform averaging. The findings connect the geometry of fine-tuning to the quality of model combinations. They support carefully directed exploration of a shared initialization's basin as a way to improve combinations built from one pretrained checkpoint.
summary.tldr: StarSSE improves transfer-learning ensembles by exploring the pretrained basin while preserving the benefits of the shared checkpoint.

title: To Stay or Not to Stay in the Pre-train Basin: Insights on Ensembling in Transfer Learning

abstract: Human communication has a multi-modal and multi-affection nature. The inter-relatedness of different emotions and sentiments poses a challenge to jointly detect multiple human affections with multi-modal clues. Recent advances in this field employed multi-task learning paradigms to render the inter-relatedness across tasks, but the scarcity of publicly available resources sets a limit to the potential of works. To fill this gap, we build the first Chinese Multi-modal Multi-Affection conversation (CMMA) dataset, which contains 3,000 multi-party conversations and 21,795 multi-modal utterances collected from various styles of TV-series. CMMA contains a wide variety of affection labels, including sentiment, emotion, sarcasm and humor, as well as the novel inter-correlations values between certain pairs of tasks. Moreover, it provides the topic and speaker information in conversations, which promotes better modeling of conversational context. On the dataset, we empirically analyze the influence of different data modalities and conversational contexts on different affection analysis tasks, and exhibit the practical benefit of inter-task correlations. The full dataset will be publicly available for research\footnote{https://github.com/annoymity2022/Chinese-Dataset}

paragraphs: Understanding a conversation can involve recognizing sentiment, emotion, sarcasm, and humor together. These qualities are related, and communication supplies multiple kinds of evidence for interpreting them. CMMA addresses a resource gap for studying these relationships in Chinese conversations, where limited public datasets have constrained work on learning several affection-analysis tasks jointly.

The dataset contains 3,000 conversations involving multiple participants and 21,795 multimodal utterances drawn from television series in different styles. It includes labels for several kinds of affection, along with values describing correlations between selected task pairs. Speaker identities and conversation topics provide additional context for interpreting an utterance within the surrounding exchange.

The authors examine how different modalities and conversational context influence the individual analysis tasks. They also report practical benefits from using relationships between tasks. This makes CMMA useful for investigating both the evidence needed to interpret conversation and the connections among its emotional and expressive dimensions. The television-derived conversations establish the concrete setting represented by the benchmark.
summary.tldr: CMMA provides Chinese multimodal conversations annotated for sentiment, emotion, sarcasm, humor, and relationships between these tasks.

title: CMMA: Benchmarking Multi-Affection Detection in Chinese Multi-Modal Conversations

abstract: Protein-ligand binding prediction is a fundamental problem in AI-driven drug discovery. Previous work focused on supervised learning methods for small molecules where binding affinity data is abundant, but it is hard to apply the same strategy to other ligand classes like antibodies where labelled data is limited. In this paper, we explore unsupervised approaches and reformulate binding energy prediction as a generative modeling task. Specifically, we train an energy-based model on a set of unlabelled protein-ligand complexes using SE(3) denoising score matching (DSM) and interpret its log-likelihood as binding affinity. Our key contribution is a new equivariant rotation prediction network called Neural Euler's Rotation Equations (NERE) for SE(3) DSM. It predicts a rotation by modeling the force and torque between protein and ligand atoms, where the force is defined as the gradient of an energy function with respect to atom coordinates. Using two protein-ligand and antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction benchmarks, we show that NERE outperforms all unsupervised baselines (physics-based potentials and protein language models) in both cases and surpasses supervised baselines in the antibody case.

paragraphs: Predicting how strongly a protein binds a ligand is important for computational drug discovery. Supervised methods depend on measured affinities, which are less available for some ligand classes, including antibodies. This paper instead learns from unlabeled protein-ligand complexes by reformulating binding-energy prediction as a generative modeling problem.

The authors train an energy-based model using denoising score matching over three-dimensional rotations and translations, then interpret its log-likelihood as binding affinity. Their central component is Neural Euler's Rotation Equations, or NERE, an equivariant network for predicting rotations. It models forces and torques between protein and ligand atoms, defining force through the gradient of an energy function with respect to atomic coordinates.

Evaluations cover protein-ligand and antibody-antigen affinity prediction. NERE outperforms all compared unsupervised baselines, including physics-based potentials and protein language models, in both cases. It also surpasses the supervised baselines in the antibody setting. These results support the proposed use of unlabeled structural complexes, especially for the evaluated setting where affinity labels are limited.
summary.tldr: NERE learns binding-affinity predictions from unlabeled complexes using an energy model and force-and-torque-based rotation prediction.

title: Unsupervised Protein-Ligand Binding Energy Prediction via Neural Euler's Rotation Equation

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data is crucial for ensuring the safe deployment of machine learning models in real-world applications. However, existing OOD detection approaches primarily rely on the feature maps or the full gradient space information to derive OOD scores neglecting the role of \textbf{most important parameters} of the pre-trained network over In-Distribution data. In this study, we propose a novel approach called GradOrth to facilitate OOD detection based on one intriguing observation that the important features to identify OOD data lie in the lower-rank subspace of in-distribution (ID) data.In particular, we identify OOD data by computing the norm of gradient projection on \textit{the subspaces considered \textbf{important} for the in-distribution data}. A large orthogonal projection value (i.e. a small projection value) indicates the sample as OOD as it captures a weak correlation of the in-distribution (ID) data. This simple yet effective method exhibits outstanding performance, showcasing a notable reduction in the average false positive rate at a 95\% true positive rate (FPR95) of up to 8\% when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a model is intended to handle. GradOrth approaches this problem through a pretrained network's gradients, focusing on directions that matter for in-distribution data. Its motivation is that feature maps or the full gradient space can overlook the special role of the network parameters most important to familiar inputs.

The method builds on the observation that useful detection information lies in a lower-rank subspace associated with in-distribution data. For a candidate input, it measures the norm of the gradient's projection onto important subspaces. A small projection indicates weak alignment with the in-distribution information and provides evidence that the input may be out of distribution.

The authors report a reduction of up to 8% in average false positive rate at a 95% true positive rate compared with existing state-of-the-art methods. This supports the value of selecting relevant gradient directions for detection. The central idea is that how a gradient aligns with important familiar-data directions can be more informative than treating every gradient direction equally.
summary.tldr: GradOrth detects unfamiliar inputs by measuring how weakly their gradients project onto subspaces important for in-distribution data.

title: GradOrth: A Simple yet Efficient Out-of-Distribution Detection with Orthogonal Projection of Gradients

abstract: Valuation methods of data and machine learning (ML) models are essential to the establishment of AI marketplaces. Importantly, certain practical considerations (e.g., operational constraints, legal restrictions) favor the use of model valuation over data valuation. Also, existing marketplaces that involve trading of pre-trained ML models call for an equitable model valuation method to price them. In particular, we investigate the black-box access setting which allows querying a model (to observe predictions) without disclosing model-specific information (e.g., architecture and parameters). By exploiting a Dirichlet abstraction of a model’s predictions, we propose a novel and equitable model valuation method called model Shapley. We also leverage a Lipschitz continuity of model Shapley to design a learning approach for predicting the model Shapley values (MSVs) of many vendors’ models (e.g., 150) in a large-scale marketplace. We perform extensive empirical validation on the effectiveness of model Shapley using various real-world datasets and heterogeneous model types.

This setting matters because operational constraints and legal restrictions may favor trading and valuing models over accessing or valuing their underlying training data.

This supplies a representation through which the authors construct their equitable model valuation approach using black-box access. The contribution focuses on assigning values from observable predictive behavior, making it applicable to models whose internal details remain undisclosed.

They empirically validate the approach across real-world datasets and heterogeneous model types. The work thus addresses both the definition of model value and the scalability of estimating that value across a collection of different models.
summary.tldr: Model Shapley values pretrained models using only their predictions and learns to estimate those values across larger marketplaces.

title: Model Shapley: Equitable Model Valuation with Black-box Access

abstract: This paper delves into stochastic optimization problems that involve Markovian noise. We present a unified approach for the theoretical analysis of first-order gradient methods for stochastic optimization and variational inequalities. Our approach covers scenarios for both non-convex and strongly convex minimization problems. To achieve an optimal (linear) dependence on the mixing time of the underlying noise sequence, we use the randomized batching scheme, which is based on the multilevel Monte Carlo method. Moreover, our technique allows us to eliminate the limiting assumptions of previous research on Markov noise, such as the need for a bounded domain and uniformly bounded stochastic gradients. Our extension to variational inequalities under Markovian noise is original. Additionally, we provide lower bounds that match the oracle complexity of our method in the case of strongly convex optimization problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization often works with noisy information about how to improve an objective. This paper considers Markovian noise, where successive noise values are dependent. It develops a unified theoretical analysis of first-order gradient methods, covering both non-convex and strongly convex minimization as well as variational inequalities.

It achieves an optimal linear dependence on the noise process's mixing time, which describes how quickly dependence on earlier states fades. This makes the influence of temporal dependence explicit in the analysis. The approach also removes earlier requirements for a bounded domain and uniformly bounded stochastic gradients.

The authors extend their framework to variational inequalities under Markovian noise and establish lower bounds for strongly convex optimization. In that setting, the lower bounds match their method's oracle complexity, supporting its optimality in the analyzed sense. The result combines broader applicability with a precise account of the computational cost imposed by correlated noise.
summary.tldr: Randomized batching enables gradient-method guarantees with optimal linear dependence on Markovian mixing time and fewer restrictive assumptions.

title: First Order Methods with Markovian Noise: from Acceleration to Variational Inequalities

abstract: Simultaneous sequence generation is a pivotal task for real-time scenarios, such as streaming speech recognition, simultaneous machine translation and simultaneous speech translation, where the target sequence is generated while receiving the source sequence. The crux of achieving high-quality generation with low latency lies in identifying the optimal moments for generating, accomplished by learning a mapping between the source and target sequences. However, existing methods often rely on task-specific heuristics for different sequence types, limiting the model’s capacity to adaptively learn the source-target mapping and hindering the exploration of multi-task learning for various simultaneous tasks. In this paper, we propose a unified segment-to-segment framework (Seg2Seg) for simultaneous sequence generation, which learns the mapping in an adaptive and unified manner. During the process of simultaneous generation, the model alternates between waiting for a source segment and generating a target segment, making the segment serve as the natural bridge between the source and target. To accomplish this, Seg2Seg introduces a latent segment as the pivot between source to target and explores all potential source-target mappings via the proposed expectation training, thereby learning the optimal moments for generating. Experiments on multiple simultaneous generation tasks demonstrate that Seg2Seg achieves state-of-the-art performance and exhibits better generality across various tasks.

paragraphs: Streaming recognition and translation must begin producing output before the full input has arrived. A central decision is when enough source information has been received to generate the next output. Existing methods often encode task-specific rules for this timing, making it harder to learn source-to-target mappings consistently across different sequence types.

Seg2Seg organizes the process around segments. The model alternates between waiting for a source segment and generating a target segment, using a latent segment as the link between them. Its expectation-training procedure explores possible source–target mappings so that generation timing can be learned within the framework.

Experiments across multiple simultaneous generation tasks report state-of-the-art performance and better generality across tasks. The approach matters because output timing is part of the learned mapping, directly addressing the balance between generation quality and latency. A shared segment-based formulation also provides a common structure for tasks such as streaming speech recognition, simultaneous machine translation, and simultaneous speech translation, whose inputs and outputs otherwise differ.
summary.tldr: Seg2Seg learns when to wait and when to generate through a shared segment-based framework for streaming sequence tasks.

title: Unified Segment-to-Segment Framework for Simultaneous Sequence Generation

abstract: Normalizing flow is a class of deep generative models for efficient sampling and likelihood estimation, which achieves attractive performance, particularly in high dimensions. The flow is often implemented using a sequence of invertible residual blocks. Existing works adopt special network architectures and regularization of flow trajectories. In this paper, we develop a neural ODE flow network called JKO-iFlow, inspired by the Jordan-Kinderleherer-Otto (JKO) scheme, which unfolds the discrete-time dynamic of the Wasserstein gradient flow. The proposed method stacks residual blocks one after another, allowing efficient block-wise training of the residual blocks, avoiding sampling SDE trajectories and score matching or variational learning, thus reducing the memory load and difficulty in end-to-end training. We also develop adaptive time reparameterization of the flow network with a progressive refinement of the induced trajectory in probability space to improve the model accuracy further. Experiments with synthetic and real data show that the proposed JKO-iFlow network achieves competitive performance compared with existing flow and diffusion models at a significantly reduced computational and memory cost.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows are generative models that support sampling and likelihood estimation, often through sequences of invertible residual blocks. Training these transformations can involve architectural restrictions, trajectory regularization, and substantial memory demands. JKO-iFlow develops a neural differential-equation flow whose design is inspired by the Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto scheme for evolving probability distributions.

The method builds the network by stacking residual blocks and training them block by block. This avoids sampling stochastic differential-equation trajectories and does not require score matching or variational learning. The resulting training procedure reduces memory demands and the difficulty of training the entire flow end to end, making the organization of training central to the contribution.

The authors additionally adapt the flow's time parameterization and progressively refine its trajectory through probability space to improve accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real data show competitive performance relative to existing flow and diffusion models, with significantly lower computational and memory costs. The reported advantage is therefore a favorable combination of generative performance and training efficiency.
summary.tldr: JKO-iFlow trains generative flow networks block by block, achieving competitive reported performance with substantially lower computation and memory costs.

title: Normalizing flow neural networks by JKO scheme

abstract: Computational predictions of mass spectra from molecules have enabled the discovery of clinically relevant metabolites. However, such predictive tools are still limited as they occupy one of two extremes, either operating (a) by fragmenting molecules combinatorially with overly rigid constraints on potential rearrangements and poor time complexity or (b) by decoding lossy and nonphysical discretized spectra vectors. In this work, we use a new intermediate strategy for predicting mass spectra from molecules by treating mass spectra as sets of molecular formulae, which are themselves multisets of atoms. After first encoding an input molecular graph, we decode a set of molecular subformulae, each of which specify a predicted peak in the mass spectrum, the intensities of which are predicted by a second model. Our key insight is to overcome the combinatorial possibilities for molecular subformulae by decoding the formula set using a prefix tree structure, atom-type by atom-type, representing a general method for ordered multiset decoding. We show promising empirical results on mass spectra prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting a molecule’s mass spectrum can help identify metabolites. Existing approaches face a trade-off: explicit fragmentation can be computationally difficult and restrictive about rearrangements, while discretized spectrum vectors lose information and physical structure. This paper introduces a representation between those two approaches.

The method first encodes the molecular graph, then predicts a set of molecular subformulae. Each subformula specifies a predicted spectral peak, and a second model predicts its intensity. Because a formula records counts of atom types, the output can be treated as a collection of multisets rather than a fixed vector of spectrum bins.

To manage the many possible subformulae, decoding follows a prefix tree and proceeds one atom type at a time. Shared partial formulas organize the output possibilities into a structured decoding process. The authors report promising empirical results on spectrum-prediction tasks and present the construction as a general approach to ordered multiset decoding, extending its conceptual relevance beyond this particular output format.
summary.tldr: A prefix-tree decoder predicts molecular subformulae for spectral peaks, with a separate model estimating their intensities.

title: Prefix-Tree Decoding for Predicting Mass Spectra from Molecules

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in diffusion models, multimodal pretraining, and efficient finetuning have led to an explosion of text-to-image generative models. Given human evaluation is expensive and difficult to scale, automated methods are critical for evaluating the increasingly large number of new models. However, most current automated evaluation metrics like FID or CLIPScore only offer a distribution-level measure of image quality or image-text alignment, and are unsuited for fine-grained or instance-level analysis. In this paper, we introduce GenEval, an object-focused framework to evaluate compositional image properties such as object co-occurrence, position, count, and color. We show that current object detection models can be leveraged to evaluate text-to-image models on a variety of generation tasks with strong human agreement, and that other discriminative vision models can be linked to this pipeline to further verify properties like object color. We then evaluate several open-source text-to-image models and analyze their relative reasoning capabilities on our benchmark. We find that recent models demonstrate significant improvement on these tasks, though they are still lacking in complex capabilities such as spatial relations and attribute binding. Finally, we demonstrate how GenEval might be used to help discover existing failure modes, in order to inform development of the next generation of text-to-image models. Our code to run the GenEval framework will be made publicly available at https://github.com/djghosh13/geneval.

paragraphs: A generated image can look convincing while failing to include the objects, counts, colors, or arrangements requested in its prompt. Broad automated scores provide limited support for diagnosing such individual failures, while human evaluation is costly to scale. GenEval introduces an object-focused framework for checking specific compositional properties.

The framework uses object detectors to evaluate whether generated images satisfy requirements involving object co-occurrence, position, and count. Other discriminative vision models can be connected to the pipeline to check properties such as color. The authors show strong agreement with human judgments across a variety of generation tasks, supporting the use of these automated checks.

GenEval makes those specific shortcomings visible instead of compressing them into one broad score. The paper demonstrates how this more detailed evaluation might identify failure modes and guide development of future models.
summary.tldr: GenEval checks object-level prompt requirements and reveals persistent spatial-relation and attribute-binding weaknesses in evaluated text-to-image models.

title: GenEval: An object-focused framework for evaluating text-to-image alignment

abstract: We study a spiked Wigner problem with an inhomogeneous noise profile. Our aim in this problem is to recover the signal passed through an inhomogeneous low-rank matrix channel. While the information-theoretic performances are well-known, we focus on the algorithmic problem. First, we derive an approximate message-passing algorithm (AMP) for the inhomogeneous problem and show that its rigorous state evolution coincides with the information-theoretic optimal Bayes fixed-point equations. Second, we deduce a simple and efficient spectral method that outperforms PCA and is shown to match the information-theoretic transition.

While the information-theoretic performances are well-known, we focus on the algorithmic problem. First, we derive an approximate message-passing algorithm (AMP) for the inhomogeneous problem and show that its rigorous state evolution coincides with the information-theoretic optimal Bayes fixed-point equations. Second, we deduce a simple and efficient spectral method that outperforms PCA and is shown to match the information-theoretic transition.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal from a low-rank matrix channel whose noise profile is inhomogeneous. The recovery problem therefore includes variation in the noise rather than a uniform noise description. Although the information-theoretic performance is already understood, the authors focus on algorithms that can recover the signal efficiently.

Their first contribution is an approximate message-passing algorithm adapted to this setting. They establish a rigorous state evolution describing its behavior and show that its fixed-point equations coincide with the information-theoretically optimal Bayes equations. This connects an explicit iterative procedure to the equations governing optimal inference in the model.

The authors then derive a simple, efficient spectral method. They show that it outperforms principal component analysis and matches the information-theoretic transition. This transition result places the method's recovery threshold at the theoretical boundary identified for the problem. Together, the contributions provide both an iterative inference algorithm with rigorous characterization and a simpler spectral approach that accounts for the inhomogeneous setting.
summary.tldr: The paper derives message-passing and spectral algorithms for inhomogeneous matrix noise, with the spectral method matching the information-theoretic transition.

title: Optimal Algorithms for the Inhomogeneous Spiked Wigner Model

abstract: We introduce a decoder-decoder architecture, YOCO, for large language models, which only caches key-value pairs once. It consists of two components, i.e., a cross-decoder stacked upon a self-decoder. The self-decoder efficiently encodes global key-value (KV) caches that are reused by the cross-decoder via cross-attention. The overall model behaves like a decoder-only Transformer, although YOCO only caches once. The design substantially reduces GPU memory demands, yet retains global attention capability. Additionally, the computation flow enables prefilling to early exit without changing the final output, thereby significantly speeding up the prefill stage. Experimental results demonstrate that YOCO achieves favorable performance compared to Transformer in various settings of scaling up model size and number of training tokens. We also extend YOCO to 1M context length with near-perfect needle retrieval accuracy. The profiling results show that YOCO improves inference memory, prefill latency, and throughput by orders of magnitude across context lengths and model sizes.

paragraphs: Language models retain key-value information during generation so they can attend to previous context. YOCO redesigns how that information is produced and reused to reduce GPU memory requirements. Its decoder-decoder architecture contains a self-decoder followed by a cross-decoder, while retaining the overall behavior of a decoder-only Transformer.

The self-decoder creates a global key-value cache that the cross-decoder reuses through cross-attention. Caching only once substantially reduces memory demand while preserving global attention. The computation also allows prompt prefilling to exit early without changing the final output, accelerating the stage that processes the supplied context before generation.

Experiments show favorable performance relative to Transformers as model size and training-token counts increase. The authors extend YOCO to a context length of one million with near-perfect needle retrieval accuracy. Profiling reports orders-of-magnitude improvements in inference memory, prefill latency, and throughput across the studied settings. These findings link cache reuse to both long-context capability and substantial inference-efficiency gains.
summary.tldr: YOCO shares one global key-value cache between two decoder components, reducing inference costs while supporting million-token context retrieval.

title: You Only Cache Once: Decoder-Decoder Architectures for Language Models

abstract: Traditional long-tailed learning methods often perform poorly when dealing with inconsistencies between training and test data distributions, and they cannot flexibly adapt to different user preferences for trade-offs between head and tail classes. To address this issue, we propose a novel long-tailed learning paradigm that aims to tackle distribution shift in real-world scenarios and accommodate different user preferences for the trade-off between head and tail classes. We generate a set of diverse expert models via hypernetworks to cover all possible distribution scenarios, and optimize the model ensemble to adapt to any test distribution. Crucially, in any distribution scenario, we can flexibly output a dedicated model solution that matches the user's preference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method not only achieves higher performance ceilings but also effectively overcomes distribution shift while allowing controllable adjustments according to user preferences. We provide new insights and a paradigm for the long-tailed learning problem, greatly expanding its applicability in practical scenarios. The code can be found here: https://github.com/DataLab-atom/PRL.

paragraphs: Long-tailed learning deals with datasets in which some classes have many examples and others have few. A model trained on one balance of common and rare classes can struggle when that balance changes at test time. Users may also prefer different compromises between performance on frequent head classes and scarce tail classes.

The proposed approach uses hypernetworks to generate a collection of diverse expert models. These experts are intended to span possible distribution scenarios, and their ensemble is optimized to adapt to the test distribution. The system also produces a dedicated model solution that reflects a user's preferred balance between head and tail performance.

The experiments report higher achievable performance, effective handling of distribution shift, and controllable adjustments to user preferences. These findings support treating adaptation and user control as connected parts of long-tailed learning. The practical contribution is a framework in which the chosen solution can vary with both the data distribution and the desired class trade-off, rather than committing to a single compromise during training.
summary.tldr: Hypernetwork-generated experts let long-tailed classifiers adapt to changing class distributions and user preferences about common versus rare classes.

title: Breaking Long-Tailed Learning Bottlenecks: A Controllable Paradigm with Hypernetwork-Generated Diverse Experts

abstract: Road network representation learning aims to learn compressed and effective vectorized representations for road segments that are applicable to numerous tasks. In this paper, we identify the limitations of existing methods, particularly their overemphasis on the distance effect as outlined in the First Law of Geography. In response, we propose to endow road network representation with the principles of the recent Third Law of Geography. To this end, we propose a novel graph contrastive learning framework that employs geographic configuration-aware graph augmentation and spectral negative sampling, ensuring that road segments with similar geographic configurations yield similar representations, and vice versa, aligning with the principles stated in the Third Law. The framework further fuses the Third Law with the First Law through a dual contrastive learning objective to effectively balance the implications of both laws. We evaluate our framework on two real-world datasets across three downstream tasks. The results show that the integration of the Third Law significantly improves the performance of road segment representations in downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Road-network representation learning compresses road segments into vectors that can support downstream tasks. The authors argue that existing methods place too much emphasis on distance, following the First Law of Geography. They propose incorporating the Third Law, emphasizing similarity of geographic configuration as another basis for learning useful representations.

Their graph contrastive framework uses geographic-configuration-aware graph augmentation and spectral negative sampling. These mechanisms encourage segments with similar configurations to receive similar representations and distinguish segments with different configurations. A dual contrastive objective also incorporates the distance-based principle, allowing the representation to balance both geographic perspectives.

Evaluation uses two real-world datasets and three downstream tasks. The reported results show significant improvements when the Third Law is included. This provides empirical support for representing roads through more than their spatial proximity: similarities in geographic configuration can contribute useful information as well. The method's central contribution is a training framework that combines those two sources of structure rather than making either one the sole organizing principle.
summary.tldr: Combining geographic configuration with distance in graph contrastive learning improves road-segment representations on the evaluated downstream tasks.

title: Road Network Representation Learning with the Third Law of Geography

abstract: Fully connected Graph Transformers (GT) have rapidly become prominent in the static graph community as an alternative to Message-Passing models, which suffer from a lack of expressivity, oversquashing, and under-reaching.However, in a dynamic context, by interconnecting all nodes at multiple snapshots with self-attention,GT loose both structural and temporal information. In this work, we introduce Supra-LAplacian encoding for spatio-temporal TransformErs (SLATE), a new spatio-temporal encoding to leverage the GT architecture while keeping spatio-temporal information.Specifically, we transform Discrete Time Dynamic Graphs into multi-layer graphs and take advantage of the spectral properties of their associated supra-Laplacian matrix.Our second contribution explicitly model nodes' pairwise relationships with a cross-attention mechanism, providing an accurate edge representation for dynamic link prediction.SLATE outperforms numerous state-of-the-art methods based on Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks combined with recurrent models (e.g, LSTM), and Dynamic Graph Transformers,on~9 datasets. Code is open-source and available at this link https://github.com/ykrmm/SLATE.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers allow broad interactions among nodes, but applying full attention across multiple graph snapshots can lose information about graph structure and time. SLATE addresses this problem by supplying an encoding that preserves both kinds of context. Its aim is to retain the advantages of Transformer attention while representing how the graph is organized and changes.

The method turns a discrete-time dynamic graph into a multilayer graph. It then uses spectral properties of the associated supra-Laplacian matrix to construct the spatiotemporal encoding. This places structural and temporal information into the representation supplied to the Transformer, helping distinguish relationships that unrestricted attention alone would not preserve.

SLATE also uses cross-attention to model relationships between pairs of nodes explicitly, producing edge representations for dynamic link prediction. Across nine datasets, it outperforms numerous leading methods, including message-passing graph networks combined with recurrent models and dynamic graph Transformers. These findings support the combined use of spatiotemporal encoding and explicit pairwise modeling for predicting links in changing graphs.
summary.tldr: SLATE preserves graph structure and time through supra-Laplacian encodings and models node pairs explicitly for dynamic link prediction.

title: Supra-Laplacian Encoding for Transformer on Dynamic Graphs

abstract: This paper considers the problem for finding the $(\delta,\epsilon)$-Goldstein stationary point of Lipschitz continuous objective, which is a rich function class to cover a great number of important applications. We construct a novel zeroth-order quantum estimator for the gradient of the smoothed surrogate. Based on such estimator, we propose a novel quantum algorithm that achieves a query complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{3/2}\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ on the stochastic function value oracle, where $d$ is the dimension of the problem. We also enhance the query complexity to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{3/2}\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-7/3})$ by introducing a variance reduction variant. Our findings demonstrate the clear advantages of utilizing quantum techniques for non-convex non-smooth optimization, as they outperform the optimal classical methods on the dependency of $\epsilon$ by a factor of $\epsilon^{-2/3}$.

Its target is a (δ, ε)-Goldstein stationary point, an approximate stationarity criterion suited to this setting. The claimed result concerns reaching that criterion efficiently through function-value queries, rather than establishing a globally optimal solution.
