paragraphs: Neural population activity changes across time, trials, and experimental conditions, making a single description of its dynamics difficult. Conditionally Linear Dynamical Systems, or CLDS, address this by allowing the dynamics to depend nonlinearly on task and behavioral variables. Once those variables are specified, the activity is described through linear dynamics.

Gaussian process priors govern how the dynamics vary with these variables. This combines flexibility across conditions with a linear model within a given condition, supporting transparent interpretation and tractable Bayesian inference. Nearby task conditions can share statistical information, so each condition does not have to supply enough observations to support an entirely separate model.

The authors find that CLDS can work well even with severely limited data, including one trial per condition. They attribute this to the Bayesian formulation and information sharing across nearby conditions. Example applications examine heading-direction encoding in thalamic neurons and motor cortical activity during cued reaching. These cases illustrate how nonlinear, condition-dependent neural activity can be studied through a collection of related linear descriptions.
summary.tldr: CLDS models nonlinear changes in neural dynamics across conditions while retaining interpretable linear dynamics within each condition.

title: Modeling Neural Activity with Conditionally Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: We argue that diffusion models' success in modeling complex distributions is, for the most part, coming from their conditioning. This paper investigates the representation used to condition diffusion models from the perspective that ideal representations should improve modeling the data distribution, be easy to generate, and be compositional to allow generalizing outside the training distribution. We introduce Discrete Latent Code (DLC), an image representation derived from Simplicial Embeddings trained with a self-supervised learning objective. DLCs are sequences of discrete tokens, as opposed to the standard continuous image embeddings. They are easy to generate and their compositionality enables sampling of novel images beyond the training distribution. Diffusion models trained with DLCs improve generation fidelity, establishing a new state-of-the-art for unconditional image generation on ImageNet. Additionally, we show that composing DLCs allows the image generator to produce interesting out-of-distribution samples that coherently combine the semantics of images in diverse ways. Finally, we showcase how DLCs can enable text-to-image generation by leveraging large-scale pretrained language models. Using only 9M image-caption pairs, we efficiently finetune a text diffusion model to generate novel DLCs that produces samples outside of the data distribution used to train the image generator.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the representation conditioning a diffusion model affects what it can generate. The authors argue that conditioning explains much of diffusion models' success, and seek representations that support accurate image modeling, are easy to generate, and can be recombined to create images beyond the training distribution.

Their Discrete Latent Code, or DLC, represents an image as a sequence of discrete tokens derived from self-supervised Simplicial Embeddings. These codes replace the usual continuous image embeddings as conditioning information. Their compositional structure allows codes to be combined so that a generator can bring together semantic content from different images.

For text-to-image generation, they use pretrained language models and fine-tune a text diffusion model on 9 million image-caption pairs to generate DLCs. This shows how a shared discrete representation can connect text-driven code generation with an image generator.
summary.tldr: Discrete Latent Codes improve diffusion image generation and enable semantic combinations beyond the image generator's training distribution.

title: Compositional Discrete Latent Code for High Fidelity, Productive Diffusion Models

abstract: Model merging provides a scalable alternative to multi-task training by combining specialized finetuned models through parameter arithmetic, enabling efficient deployment without the need for joint training or access to all task data. While recent methods have shown promise, existing evaluations are limited in both model scale and task diversity, leaving open questions about their applicability to large, domain-specialized LLMs. To tackle the challenges, we introduce MergeBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite designed to assess model merging at scale. MergeBench builds on state-of-the-art open-source language models, including Llama and Gemma families at 2B to 9B scales, and covers five key domains: instruction following, mathematics, multilingual understanding, coding and safety. We standardize finetuning and evaluation protocols, and assess eight representative merging methods across multi-task performance, forgetting and runtime efficiency. Based on extensive experiments, we provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and share insights showing that model merging tends to perform better on stronger base models, with techniques such as merging coefficient tuning and sparsification improving knowledge retention. However, several challenges remain, including the computational cost on large models, the gap for in-domain performance compared to multi-task models, and the underexplored role of model merging in standard LLM training pipelines. We hope MergeBench provides a foundation for future research to advance the understanding and practical application of model merging.

title: MergeBench: A Benchmark for Merging Domain-Specialized LLMs

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated impressive performance in novel view synthesis under dense-view settings. However, in sparse-view scenarios, despite the realistic renderings in training views, 3DGS occasionally manifests appearance artifacts in novel views. This paper investigates the appearance artifacts in sparse-view 3DGS and uncovers a core limitation of current approaches: the optimized Gaussians are overly-entangled with one another to aggressively fit the training views, which leads to a neglect of the real appearance distribution of the underlying scene and results in appearance artifacts in novel views. The analysis is based on a proposed metric, termed Co-Adaptation Score (CA), which quantifies the entanglement among Gaussians, i.e., co-adaptation, by computing the pixel-wise variance across multiple renderings of the same viewpoint, with different random subsets of Gaussians. The analysis reveals that the degree of co-adaptation is naturally alleviated as the number of training views increases. Based on the analysis, we propose two lightweight strategies to explicitly mitigate the co-adaptation in sparse-view 3DGS: (1) random gaussian dropout; (2) multiplicative noise injection to the opacity. Both strategies are designed to be plug-and-play, and their effectiveness is validated across various methods and benchmarks. We hope that our insights into the co-adaptation effect will inspire the community to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of sparse-view 3DGS.

paragraphs: With only a few training views, 3D Gaussian Splatting can reproduce observed images convincingly yet show artifacts from new viewpoints. This paper investigates excessive dependence among the optimized Gaussians as a source of that behavior. The authors argue that tightly coordinated fitting to training images can neglect the scene's underlying appearance distribution.

They introduce a Co-Adaptation Score to quantify this dependence. The score measures pixel-wise variance across renderings of the same viewpoint made with different random subsets of Gaussians. This provides a way to study how rendering depends on combinations of components. Their analysis finds that co-adaptation naturally decreases as more training views become available.

Based on this diagnosis, the authors propose randomly dropping Gaussians and injecting multiplicative noise into opacity. Both lightweight interventions are designed to reduce co-adaptation and integrate with existing methods. Experiments across multiple methods and benchmarks validate their effectiveness. The contribution links a measurable internal property of the representation to sparse-view artifacts and supplies two practical ways to address it.
summary.tldr: A new co-adaptation measure links sparse-view Gaussian-splatting artifacts to entangled components and motivates effective dropout and opacity-noise interventions.

title: Quantifying and Alleviating Co-Adaptation in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a high-fidelity and efficient paradigm for online free-viewpoint video (FVV) reconstruction, offering viewers rapid responsiveness and immersive experiences. However, existing online methods face challenge in prohibitive storage requirements primarily due to point-wise modeling that fails to exploit the motion properties. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Compact Gaussian Streaming (ComGS) framework, leveraging the locality and consistency of motion in dynamic scene, that models object-consistent Gaussian point motion through keypoint-driven motion representation. By transmitting only the keypoint attributes, this framework provides a more storage-efficient solution. Specifically, we first identify a sparse set of motion-sensitive keypoints localized within motion regions using a viewspace gradient difference strategy. Equipped with these keypoints, we propose an adaptive motion-driven mechanism that predicts a spatial influence field for propagating keypoint motion to neighboring Gaussian points with similar motion. Moreover, ComGS adopts an error-aware correction strategy for key frame reconstruction that selectively refines erroneous regions and mitigates error accumulation without unnecessary overhead. Overall, ComGS achieves a remarkable storage reduction of over 159 × compared to 3DGStream and 14 × compared to the SOTA method QUEEN, while maintaining competitive visual fidelity and rendering speed. Project page: https://chenjiacong-1005.github.io/ComGS/.

The paper argues that representing motion point by point misses an opportunity: neighboring points on a moving object often move consistently. ComGS uses a sparse set of keypoints to represent that shared motion more compactly.

A viewspace gradient difference strategy identifies motion-sensitive keypoints within moving regions. The method then predicts a spatial influence field that propagates each keypoint’s motion to neighboring Gaussian points with similar movement. Transmitting keypoint attributes provides a smaller representation of the scene’s motion. An error-aware correction mechanism selectively refines inaccurate regions during key-frame reconstruction to reduce accumulated errors.

The reported results show storage reductions of over 159 times relative to 3DGStream and 14 times relative to QUEEN, while retaining competitive visual fidelity and rendering speed. These findings support exploiting local motion consistency as a way to compress dynamic Gaussian representations without giving up the responsiveness sought in free-viewpoint video.
summary.tldr: ComGS represents shared Gaussian-point motion through sparse keypoints, sharply reducing video storage while maintaining competitive rendering quality and speed.

title: Motion Matters: Compact Gaussian Streaming for Free-Viewpoint Video Reconstruction

abstract: Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) has successfully integrated mechanistic understanding into machine learning, particularly in domains governed by well-known physical laws.This success has motivated efforts to apply PIML to biology, a field rich in dynamical systems but shaped by different constraints.Biological modeling, however, presents unique challenges: multi-faceted and uncertain prior knowledge, heterogeneous and noisy data, partial observability, and complex, high-dimensional networks.\textbf{In this position paper, we argue that these challenges should not be seen as obstacles to PIML, but as catalysts for its evolution. We propose Biology-Informed Machine Learning (BIML): a principled extension of PIML that retains its structural grounding while adapting to the practical realities of biology.}Rather than replacing PIML, BIML retools its methods to operate under softer, probabilistic forms of prior knowledge.We outline four foundational pillars as a roadmap for this transition: uncertainty quantification, contextualization, constrained latent structure inference, and scalability.Foundation Models and Large Language Models will be key enablers, bridging human expertise with computational modeling.We conclude with concrete recommendations to build the BIML ecosystem and channel PIML-inspired innovation toward challenges of high scientific and societal relevance.

paragraphs: Physics-informed machine learning incorporates mechanistic knowledge into learned models, with successes in settings governed by well-understood physical laws. This position paper argues that biology calls for an evolution of that approach. Biological knowledge can be uncertain and multifaceted, while observations are noisy, heterogeneous, and incomplete.

The proposed Biology-Informed Machine Learning retains structural guidance but allows prior knowledge to take softer, probabilistic forms. The authors organize their roadmap around four pillars: uncertainty quantification, contextualization, constrained inference of latent structure, and scalability. Together, these address how models represent uncertainty, account for context, infer hidden organization, and handle complex biological networks.

The paper presents foundation models and large language models as prospective enablers for connecting human expertise with computational modeling. It also outlines recommendations for developing a BIML ecosystem. Its contribution is a research position and roadmap: biological difficulties are presented as opportunities to extend physics-informed methods toward settings where mechanistic knowledge cannot always be treated as precise or fully observed.
summary.tldr: This position paper proposes biology-informed machine learning that combines structural guidance with uncertain, contextual, and incomplete biological knowledge.

title: Position: Biology is the Challenge Physics-Informed ML Needs to Evolve

abstract: Most counterfactual inference frameworks traditionally assume acyclic structural causal models (SCMs), i.e. directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). However, many real-world systems (e.g. biological systems) contain feedback loops or cyclic dependencies that violate acyclicity. In this work, we study counterfactual inference in cyclic SCMs under shift–scale interventions, i.e., soft, policy-style changes that rescale and/or shift a variable’s mechanism.

However, many real-world systems (e.g. biological systems) contain feedback loops or cyclic dependencies that violate acyclicity. In this work, we study counterfactual inference in cyclic SCMs under shift–scale interventions, i.e., soft, policy-style changes that rescale and/or shift a variable’s mechanism.

paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks how an outcome would differ under a change to the system that produced it. This paper studies that question for structural causal models containing cycles. Its motivation is that many real systems, including biological systems, have feedback loops, whereas most counterfactual frameworks traditionally assume an acyclic structure.

The distinction matters because an acyclic graph rules out a chain of dependencies that returns to its starting point. A cyclic model allows that feedback structure. The paper therefore places counterfactual questions in a setting where dependencies need not follow a one-way ordering, bringing the modeling setup closer to the feedback systems highlighted in the abstract.

Within this setting, the work considers shift–scale interventions: soft, policy-style changes that shift or rescale a variable’s mechanism, or do both. The stated contribution is the study of counterfactual inference under this combination of cyclic dependencies and mechanism adjustments. It broadens the problem setting beyond acyclic models to examine changes within systems that contain feedback.
summary.tldr: The paper studies counterfactual inference in causal systems with feedback loops under interventions that shift or rescale variable mechanisms.

title: Cyclic Counterfactuals under Shift–Scale Interventions

abstract: Generative models trained on natural sequences are increasingly used to predict the effects of genetic variation, enabling progress in therapeutic design, disease risk prediction, and synthetic biology. In the zero-shot setting, variant impact is estimated by comparing the likelihoods of sequences, under the assumption that likelihood serves as a proxy for fitness. However, this assumption often breaks down in practice: sequence likelihood reflects not only evolutionary fitness constraints, but also phylogenetic structure and sampling biases, especially as model capacity increases. We introduce Likelihood-Fitness Bridging (LFB), a simple and general strategy that improves variant effect prediction by averaging model scores across sequences subject to similar selective pressures. Assuming an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model of evolution, LFB can be viewed as a way to marginalize the effects of genetic drift, although its benefits appear to extend more broadly. LFB applies to existing protein and genomic language models without requiring retraining, and incurs only modest computational overhead. Evaluated on large-scale deep mutational scans and clinical benchmarks, LFB consistently improves predictive performance across model families and sizes. Notably, it reverses the performance plateau observed in larger protein language models, making the largest models the most accurate when combined with LFB. These results suggest that accounting for phylogenetic and sampling biases is essential to realizing the full potential of large sequence models in variant effect prediction.

paragraphs: Sequence language models often predict a genetic variant's effect by comparing how likely different sequences are. This treats likelihood as a proxy for biological fitness. The paper explains why that proxy can fail: likelihood also reflects evolutionary ancestry and which sequences were sampled, with these influences becoming especially consequential as model capacity grows.

Likelihood-Fitness Bridging averages model scores across sequences exposed to similar selective pressures. It works with existing protein and genomic language models without retraining and adds modest computation. Under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model of evolution, the averaging can be interpreted as marginalizing genetic drift; the authors report benefits that appear to extend beyond that modeling assumption.

Across large-scale mutational scans and clinical benchmarks, the method consistently improves prediction for different model families and sizes. It also reverses the observed plateau in larger protein models, making the largest models most accurate when combined with the method. These findings suggest that correcting ancestry and sampling effects can help translate additional modeling capacity into better variant predictions.
summary.tldr: Likelihood-Fitness Bridging improves genetic variant predictions by averaging sequence-model scores across sequences under similar selective pressures.

title: From Likelihood to Fitness: Improving Variant Effect Prediction in Protein and Genome Language Models

abstract: Seeking high-quality representations with latent variable models (LVMs) to reveal the intrinsic correlation between neural activity and behavior or sensory stimuli has attracted much interest. In the study of the biological visual system, naturalistic visual stimuli are inherently high-dimensional and time-dependent, leading to intricate dynamics within visual neural activity. However, most work on LVMs has not explicitly considered neural temporal relationships. To cope with such conditions, we propose Time-Evolving Visual Dynamical System (TE-ViDS), a sequential LVM that decomposes neural activity into low-dimensional latent representations that evolve over time. To better align the model with the characteristics of visual neural activity, we split latent representations into two parts and apply contrastive learning to shape them. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets and real neural datasets from the mouse visual cortex demonstrate that TE-ViDS achieves the best decoding performance on naturalistic scenes/movies, extracts interpretable latent trajectories that uncover clear underlying neural dynamics, and provides new insights into differences in visual information processing between subjects and between cortical regions. In summary, TE-ViDS is markedly competent in extracting stimulus-relevant embeddings from visual neural activity and contributes to the understanding of visual processing mechanisms. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Grasshlw/Time-Evolving-Visual-Dynamical-System.

paragraphs: Natural scenes and movies create complex patterns of activity in the visual brain. Those patterns change over time, so a useful compact representation needs to account for temporal relationships. This paper introduces TE-ViDS, a sequential latent-variable model designed to extract such representations from visual neural activity.

TE-ViDS maps neural recordings into low-dimensional latent states that evolve over time. It divides those states into two parts and uses contrastive learning to shape their representations. abstract: Retrosynthesis planning aims to decompose target molecules into available building blocks, forming a synthetic tree where each internal node represents an intermediate compound and each leaf ideally corresponds to a purchasable reactant. However, this tree becomes invalid if any leaf node is not a valid building block, making the planning process vulnerable to the "weakest link" in the synthetic route. Existing methods often optimise for average performance across branches, failing to account for this worst-case sensitivity. In this paper, we reframe retrosynthesis as a worst-path optimisation problem within tree-structured Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We prove that this formulation admits a unique optimal solution and provides monotonic improvement guarantees. Building on this insight, we introduce Interactive Retrosynthesis Planning (InterRetro), a method that interacts with the tree MDP, learns a value function for worst-path outcomes, and improves its policy through self-imitation, preferentially reinforcing past decisions with high estimated advantage. Empirically, InterRetro achieves state-of-the-art results — solving 100\% of targets on the Retro*-190 benchmark, shortening synthetic routes by 4.9\%, and achieving promising performance using only 10\% of the training data.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis plans how to build a target molecule by working backward toward available starting materials. The plan forms a tree, and every terminal branch must reach a valid building block. A single unresolved branch invalidates the whole route, making average performance across branches an incomplete guide to planning quality.

The authors formulate this weakest-link problem as worst-path optimization in a tree-structured Markov decision process. These findings support aligning the learning objective with the branch that can cause an entire plan to fail. The complete success result applies to the named benchmark, while the theoretical guarantees concern the proposed optimization formulation.
summary.tldr: InterRetro improves retrosynthesis planning by optimizing the weakest branch of a synthesis tree and reinforcing successful past decisions.

title: Retrosynthesis Planning via Worst-path Policy Optimisation in Tree-structured MDPs

abstract: Evolutionary multi-view classification (EMVC) methods have gained wide recognition due to their adaptive mechanisms. Fitness evaluation (FE), which aims to calculate the classification performance of each individual in the population and provide reliable performance ranking for subsequent operations, is a core step in such methods. Its accuracy directly determines the correctness of the evolutionary direction. That is, when FE fails to correctly reflect the superiority-inferiority relationship among individuals, it will lead to confusion in individual performance ranking, which in turn misleads the evolutionary direction and results in trapping into local optima. This paper is the first to identify the aforementioned issue in the field of EMVC and call it as fitness evaluation bias (FEB). FEB may be caused by a variety of factors, and this paper approaches the issue from the perspective of view information content: existing methods generally adopt joint training strategies, which restrict the exploration of key information in views with low information content. This makes it difficult for multi-view model (MVM) to achieve optimal performance during convergence, which in turn leads to FE failing to accurately reflect individual performance rankings and ultimately triggering FEB. To address this issue, we propose an evolutionary multi-view classification via eliminating individual fitness bias (EFB-EMVC) method, which alleviates the FEB issue by introducing evolutionary navigators for each MVM, thereby providing more accurate individual ranking. Experimental results fully verify the effectiveness of the proposed method in alleviating the FEB problem, and the EMVC method equipped with this strategy exhibits more superior performance compared with the original EMVC method. (The code is available at https://github.com/LiShuailzn/Neurips-2025-EFB-EMVC)

paragraphs: Evolutionary multi-view classification relies on ranking candidate models so that later search steps favor better candidates. If the fitness evaluation misrepresents their relative quality, the search can move in an unhelpful direction and become trapped in local optima. This paper names that problem fitness evaluation bias and examines one source of it.

The proposed explanation concerns differences in information content across views. Joint training can restrict the discovery of useful signals in views that contain less information. A multi-view model may consequently converge below its potential, causing its measured fitness to misrepresent how it compares with other candidates. The issue therefore affects both individual model learning and the evolutionary decisions based on that learning.

EFB-EMVC introduces evolutionary navigators for each multi-view model to alleviate this bias and produce more accurate rankings. Experiments show that the strategy reduces the identified problem and improves performance relative to the original evolutionary method. The contribution highlights evaluation quality as an active part of evolutionary search: improving how candidates are judged can improve the direction of the search itself.
summary.tldr: EFB-EMVC improves evolutionary multi-view classification by reducing fitness-ranking bias associated with uneven learning across views.

title: Improving Evolutionary Multi-View Classification via Eliminating Individual Fitness Bias

abstract: Subject-to-Video (S2V) generation aims to create videos that faithfully incorporate reference content, providing enhanced flexibility in the production of videos. To establish the infrastructure for S2V generation, we propose **OpenS2V-Nexus**, consisting of (i) **OpenS2V‑Eval**, a fine‑grained benchmark, and (ii) **OpenS2V‑5M**, a million‑scale dataset.In contrast to existing S2V benchmarks inherited from VBench that focus on global and coarse-grained assessment of generated videos, *OpenS2V-Eval* focuses on the model's ability to generate subject-consistent videos with natural subject appearance and identity fidelity. For these purposes, *OpenS2V-Eval* introduces 180 prompts from seven major categories of S2V, which incorporate both real and synthetic test data. Furthermore, to accurately align human preferences with S2V benchmarks, we propose three automatic metrics, NexusScore, NaturalScore and GmeScore, to separately quantify subject consistency, naturalness, and text relevance in generated videos. Building on this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 18 representative S2V models, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses across different content. Moreover, we create the first open-source large-scale S2V generation dataset *OpenS2V-5M*, which consists of five million high-quality 720P subject-text-video triplets. Specifically, we ensure subject‐information diversity in our dataset by (1) segmenting subjects and building pairing information via cross‐video associations and (2) prompting GPT-4o on raw frames to synthesize multi-view representations. Through *OpenS2V-Nexus*, we deliver a robust infrastructure to accelerate future S2V generation research.

paragraphs: Subject-to-video generation creates videos that incorporate reference content faithfully. Evaluating these systems requires attention to whether the subject retains its identity and appears natural, beyond broad judgments about overall video quality. OpenS2V-Nexus provides two resources for this problem: a detailed evaluation benchmark and a large dataset for generation research.

OpenS2V-Eval contains 180 prompts spanning seven major subject-to-video categories, with both real and synthetic test data. Three proposed metrics separately assess subject consistency, naturalness, and relevance to the text. The authors use the benchmark to evaluate 18 representative models, examining how their strengths and weaknesses vary across content.

OpenS2V-5M supplies five million subject-text-video triplets at 720P resolution. Its construction uses subject segmentation, associations across videos, and GPT-4o prompting on raw frames to synthesize multiple views and diversify subject information. Together, the resources connect more specific evaluation criteria with large-scale training material. The contribution is infrastructure for studying reference fidelity and generation quality rather than a single new video-generation model.
summary.tldr: OpenS2V-Nexus provides a detailed subject-to-video benchmark and five million training triplets focused on reference fidelity, naturalness, and text relevance.

title: OpenS2V-Nexus: A Detailed Benchmark and Million-Scale Dataset for Subject-to-Video Generation

abstract: Eliciting reliable human feedback is essential for many machine learning tasks, such as learning from noisy labels and aligning AI systems with human preferences. Peer prediction mechanisms incentivize truthful reporting without ground truth verification by scoring agents based on correlations with peers. Traditional mechanisms, which ensure that truth-telling maximizes the \textbf{expected scores} in equilibrium, can elicit honest information while assuming agents' utilities are \textbf{linear functions} of their scores. However, in practice, non-linear payment rules are usually preferred, or agents' utilities are inherently non-linear. We propose \emph{stochastically dominant truthfulness (SD-truthfulness)} as a stronger guarantee: the score distribution of truth-telling stochastically dominates all other strategies, incentivizing truthful reporting for a wide range of monotone utility functions. Our first observation is that no existing peer prediction mechanism naturally satisfies this criterion without strong assumptions. A simple solution - rounding scores into binary lotteries — can enforce SD-truthfulness, but often degrades \emph{sensitivity}, a key property related to fairness and statistical efficiency. We demonstrate how a more careful application of rounding can better preserve sensitivity. Furthermore, we introduce a new enforced agreement (EA) mechanism that is theoretically guaranteed to be SD-truthful in binary-signal settings and, under mild assumptions, empirically achieves the highest sensitivity among all known SD-truthful mechanisms.

paragraphs: Peer prediction encourages honest feedback by comparing participants' reports with those of their peers when ground truth cannot be checked. Traditional guarantees make honesty maximize expected scores in equilibrium. Those guarantees fit linear utility, but nonlinear payment rules or personal preferences can change how participants value the same score distribution.

The paper proposes stochastically dominant truthfulness, requiring the distribution of honest-reporting scores to dominate those from alternative strategies. This supports honesty for a broad range of monotone utility functions. Converting scores into binary lotteries can enforce the property, but often weakens sensitivity, which matters for fairness and statistical efficiency. The authors show how more careful rounding better preserves that sensitivity.

They also introduce an enforced agreement mechanism with a theoretical guarantee of this stronger truthfulness in binary-signal settings. Under mild assumptions, it empirically achieves the highest sensitivity among known mechanisms satisfying the criterion. The work separates the strength of an honesty guarantee from the sensitivity of the scoring system, then develops mechanisms intended to achieve both.
summary.tldr: The paper develops stronger peer-prediction incentives that support honest reporting under nonlinear utilities while better preserving score sensitivity.

title: Stochastically Dominant Peer Prediction

abstract: In studies of transferable learning, scaling laws are obtained for various important foundation models to predict their properties and performance at larger scales. Taking language-vision learning as example, we show here how scaling law derivation can also be used for model and dataset comparison, allowing to decide which procedure is to be preferred for pre-training. Full scaling laws based on dense measurements across a wide span of model and samples seen scales are derived for two important language-vision learning procedures, CLIP and MaMMUT, that use either contrastive only or contrastive and captioning text generative loss. For the first time, we use derived scaling laws to compare both models and three open datasets, DataComp-1.4B, Re-LAION-1.4B and DFN-1.4B, while ensuring sufficient prediction accuracy on held out points. From comparison, we obtain evidence for (i) MaMMUT's stronger improvement with scale and better sample efficiency than standard CLIP (ii) DFN-1.4B outperforming other open datasets. To strengthen validity of the comparison, we show scaling laws for various downstream tasks, classification, retrieval, and segmentation, observing consistently the same scaling trends for models and datasets across tasks. We show that comparison can also be performed when deriving scaling laws with a constant learning rate schedule, reducing compute cost. Accurate derivation of scaling laws provides thus means to perform model and dataset comparison on aligned common compute axis across large scale span, avoiding misleading conclusions based on measurements from few isolated single reference scales only. This paves road for guided collective improvement of open foundation models and training datasets, as scaling law based comparisons from various studies executed in common frame can be combined to identify overall better procedures. We release all the pre-trained models with their intermediate checkpoints, including openMaMMUT-L/14, which achieves 80.3% zero-shot ImageNet-1k accuracy, trained on 12.8B samples from DataComp-1.4B. Code for reproducing experiments in the paper and raw experiments data can be found at https://github.com/LAION-AI/scaling-laws-for-comparison.

abstract: Let X denote the feature and Y the target. We consider domain adaptation under three possible scenarios: (1) the marginal P_Y changes, while the conditional P_X|Y stays the same (\it target shift), (2) the marginal P_Y is fixed, while the conditional P_X|Y changes with certain constraints (\it conditional shift), and (3) the marginal P_Y changes, and the conditional P_X|Y changes with constraints (\it generalized target shift). Using background knowledge, causal interpretations allow us to determine the correct situation for a problem at hand. We exploit importance reweighting or sample transformation to find the learning machine that works well on test data, and propose to estimate the weights or transformations by \it reweighting or transforming training data to reproduce the covariate distribution on the test domain. Thanks to kernel embedding of conditional as well as marginal distributions, the proposed approaches avoid distribution estimation, and are applicable for high-dimensional problems. Numerical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation requires understanding how training and test distributions differ. This paper separates three possibilities using features X and targets Y. Target shift changes the distribution of Y while preserving the distribution of X given Y. Conditional shift preserves the target distribution but changes the conditional distribution under constraints. Generalized target shift permits both kinds of change, again constraining the conditional change.

The authors use causal interpretations and background knowledge to determine which situation fits a problem. They then adapt learning through importance reweighting or transformations of the samples. The weights or transformations are estimated by making the adjusted training data reproduce the feature distribution observed in the test domain.

Kernel embeddings represent both conditional and marginal distributions, allowing the methods to avoid explicit distribution estimation. This makes the proposed approaches applicable to high-dimensional problems. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Its central contribution is to connect different assumptions about distribution change with corresponding ways to adjust training data.
summary.tldr: A domain adaptation framework uses shift-specific assumptions, reweighting or sample transformations, and kernel embeddings to match training data to the test domain.

title: Domain Adaptation under Target and Conditional Shift

abstract: We initiate the study of fairness in reinforcement learning, where the actions of a learning algorithm may affect its environment and future rewards. Our fairness constraint requires that an algorithm never prefers one action over another if the long-term (discounted) reward of choosing the latter action is higher. Our first result is negative: despite the fact that fairness is consistent with the optimal policy, any learning algorithm satisfying fairness must take time exponential in the number of states to achieve non-trivial approximation to the optimal policy. We then provide a provably fair polynomial time algorithm under an approximate notion of fairness, thus establishing an exponential gap between exact and approximate fairness.

Our fairness constraint requires that an algorithm never prefers one action over another if the long-term (discounted) reward of choosing the latter action is higher. Our first result is negative: despite the fact that fairness is consistent with the optimal policy, any learning algorithm satisfying fairness must take time exponential in the number of states to achieve non-trivial approximation to the optimal policy. We then provide a provably fair polynomial time algorithm under an approximate notion of fairness, thus establishing an exponential gap between exact and approximate fairness.

paragraphs: The paper studies a fairness requirement for reinforcement learning, where an action can change both the environment and future rewards. Its definition says that a learning algorithm must never favor one action over another when the latter has greater long-term discounted reward. Fairness is therefore tied to the actions' future value.

An optimal policy is compatible with this requirement, but learning under it can be difficult. The authors prove that any algorithm satisfying exact fairness must take time exponential in the number of states to obtain a nontrivial approximation to the optimal policy. Compatibility with the eventual best behavior does not by itself make the learning process efficient.

The paper then relaxes the requirement to an approximate notion of fairness and provides a polynomial-time algorithm that is provably fair under that definition. This establishes an exponential separation between exact and approximate fairness. The finding identifies a consequential tradeoff in the stated framework: how strictly fairness is required during learning can fundamentally change the time needed to learn useful behavior.
summary.tldr: Exact reward-based fairness can make reinforcement learning exponentially slow, while an approximate fairness requirement permits polynomial-time learning.

title: Fairness in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite the success of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for image generation, the trade-off between visual quality and image diversity remains a significant issue. This paper achieves both aims simultaneously by improving the stability of training GANs. The key idea of the proposed approach is to implicitly regularize the discriminator using representative features. Focusing on the fact that standard GAN minimizes reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, we transfer the representative feature, which is extracted from the data distribution using a pre-trained autoencoder (AE), to the discriminator of standard GANs. Because the AE learns to minimize forward KL divergence, our GAN training with representative features is influenced by both reverse and forward KL divergence. Consequently, the proposed approach is verified to improve visual quality and diversity of state of the art GANs using extensive evaluations.

paragraphs: Generating images that are both visually convincing and diverse remains a challenge for generative adversarial networks. This paper addresses those goals by improving training stability. Its central intervention is to give the discriminator representative features learned from the data distribution, using those features as a form of implicit regularization.

A pretrained autoencoder supplies the representative features, which are transferred to a standard GAN's discriminator. The paper explains this design through two directions of Kullback-Leibler divergence. In the authors' account, standard GAN training minimizes reverse KL divergence, while the autoencoder learns through forward KL divergence. Transferring its features brings influences from both into GAN training.

Extensive evaluations report improvements in both visual quality and diversity for the evaluated state-of-the-art GANs. The result supports using an additional learned representation to shape discriminator behavior and stabilize adversarial training. The paper's proposed mechanism ties the feature transfer to complementary distribution-matching influences, connecting its training modification to the two image-generation objectives it seeks to improve.
summary.tldr: Transferring pretrained autoencoder features to GAN discriminators stabilizes training and improves image quality and diversity in the reported evaluations.

title: Improved Training of Generative Adversarial Networks Using Representative Features

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning algorithms that estimate state and state-action value functions have been shown to be effective in a variety of challenging domains, including learning control strategies from raw image pixels. However, algorithms that estimate state and state-action value functions typically assume a fully observed state and must compensate for partial observations by using finite length observation histories or recurrent networks. In this work, we propose a new deep reinforcement learning algorithm based on counterfactual regret minimization that iteratively updates an approximation to an advantage-like function and is robust to partially observed state. We demonstrate that this new algorithm can substantially outperform strong baseline methods on several partially observed reinforcement learning tasks: learning first-person 3D navigation in Doom and Minecraft, and acting in the presence of partially observed objects in Doom and Pong.

In this work, we propose a new deep reinforcement learning algorithm based on counterfactual regret minimization that iteratively updates an approximation to an advantage-like function and is robust to partially observed state. We demonstrate that this new algorithm can substantially outperform strong baseline methods on several partially observed reinforcement learning tasks: learning first-person 3D navigation in Doom and Minecraft, and acting in the presence of partially observed objects in Doom and Pong.

paragraphs: An agent often has to act without seeing the complete state of its environment. The paper notes that reinforcement-learning algorithms based on state or state-action values typically assume full observation, then compensate for missing information using short observation histories or recurrent networks. It proposes a different learning algorithm designed to be robust to partial observation.

The method builds on counterfactual regret minimization. It repeatedly updates an approximation to an advantage-like function, making that quantity central to learning. This changes the object the algorithm learns compared with approaches organized around estimates of state and state-action value functions, directly addressing the setting in which the agent's observations leave part of the state hidden.

Experiments cover first-person three-dimensional navigation in Doom and Minecraft, along with tasks involving partially observed objects in Doom and Pong. The authors demonstrate that the algorithm can substantially outperform strong baselines on several such tasks. These results provide empirical evidence that regret-based learning can be effective across different forms of incomplete observation in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: A deep reinforcement-learning algorithm based on counterfactual regret minimization substantially outperforms strong baselines on several partially observed tasks.

title: Regret Minimization for Partially Observable Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Theory of mind (ToM) broadly refers to humans’ ability to represent the mental states of others, including their desires, beliefs, and intentions. We design a Theory of Mind neural network {–} a ToMnet {–} which uses meta-learning to build such models of the agents it encounters. The ToMnet learns a strong prior model for agents’ future behaviour, and, using only a small number of behavioural observations, can bootstrap to richer predictions about agents’ characteristics and mental states. We apply the ToMnet to agents behaving in simple gridworld environments, showing that it learns to model random, algorithmic, and deep RL agents from varied populations, and that it passes classic ToM tasks such as the "Sally-Anne" test of recognising that others can hold false beliefs about the world.

paragraphs: Predicting another agent's behavior can require reasoning about its desires, beliefs, and intentions. This paper develops a Theory of Mind neural network, or ToMnet, that learns models of other agents through meta-learning. The aim is to use experience across agents to interpret a newly encountered agent from limited observations.

ToMnet learns a prior model of how agents behave. A small number of behavioral observations then supports richer predictions about a particular agent's characteristics and mental states. This combines general expectations learned across a population with evidence from the individual being observed, providing a basis for anticipating its future behavior.

The authors test the system in simple gridworlds with random, algorithmic, and deep reinforcement learning agents. ToMnet learns to model these varied populations and passes classic theory-of-mind tasks, including the Sally-Anne test for recognizing false beliefs. These results demonstrate the reported capacities in controlled agent environments, where another agent's belief can differ from the actual world.
summary.tldr: ToMnet meta-learns models of other agents and uses limited observations to predict behavior and recognize false beliefs in gridworld tasks.

title: Machine Theory of Mind

abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a core component of data science pipelines. From collected noisy worker labels, aggregation models that incorporate worker reliability parameters aim to infer a latent true annotation. In this paper, we argue that existing crowdsourcing approaches do not sufficiently model worker correlations observed in practical settings; we propose in response an enhanced Bayesian classifier combination (EBCC) model, with inference based on a mean-field variational approach. An introduced mixture of intra-class reliabilities—connected to tensor decomposition and item clustering—induces inter-worker correlation. EBCC does not suffer the limitations of existing correlation models: intractable marginalisation of missing labels and poor scaling to large worker cohorts. Extensive empirical comparison on 17 real-world datasets sees EBCC achieving the highest mean accuracy across 10 benchmark crowdsourcing methods.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing often produces several noisy labels for the same item, leaving an aggregation model to infer the underlying annotation. Such models commonly account for differences in worker reliability. This paper argues that they also need to capture correlations between workers, which existing approaches do not adequately represent in practical settings.

The proposed enhanced Bayesian classifier combination model, or EBCC, introduces a mixture of reliability patterns within each class. This construction induces dependence between workers and connects the model to item clustering and tensor decomposition. Inference uses a mean-field variational approach, providing a computational way to estimate the model from the collected labels.

The authors report that EBCC avoids two problems affecting existing correlation models: intractable treatment of missing labels and poor scaling to large groups of workers. Across 17 real-world datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy in a comparison involving 10 benchmark crowdsourcing methods. That aggregate finding supports the value of modeling worker relationships without claiming that EBCC wins on every individual dataset.
summary.tldr: EBCC models correlations among crowd workers while handling missing labels and large worker groups, achieving the highest mean accuracy in the reported comparison.

title: Exploiting Worker Correlation for Label Aggregation in Crowdsourcing

abstract: Deep generative models are becoming a cornerstone of modern machine learning. Recent work on conditional generative adversarial networks has shown that learning complex, high-dimensional distributions over natural images is within reach. While the latest models are able to generate high-fidelity, diverse natural images at high resolution, they rely on a vast quantity of labeled data. In this work we demonstrate how one can benefit from recent work on self- and semi-supervised learning to outperform the state of the art on both unsupervised ImageNet synthesis, as well as in the conditional setting. In particular, the proposed approach is able to match the sample quality (as measured by FID) of the current state-of-the-art conditional model BigGAN on ImageNet using only 10% of the labels and outperform it using 20% of the labels.

Conditional generative adversarial networks have demonstrated the ability to model complex natural-image distributions, but their demand for labels makes supervision an important resource. This paper investigates how self-supervised and semi-supervised learning can reduce that dependence while maintaining strong image-generation results.

The proposed approach draws on these learning methods to improve both unsupervised ImageNet synthesis and conditional generation. Its central focus is how effectively a generative model can use the available supervision. The two settings matter because the work addresses image synthesis without labels as well as generation in a setting that uses conditioning information.

On ImageNet, the approach matches BigGAN's sample quality, measured by FID, using only 10% of the labels, and exceeds it using 20%. The authors also report outperforming the state of the art in unsupervised synthesis. These findings establish a substantial reduction in label requirements for the reported quality comparison, with the specific matching and improvement claims tied to FID.
summary.tldr: Self- and semi-supervised learning match BigGAN's ImageNet FID with 10% of the labels and improve on it with 20%.

title: High-Fidelity Image Generation With Fewer Labels

abstract: We propose the labeled Cech complex, the plain labeled Vietoris-Rips complex, and the locally scaled labeled Vietoris-Rips complex to perform persistent homology inference of decision boundaries in classification tasks. We provide theoretical conditions and analysis for recovering the homology of a decision boundary from samples. Our main objective is quantification of deep neural network complexity to enable matching of datasets to pre-trained models to facilitate the functioning of AI marketplaces; we report results for experiments using MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10.

paragraphs: A classifier's decision boundary separates regions assigned different labels. This paper studies the boundary through topology, focusing on structural features such as connected components and holes. Its aim is to infer those features from labeled samples and use them to quantify the complexity of deep neural networks.

The authors propose three constructions: a labeled Cech complex, a plain labeled Vietoris-Rips complex, and a locally scaled labeled Vietoris-Rips complex. These provide structures on which persistent homology can examine topological features across scales. The paper gives theoretical conditions and analysis for recovering the homology of a decision boundary from samples, making that recovery a conditional mathematical result.

The intended application is matching datasets with pretrained models in AI marketplaces. A description of boundary complexity supplies a way to study how a model relates to a classification task. The authors report experiments using MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10. The contribution combines tools for estimating boundary topology with a model-selection objective, rather than stating a universal performance improvement from topological matching.
summary.tldr: The paper develops labeled topological constructions to recover decision-boundary structure and study matching datasets with pretrained neural networks.

title: Topological Data Analysis of Decision Boundaries with Application to Model Selection

abstract: Real-world datasets are often biased with respect to key demographic factors such as race and gender. Due to the latent nature of the underlying factors, detecting and mitigating bias is especially challenging for unsupervised machine learning. We present a weakly supervised algorithm for overcoming dataset bias for deep generative models. Our approach requires access to an additional small, unlabeled reference dataset as the supervision signal, thus sidestepping the need for explicit labels on the underlying bias factors. Using this supplementary dataset, we detect the bias in existing datasets via a density ratio technique and learn generative models which efficiently achieve the twin goals of: 1) data efficiency by using training examples from both biased and reference datasets for learning; and 2) data generation close in distribution to the reference dataset at test time. Empirically, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach which reduces bias w.r.t. latent factors by an average of up to 34.6% over baselines for comparable image generation using generative adversarial networks.

Addressing this is difficult in unsupervised learning because the factors associated with bias may not be explicitly labeled. This paper introduces a weakly supervised method that uses a small additional reference dataset as guidance without requiring labels for those underlying factors.

The method compares the biased and reference datasets through a density ratio technique to detect distributional bias. It then learns from examples in both datasets, combining the larger training collection with the reference signal. The intended output distribution is close to the reference dataset's distribution, so that reference supplies the direction of the correction.

In image generation experiments with generative adversarial networks, the authors report average bias reductions of up to 34.6% relative to baselines for comparable generation. The result supports using a small unlabeled reference collection to improve the evaluated bias measures while retaining data from the original collection for training.
summary.tldr: A small unlabeled reference dataset guides generative training toward its distribution, reducing measured latent-factor bias in the reported image experiments.

title: Fair Generative Modeling via Weak Supervision

abstract: Off-policy policy estimators that use importance sampling (IS) can suffer from high variance in long-horizon domains, and there has been particular excitement over new IS methods that leverage the structure of Markov decision processes. We analyze the variance of the most popular approaches through the viewpoint of conditional Monte Carlo. Surprisingly, we find that in finite horizon MDPs there is no strict variance reduction of per-decision importance sampling or marginalized importance sampling, comparing with vanilla importance sampling. We then provide sufficient conditions under which the per-decision or marginalized estimators will provably reduce the variance over importance sampling with finite horizons. For the asymptotic (in terms of horizon $T$) case, we develop upper and lower bounds on the variance of those estimators which yields sufficient conditions under which there exists an exponential v.s. polynomial gap between the variance of importance sampling and that of the per-decision or stationary/marginalized estimators. These results help advance our understanding of if and when new types of IS estimators will improve the accuracy of off-policy estimation.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using experience collected under another policy. Importance sampling can make such estimates highly variable when trajectories are long. This paper uses conditional Monte Carlo to analyze whether structured alternatives, including per-decision and marginalized importance sampling, actually reduce that variance.

For finite-horizon Markov decision processes, the authors find that these alternatives do not have an unconditional strict variance-reduction guarantee over ordinary importance sampling. They then establish sufficient conditions under which per-decision or marginalized estimators do reduce variance. The distinction matters: using more of the problem’s structure can help, but the estimator’s form alone does not establish the improvement.

The authors also analyze how variance behaves as the horizon grows, deriving upper and lower bounds. These yield sufficient conditions for an exponential-versus-polynomial separation between ordinary importance sampling and the studied alternatives. The paper therefore clarifies both the potential size of the benefit and the circumstances needed to establish it, rather than treating long-horizon variance reduction as automatic.
summary.tldr: Structured importance-sampling estimators reduce variance under sufficient conditions, but strict improvement is not guaranteed for every finite-horizon problem.

title: Understanding the Curse of Horizon in Off-Policy Evaluation via Conditional Importance Sampling

abstract: Neural processes (NPs) constitute a family of variational approximate models for stochastic processes with promising properties in computational efficiency and uncertainty quantification. These processes use neural networks with latent variable inputs to induce a predictive distribution. However, the expressiveness of vanilla NPs is limited as they only use a global latent variable, while target-specific local variation may be crucial sometimes. To address this challenge, we investigate NPs systematically and present a new variant of NP model that we call Doubly Stochastic Variational Neural Process (DSVNP). This model combines the global latent variable and local latent variables for prediction. We evaluate this model in several experiments, and our results demonstrate competitive prediction performance in multi-output regression and uncertainty estimation in classification.

paragraphs: Neural processes use neural networks and latent variables to produce predictive distributions. This makes them promising for efficient prediction with uncertainty estimates. The paper examines a restriction of the standard formulation: it uses a global latent variable, even though some prediction problems also contain variation specific to individual targets.

The authors introduce the Doubly Stochastic Variational Neural Process, or DSVNP. Its prediction model combines a global latent variable with local latent variables. The global component represents shared variation, while the local components allow target-specific variation to enter the prediction. This hierarchical structure addresses the expressiveness limitation identified in models that rely only on a shared global variable.

Experiments demonstrate competitive prediction performance for regression with multiple outputs and competitive uncertainty estimation for classification. The results support using both shared and local latent structure when target-specific variation matters. The stated finding is competitive performance across these evaluated tasks, with the architectural contribution providing a more expressive way to organize latent information in neural processes.
summary.tldr: DSVNP combines global and target-specific latent variables to make neural process predictions more expressive.

title: Doubly Stochastic Variational Inference for Neural Processes with Hierarchical Latent Variables

abstract: Selective classification is a powerful tool for decision-making in scenarios where mistakes are costly but abstentions are allowed. In general, by allowing a classifier to abstain, one can improve the performance of a model at the cost of reducing coverage and classifying fewer samples. However, recent work has shown, in some cases, that selective classification can magnify disparities between groups, and has illustrated this phenomenon on multiple real-world datasets. We prove that the sufficiency criterion can be used to mitigate these disparities by ensuring that selective classification increases performance on all groups, and introduce a method for mitigating the disparity in precision across the entire coverage scale based on this criterion. We then provide an upper bound on the conditional mutual information between the class label and sensitive attribute, conditioned on the learned features, which can be used as a regularizer to achieve fairer selective classification. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated on the Adult, CelebA, Civil Comments, and CheXpert datasets.

paragraphs: A selective classifier can abstain when it would otherwise make a prediction. Accepting fewer examples can improve performance on those it does classify, but the benefits need not be shared across groups. In some cases, abstention can increase existing disparities even while the model's overall performance improves.

This paper proves that the sufficiency criterion can mitigate that problem by ensuring that selective classification improves performance for every group. It then develops a method based on this criterion to reduce differences in precision across the full coverage scale. Coverage describes how many examples receive predictions, so the method addresses fairness across different degrees of abstention.

To make the criterion useful during learning, the authors bound the conditional mutual information between the label and sensitive attribute given the learned features. That bound can serve as a regularizer, encouraging features that support fairer selective prediction. Experiments on Adult, CelebA, Civil Comments, and CheXpert demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution connects a formal fairness criterion to a trainable approach for managing group disparities as coverage changes.
summary.tldr: A sufficiency-based method reduces group precision disparities across abstention levels, supported by theory and experiments on four datasets.

title: Fair Selective Classification Via Sufficiency

abstract: Learning with adversarial robustness has been a challenge in contemporary machine learning, and recent years have witnessed increasing attention on robust decision trees and ensembles, mostly working with high computational complexity or without guarantees of provable robustness. This work proposes the Fast Provably Robust Decision Tree (FPRDT) with the smallest computational complexity O(n log n), a tradeoff between global and local optimizations over the adversarial 0/1 loss. We further develop the Provably Robust AdaBoost (PRAdaBoost) according to our robust decision trees, and present convergence analysis for training adversarial 0/1 loss. We conduct extensive experiments to support our approaches; in particular, our approaches are superior to those unprovably robust methods, and achieve better or comparable performance to those provably robust methods yet with the smallest running time.

paragraphs: Training decision trees to withstand adversarial changes can be computationally expensive, and some existing methods lack provable robustness guarantees. This paper aims to address both issues together. It introduces Fast Provably Robust Decision Tree, or FPRDT, with reported computational complexity of O(n log n).

FPRDT balances global and local optimization of the adversarial 0/1 loss, which evaluates classification mistakes under adversarial conditions. This tradeoff is central to making robust training efficient. The authors then build a boosting method, PRAdaBoost, from these robust trees and analyze convergence of its training adversarial 0/1 loss. The contribution therefore covers both individual trees and their combination into an ensemble.

Experiments support the proposed methods on performance and speed. They outperform the compared methods without provable robustness and achieve better or comparable performance to the compared provably robust methods, with the shortest reported running time. These findings suggest that robustness guarantees and practical training efficiency can coexist in the studied tree-based approaches, rather than requiring the computational costs associated with the comparison methods.
summary.tldr: FPRDT and PRAdaBoost combine provable adversarial robustness with efficient tree training and strong comparative experimental performance.

title: Fast Provably Robust Decision Trees and Boosting

abstract: This article introduces a random matrix framework for the analysis of clustering on high-dimensional data streams, a particularly relevant setting for a more sober processing of large amounts of data with limited memory and energy resources. Assuming data $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ arrives as a continuous flow and a small number $L$ of them can be kept in the learning pipeline, one has only access to the diagonal elements of the Gram kernel matrix: $\left[ \mathbf{K}_L \right]_{i, j} = \frac{1}{p} \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j \mathbf{1}_{\left\lvert i - j \right\rvert < L}$. Under a large-dimensional data regime, we derive the limiting spectral distribution of the banded kernel matrix $\mathbf{K}_L$ and study its isolated eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which behave in an unfamiliar way. We detail how these results can be used to perform efficient online kernel spectral clustering and provide theoretical performance guarantees. Our findings are empirically confirmed on image clustering tasks. Leveraging on optimality results of spectral methods for clustering, this work offers insights on efficient online clustering techniques for high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Clustering a continuous stream of high-dimensional data becomes difficult when only a small number of observations can remain in memory. This paper studies what can still be learned when comparisons between observations are available only within a limited window. Those comparisons form a banded kernel matrix, with entries outside the accessible window set to zero.

The authors develop a random matrix framework for understanding this matrix in a large-dimensional regime. They derive the limiting distribution of its eigenvalues and investigate isolated eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors. These spectral features behave differently from familiar settings, making their analysis important for understanding how restricted memory changes the information available for clustering.

The paper uses these results to construct efficient online kernel spectral clustering methods and provide theoretical performance guarantees. Image clustering experiments support the analysis. The contribution connects a concrete resource constraint to the mathematical behavior of the clustering machinery, offering guidance for processing high-dimensional streams when retaining and comparing the full dataset is impractical.
summary.tldr: A random matrix analysis explains how limited memory changes streaming spectral clustering and supports efficient methods with theoretical guarantees.

title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Data Stream Clustering: Coping With Limited Memory Resources

abstract: Message passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are a popular learning architectures for graph-structured data. However, one problem GNNs experience is oversquashing, where a GNN has difficulty sending information between distant nodes. Understanding and mitigating oversquashing has recently received significant attention from the research community. In this paper, we continue this line of work by analyzing oversquashing through the lens of the effective resistance between nodes in the input graph. Effective resistance intuitively captures the “strength” of connection between two nodes by paths in the graph, and has a rich literature spanning many areas of graph theory. We propose to use total effective resistance as a bound of the total amount of oversquashing in a graph and provide theoretical justification for its use. We further develop an algorithm to identify edges to be added to an input graph to minimize the total effective resistance, thereby alleviating oversquashing. We provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of our total effective resistance based rewiring strategies for improving the performance of GNNs.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph neural networks can struggle to transmit useful information between distant nodes, a problem known as oversquashing. This paper examines that difficulty through effective resistance, a graph quantity that captures how strongly two nodes are connected through the paths available between them.

The authors propose total effective resistance as a bound on the graph's overall oversquashing and provide theoretical justification for this use. This links a learning problem to a structural property of the input graph. It also gives a concrete quantity to target when trying to improve the routes through which a network exchanges information.

Building on that connection, the paper develops an algorithm that identifies edges to add so as to minimise total effective resistance. The resulting rewiring aims to alleviate oversquashing by changing the input graph's connectivity. Experiments provide evidence that these strategies improve GNN performance. The contribution combines a theoretically motivated diagnostic with an actionable graph modification, showing how understanding communication constraints can guide changes that help the evaluated networks learn.
summary.tldr: Total effective resistance provides a theoretically motivated oversquashing bound and guides graph rewiring that empirically improves GNN performance.

title: Understanding Oversquashing in GNNs through the Lens of Effective Resistance

abstract: In Multi-Task Learning (MTL), tasks may compete and limit the performance achieved on each other, rather than guiding the optimization to a solution, superior to all its single-task trained counterparts. Since there is often not a unique solution optimal for all tasks, practitioners have to balance tradeoffs between tasks’ performance, and resort to optimality in the Pareto sense. Most MTL methodologies either completely neglect this aspect, and instead of aiming at learning a Pareto Front, produce one solution predefined by their optimization schemes, or produce diverse but discrete solutions. Recent approaches parameterize the Pareto Front via neural networks, leading to complex mappings from tradeoff to objective space. In this paper, we conjecture that the Pareto Front admits a linear parameterization in parameter space, which leads us to propose Pareto Manifold Learning , an ensembling method in weight space. Our approach produces a continuous Pareto Front in a single training run, that allows to modulate the performance on each task during inference. Experiments on multi-task learning benchmarks, ranging from image classification to tabular datasets and scene understanding, show that Pareto Manifold Learning outperforms state-of-the-art single-point algorithms, while learning a better Pareto parameterization than multi-point baselines.

paragraphs: Tasks trained together can compete, so improving one task may reduce performance on another. Multi-task learning therefore often involves selecting among tradeoffs rather than finding a single solution that is best for every task. The paper focuses on learning a continuous Pareto front, allowing users to adjust those tradeoffs instead of receiving one fixed solution or several discrete choices.

The approach produces a continuous front in one training run and allows task performance to be modulated during inference. The proposed linear structure is presented as a conjecture, rather than a universal theorem.

Experiments span image classification, tabular data, and scene understanding. The method outperforms state-of-the-art single-point algorithms and learns a better Pareto parameterization than the evaluated multi-point baselines. These results support weight-space ensembling as a practical way to expose adjustable task tradeoffs without separately training each desired operating point.
summary.tldr: Pareto Manifold Learning ensembles model weights to learn continuous, inference-time-adjustable task tradeoffs in a single training run.

title: Pareto Manifold Learning: Tackling multiple tasks via ensembles of single-task models

abstract: Recently, the impressive empirical success of policy gradient (PG) methods has catalyzed the development of their theoretical foundations. Despite the huge efforts directed at the design of efficient stochastic PG-type algorithms, the understanding of their convergence to a globally optimal policy is still limited. In this work, we develop improved global convergence guarantees for a general class of Fisher-non-degenerate parameterized policies which allows to address the case of continuous state action spaces. First, we propose a Normalized Policy Gradient method with Implicit Gradient Transport (N-PG-IGT) and derive a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-2.5})$ sample complexity of this method for finding a global $\varepsilon$-optimal policy. Improving over the previously known $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ complexity, this algorithm does not require the use of importance sampling or second-order information and samples only one trajectory per iteration. Second, we further improve this complexity to $\tilde{ \mathcal{\mathcal{O}} }(\varepsilon^{-2})$ by considering a Hessian-Aided Recursive Policy Gradient ((N)-HARPG) algorithm enhanced with a correction based on a Hessian-vector product. Interestingly, both algorithms are $(i)$ simple and easy to implement: single-loop, do not require large batches of trajectories and sample at most two trajectories per iteration; $(ii)$ computationally and memory efficient: they do not require expensive subroutines at each iteration and can be implemented with memory linear in the dimension of parameters.

title: Stochastic Policy Gradient Methods: Improved Sample Complexity for Fisher-non-degenerate Policies

abstract: It is believed that Gradient Descent (GD) induces an implicit bias towards good generalization in training machine learning models. This paper provides a fine-grained analysis of the dynamics of GD for the matrix sensing problem, whose goal is to recover a low-rank ground-truth matrix from near-isotropic linear measurements. It is shown that GD with small initialization behaves similarly to the greedy low-rank learning heuristics and follows an incremental learning procedure: GD sequentially learns solutions with increasing ranks until it recovers the ground truth matrix. Compared to existing works which only analyze the first learning phase for rank-1 solutions, our result provides characterizations for the whole learning process. Moreover, besides the over-parameterized regime that many prior works focused on, our analysis of the incremental learning procedure also applies to the under-parameterized regime. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to confirm our theoretical findings.
