These findings show that neural construction can improve measured space coverage while supporting diverse applications. The stated contribution concerns finite sequences, with prefix quality built into the learning objective rather than evaluating only the complete point set.
summary.tldr: NeuroLDS learns finite point sequences with strong uniform coverage across prefixes, improving discrepancy measures and demonstrating usefulness in several computational applications.

title: Neural Low-Discrepancy Sequences

abstract: Text-to-video diffusion transformers encode semantic information unevenly across model depth, which constrains effective concept erasure. We identify a representational bottleneck, termed concept–layer topological alignment, under which target concepts exhibit higher separability at certain representational depths. Outside these depths, concept and non-target signals remain strongly entangled, limiting the effectiveness of depth-specific erasure. This observation reframes concept erasure as the problem of identifying representational depths where concept–non-target separation naturally emerges. Motivated by this structural constraint, we introduce CLEAR, a separability-driven optimization framework for concept erasure that explicitly enforces concept–layer alignment. CLEAR operationalizes this principle by formulating layer selection as an optimization problem over concept–non-target separability, rather than relying on layer-agnostic or heuristic choices. To enable this, we introduce a separability-aware objective that favors layers exhibiting stronger concept–non-target separation. Experiments on large-scale text-to-video diffusion models demonstrate that enforcing concept–layer alignment leads to more precise concept suppression while preserving overall generative quality.

paragraphs: Removing a concept from a text-to-video diffusion model depends on where that concept is represented. This paper finds that semantic information is distributed unevenly across model depth. At some layers, the target concept is more separable from other information; elsewhere, target and non-target signals remain strongly entangled.

The authors call this relationship concept–layer topological alignment. It explains a structural difficulty for depth-specific erasure: editing a layer where the relevant signals are entangled limits the effectiveness of the intervention. The proposed CLEAR framework therefore treats identifying suitable representational depths as part of the concept-erasure problem itself.

CLEAR formulates layer selection as an optimization over target-versus-non-target separability. Its objective favors layers where this separation is stronger, explicitly enforcing the alignment principle. Experiments on large-scale text-to-video diffusion models report more precise concept suppression while preserving overall generative quality. The findings support choosing intervention locations according to the model’s existing representation structure, so that suppression can be more selective.
summary.tldr: CLEAR selects layers where target concepts are more separable from other content to improve concept erasure while preserving video-generation quality.

title: Where Concept Erasure Should Occur: Concept–Layer Alignment in Text-to-Video Diffusion Models

abstract: While frontier formal mathematics systems now routinely develop repository-scale proof engineering artifacts requiring multi-file coordination and semantic correctness beyond compilation, existing evaluation benchmarks remain focused on isolated theorem proving. We introduce Automated Proof Engineering (APE), the first systematic framework for evaluating repository-scale proof engineering through dual verification that validates both syntactic compilation and semantic requirement satisfaction in pinned library environments. We present a complete infrastructure comprising APE-Bench, which automatically extracts proof engineering tasks from real library commit histories, and APE-Harness, a unified execution framework based on task contract abstraction. This contract-based design enables standardized evaluation across diverse formal mathematics tasks and fair systematic comparison of different agent implementations (including our APE-Agent reference scaffold alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI) on identical task specifications. We demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness through comprehensive evaluation. All code, benchmarks, and infrastructure will be open-sourced.

paragraphs: APE-Bench addresses the gap between proving an isolated theorem and modifying a formal mathematics library. Repository work can require coordinated changes across several files, and a result that compiles may still fail to satisfy the requested mathematical or engineering requirements. The paper makes those broader obligations part of evaluation.

The proposed Automated Proof Engineering framework checks two things: whether the artifact compiles and whether it fulfills its semantic requirements. Evaluations use fixed library environments so that agents face consistent conditions. APE-Bench extracts tasks automatically from actual library commit histories, while APE-Harness provides a common execution framework organized around explicit task contracts.

Those contracts allow different agent implementations to be compared on identical specifications. The evaluation includes the authors’ APE-Agent scaffold alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI. The authors report that their evaluation demonstrates the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution is an infrastructure for assessing repository-scale proof engineering, with both executable validity and requirement satisfaction represented in the assessment.
summary.tldr: APE-Bench evaluates formal mathematics agents on repository tasks using both compilation checks and semantic requirement checks.

title: APE-Bench: Evaluating Automated Proof Engineering for Formal Math Libraries

abstract: Traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training typically proceeds without any structural priors, effectively requiring the model to simultaneously train expert weights while searching for an optimal routing policy within a vast combinatorial space. This entanglement often leads to sluggish convergence and training instabilities. This paper introduces Grouter a preemptive routing method that by distilling high-quality structures from fully-trained MoE models and serving as a fixed router for target models. By decoupling structural optimization from weight updates, Grouter significantly accelerates both the speed and quality of model convergence. To ensure the framework’s versatility, we also introduce expert folding to adapt Grouter across varying model configurations and expert tuning to rebalance workloads across different data distributions. Furthermore, by leveraging the structural priors provided by preemptive routing, we can implement targeted optimizations to further enhance training throughput. Experiments demonstrate that Grouter achieves superior performance and efficiency which boosts pre-training data utilization by $\textbf{4.28$\times$}$ and achieves up to $\textbf{33.5$%$}$ throughput acceleration, establishing preemptive routing as a fundamental paradigm for scalable MoE training. We publicly release our code and pretrained Grouter checkpoints.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts training must develop expert weights while also learning which experts should process inputs. Grouter addresses the slow convergence and instability associated with searching for that routing structure at the same time as updating the experts. It supplies routing information obtained from already trained mixture-of-experts models.

The method distills those learned structures into a router that remains fixed for a target model. Expert folding adapts the router to different model configurations, while expert tuning rebalances workloads when the data distribution changes. The resulting routing structure also enables targeted optimizations intended to increase training throughput.

Experiments report improved performance and efficiency, including 4.28 times better pre-training data utilization and throughput acceleration of up to 33.5%. These are distinct benefits: learning can make better use of training data, and the training system can process work faster. The contribution is an approach to reusing learned routing structure so that target-model training need not jointly discover that structure and learn expert representations.
summary.tldr: Grouter transfers routing structures from trained mixture-of-experts models to accelerate target-model learning and throughput.

title: Grouter: Decoupling Routing from Representation for Accelerated MoE Training

abstract: We study the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learnability of partial concept classes in the multiclass setting, where the label space can be infinite. While the Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability for finite label spaces, we show it fails when the label space is unbounded. Instead, we prove that the Daniely-Shalev (DS) dimension provides a characterization of learnability for partial concept classes in the general multiclass setting. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a surprising phenomenon we call the “Disambiguation Paradox”: disambiguation schemes with simple label space can destroy learnability, while richer labeling may preserves it. We further characterize how the number and structure of disambiguation labels control the induced DS dimension, yielding a trade-off between label complexity and sample complexity.

While the Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability for finite label spaces, we show it fails when the label space is unbounded. Instead, we prove that the Daniely-Shalev (DS) dimension provides a characterization of learnability for partial concept classes in the general multiclass setting. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a surprising phenomenon we call the “Disambiguation Paradox”: disambiguation schemes with simple label space can destroy learnability, while richer labeling may preserves it. We further characterize how the number and structure of disambiguation labels control the induced DS dimension, yielding a trade-off between label complexity and sample complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies when multiclass partial concept classes can be learned in the Probably Approximately Correct framework. Partial concepts leave some inputs without a specified label, and the label space considered here may be infinite. The central question is which mathematical measure of class complexity correctly captures learnability across this general setting.

For finite label spaces, Natarajan dimension provides a characterization, but the authors show that it fails when the label space is unbounded. They prove that Daniely-Shalev dimension supplies the characterization for general multiclass partial concept classes. This identifies the complexity measure needed when moving beyond a fixed finite collection of possible labels.

The paper also analyzes disambiguation, which resolves the unspecified portions of partial concepts through labeling. Surprisingly, using a simple label space can destroy learnability, whereas richer labeling may preserve it. The authors characterize how the number and arrangement of disambiguation labels affect the resulting Daniely-Shalev dimension. This reveals a trade-off between label complexity and the amount of data needed for learning.
summary.tldr: Daniely-Shalev dimension characterizes general multiclass partial learnability, and simpler disambiguation labels can unexpectedly make a class unlearnable.

title: On Learnability and Disambiguation of Multiclass Partial Concept Classes

abstract: Most post-training backdoor detection methods rely on attacked models exhibiting extreme outlier detection statistics for the target class of an attack, compared to non-target classes. However, these approaches may fail: (1) when some (non-target) classes are easily discriminable from all others, in which case they may naturally achieve extreme detection statistics (e.g., decision confidence); and (2) when the backdoor is subtle, i.e., with its features weak relative to intrinsic class-discriminative features. A key observation is that the backdoor target class has contributions to its detection statistic from both the backdoor trigger and from its intrinsic features, whereas non-target classes only have contributions from their intrinsic features. To achieve more sensitive detectors, we thus propose to suppress intrinsic features while optimizing the detection statistic for a given class. For non-target classes, such suppression will drastically reduce the achievable statistic, whereas for the target class the (significant) contribution from the backdoor trigger remains. In practice, we formulate a constrained optimization problem, leveraging a small set of clean examples from a given class, and optimizing the detection statistic while orthogonalizing with respect to the class’s intrinsic features. We dub this approach ”class subspace orthogonalization” (CSO). CSO can be ”plug-and-play” applied to a wide variety of existing detectors. We demonstrate its effectiveness in improving several well-known detectors, comparing with a variety of baseline detectors, against a variety of attacks, on the CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and TinyImageNet domains. Moreover, to make the detection problem even more challenging, we also evaluate against a novel mixed clean/dirty-label poisoning attack that is more surgical and harder to detect than traditional dirty-label attacks. Finally, we evaluate CSO against an adaptive attack designed to defeat it, with promising detection results.

This can be misleading when an ordinary class is naturally easy to distinguish, or when a backdoor signal is weak relative to legitimate class features. title: Improving the Sensitivity of Backdoor Detectors via Class Subspace Orthogonalization

abstract: Online convex optimization in non-stationary environments has garnered considerable attention in the literature. Recently, Pasteris et al. (2024) investigate online convex optimization with the optimal switching regret, defined as the sum of the static regret over each segment, where the segmentation is an arbitrary partition of the entire time horizon. For general convex functions, their work has established an optimal switching regret bound. However, it remains open whether similar bounds are attainable for other types of convex functions, such as exponentially concave or strongly convex functions. In this paper, we affirmatively answer this question by proposing a novel meta-algorithm, termed IRESET, which is used to aggregate the decisions from a group of experts. The essence of our method lies in running multiple experts over a set of intervals, and then employing a meta-algorithm equipped with second-order bounds to sequentially combine their decisions. We leverage the segment tree structure to analyze the switching regret over the entire time horizon, and offer new insights into utilizing recursive equations over the segment tree. By choosing appropriate expert-algorithms for IRESET, our methods achieve logarithmic switching regret bounds for exponentially concave or strongly convex functions, respectively.

paragraphs: Online optimization in a changing environment needs a performance measure that allows the best decision to change over time. Switching regret sums the static regret within segments of the time horizon, for an arbitrary partition into segments. This paper asks whether stronger convexity properties permit logarithmic switching-regret bounds.

The authors introduce IRESET, a meta-algorithm that combines decisions from multiple experts operating over different intervals. Its aggregation procedure uses second-order bounds to combine those decisions sequentially. A segment-tree structure organizes the analysis across the full horizon, with recursive equations helping relate performance on individual intervals to the overall switching regret.

This resolves the stated open question for those function classes, extending the available theory beyond the general-convex setting discussed in the abstract. The significance is conditional on the objective’s structure: the framework shows how suitable experts and interval aggregation can exploit these stronger properties in non-stationary online optimization.
summary.tldr: IRESET combines interval-based experts to obtain logarithmic switching-regret bounds for exponentially concave and strongly convex online objectives.

title: Logarithmic Switching Regret for Online Convex Optimization

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely used in various graph machine learning scenarios. Existing literature primarily assumes well-annotated training graphs, while the reliability of labels is not guaranteed in real-world scenarios. Recently, efforts have been made to address the problem of graph learning with label noise. However, existing methods often (i) struggle to distinguish between reliable and unreliable nodes, and (ii) overlook the relational information embedded in the graph topology. To tackle this problem, this paper proposes a novel method, Dual-Standard Semantic Homogeneity with Dynamic Optimization (DREAM), for reliable, relation-informed optimization on graphs with label noise. Specifically, we design a relation-informed dynamic optimization framework that iteratively reevaluates the reliability of each labeled node in the graph during the optimization process according to the relation of the target node and other nodes. To measure this relation comprehensively, we propose a dual-standard selection strategy that selects a set of anchor nodes based on both node proximity and graph topology. Subsequently, we compute the semantic homogeneity between the target node and the anchor nodes, which serves as guidance for optimization. We also provide a rigorous theoretical analysis to justify the design of DREAM. Extensive experiments are performed on six graph datasets across various domains under three types of graph label noise against competing baselines, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DREAM.

paragraphs: Graph learning often assumes that training labels are trustworthy, although real datasets can contain mislabeled nodes. The paper identifies two connected weaknesses in existing approaches: difficulty distinguishing dependable labels from unreliable ones, and insufficient use of relationships encoded by the graph. DREAM uses those relationships to guide how training handles labeled nodes.

During optimization, DREAM repeatedly reassesses each labeled node's reliability by comparing it with selected anchor nodes. Anchor selection follows two standards, considering both node proximity and graph topology. The method then measures semantic homogeneity between the target and its anchors, using their agreement as guidance for optimization. Reliability is therefore reconsidered as training progresses rather than assigned only once.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting this design and evaluate it on six graph datasets from different domains under three types of label noise. Comparisons with competing baselines demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The central contribution is to make label-noise handling responsive to both evolving training information and the relational structure that distinguishes graph data from isolated examples.
summary.tldr: DREAM repeatedly assesses noisy graph labels using semantic agreement with anchors selected through node proximity and graph topology.

title: DREAM: Dual-Standard Semantic Homogeneity with Dynamic Optimization for Graph Learning with Label Noise

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional general language processing capabilities, but their memory and compute costs hinder deployment. Ternarization has emerged as a promising compression technique, offering significant reductions in model size and inference complexity. However, existing methods struggle with heavy-tailed activation distributions and therefore keep activations in high precision, fundamentally limiting end-to-end inference acceleration. To overcome this limitation, we propose TWLA, a post-training quantization (PTQ) framework that achieves 1.58-bit weight compression and 4-bit activation quantization while maintaining high accuracy. TWLA comprises three components: (1) Euclidean-to-Manifold Asymmetric Ternary Quantizer (E2M-ATQ) minimizes layer-output error under weight ternarization via a two-stage optimization from Euclidean initialization to manifold relocation; (2) Kronecker Orthogonal Tri-Modal Shaping (KOTMS) applies a Kronecker-structured orthogonal rotation to reshape weights into ternary-friendly tri-modal distributions, while the shared rotation statistically suppresses activation outliers; and (3) Inter-Layer Aware Activation Mixed Precision (ILA-AMP) explicitly introduces adjacent-layer second-order interaction costs in bit allocation and jointly optimizes for the layer-wise disparity of activation quantization gains induced by the shared orthogonal transform, preventing cascades triggered by a few weak layers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TWLA is a PTQ method that maintains high accuracy under the W1.58A4 configuration, while delivering significant inference acceleration. The code is available at TWLA.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model's weights to three values can reduce storage and computation, but high-precision activations can still limit inference speed. Activation outliers make lowering their precision difficult. TWLA is a post-training quantization framework that addresses weights and activations together, targeting 1.58-bit weights and 4-bit activations while maintaining high accuracy.

Its ternary quantizer minimizes layer-output error through an initial Euclidean optimization followed by manifold relocation. A structured orthogonal rotation reshapes weights toward three clusters suitable for ternarization and statistically suppresses activation outliers. These components make the model's numerical distributions more compatible with the desired precision.

A third component allocates activation precision using interactions between adjacent layers and differences in how much individual layers benefit from quantization after rotation. This is intended to prevent a few vulnerable layers from triggering cascading errors. Experiments report high accuracy under the W1.58A4 configuration alongside significant inference acceleration. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of weight compression, activation outliers, and cross-layer sensitivity rather than weight ternarization alone.
summary.tldr: TWLA combines ternary weight quantization, distribution-shaping rotations, and layer-aware activation precision to accelerate language-model inference while maintaining high accuracy.

title: TWLA: Achieving Ternary Weights and Low-Bit Activations for LLMs via Post-Training Quantization

abstract: In this paper, we study solution operators of physical field equations on geometric meshes from a function-space perspective. We reveal that Hodge orthogonality fundamentally resolves spectral interference by isolating unlearnable topological degrees of freedom from learnable geometric dynamics, enabling an additive approximation confined to structure-preserving subspaces. Building on Hodge theory and operator splitting, we derive a principled operator-level decomposition. The result is a Hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian architecture with an algebraic-level inductive bias we call Hodge Spectral Duality (HSD). In our framework, we use discrete differential forms to capture topology-dominated components and an orthogonal auxiliary ambient space to represent complex local dynamics. Our method achieves superior accuracy and efficiency on geometric graphs with enhanced fidelity to physical invariants.

summary.tldr: A Hodge-based operator decomposition separates topology from learnable geometric dynamics, improving reported accuracy, efficiency, and physical-invariant fidelity.

title: Topology-Preserving Neural Operator Learning via Hodge Decomposition

abstract: Most current paradigms in visual mechanistic interpretability (MI) remain confined to interpreting internal units of the vision model via heuristic methods (e.g., top-$K$ activation retrieval or optimization with regularization). In this work, we establish a theoretical distributional view for visual MI, which models the influence of a feature activation on the natural image distribution, thereby formulating a Kullback-Leibler (KL)-minimal optimization problem to model the MI task. Under this framework, statistical biases are identified within previous MI paradigms, which reveal that they may either be perceptually uninterpretable to humans (i.e., deviate from the natural image distribution), or mechanistically unfaithful to the vision models (i.e., unable to activate model features). To resolve the biases under the distributional view, we propose a model with a KL-minimal soft-constraint principle for visual MI that theoretically balances interpretability and faithfulness. We realize this principle via energy-guided diffusion posterior sampling. Extensive experiments validate the theoretical soundness of the proposed distributional view and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our paradigm on the DINOv3 vision model. The code is available at https://github.com/SII-ZhouGC/EnergyDPS.

paragraphs: Visual mechanistic interpretability tries to explain what internal features of a vision model respond to. Common approaches retrieve highly activating images or optimize an image to excite a feature. This paper reframes that task around distributions: how should the distribution of natural images change when a particular feature’s activation is encouraged?

The authors formulate an optimization problem using Kullback–Leibler divergence, which measures a difference between distributions. Their analysis identifies biases in earlier approaches that can produce images people struggle to interpret or images that fail to activate the intended feature. Their proposed soft constraint balances feature activation against remaining close to the natural image distribution.

The method implements this principle through energy-guided diffusion posterior sampling, using image generation to realize the distributional objective. Experiments on DINOv3 support its practical effectiveness. The contribution is both a theoretical account of why familiar visualization methods can become misleading and a generation procedure designed to balance human interpretability with faithfulness to the model.
summary.tldr: A distributional framework generates feature visualizations that balance natural-looking images with faithful activation of a vision model.

title: A Distributional View for Visual Mechanistic Interpretability: KL-Minimal Soft-Constraint Principle

abstract: With the rapid advancement of high-fidelity video generation models, robust AI-generated video (AIGV) detection has become increasingly needed. While most AIGV detection methods operate in the decoded pixel domain, we observe that detection in the pixel domain inevitably entangles task-irrelevant semantic information, leading to substantial semantic redundancy and extensive redundant computation, while overlooking free-to-use signals in compressed bitstreams. In particular, motion vectors and residuals directly encode temporal and spatial generative artifacts but remain largely underexplored. To address these issues, we propose a unified framework for Spatio-Temporal REsidual and Artifact Mining, namely STREAM, which enables AIGV detection directly from compressed bitstreams. STREAM leverages I-frames, motion vectors, and residual errors to capture spatiotemporal artifacts that are typically smoothed out by decompression filters. In particular, we design a lightweight network with a motion-guided alignment module and a gated fusion mechanism, enabling adaptive fusion of spatial artifacts and nonlinear temporal dynamics. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that STREAM achieves SOTA performance with an mAP of 0.965, with 2.5$\times$ faster inference than previous SOTA baselines.

paragraphs: STREAM detects AI-generated videos using information already present in compressed video files. The paper argues that analyzing decoded pixels mixes useful forensic clues with semantic content unrelated to detection, creating redundant computation. It instead focuses on motion vectors and residual errors, which contain information about temporal and spatial generation artifacts.

The framework combines these signals with I-frames in a lightweight network. A motion-guided alignment module helps relate evidence across movement, while a gated fusion mechanism adaptively combines spatial artifacts and nonlinear temporal behavior. This design matters because the authors identify useful compressed-domain traces that decompression filters can smooth away before a conventional detector sees them.

In the reported experiments, STREAM reaches a mean average precision of 0.965 and runs inference 2.5 times faster than previous leading baselines. These results support the paper’s central claim that compressed representations can improve both detection quality and efficiency. The contribution is therefore a change in the evidence the detector examines, together with a network designed to combine that evidence effectively.
summary.tldr: STREAM detects AI-generated video from compressed-file signals, reporting leading detection performance and 2.5 times faster inference.

title: Beyond Pixels: Mining Compressed Domain Artifacts for Efficient AI-Generated Video Detection

abstract: Sociopolitical AI risks are threats to collective self-determination: a society’s capacity to articulate its interests and realize them through institutions. We argue that sociopolitical AI risks emerge when general-purpose AI systems are integrated into society in ways that disproportionately amplify the scale, speed, and opacity of institutional operations, thereby degrading their capacity to function. Unlike model-level harms (toxicity, bias, discrimination), sociopolitical risks arise from widespread deployment rather than individual outputs. And unlike existential risks involving loss of control or complete labor automation, they manifest with current AI capabilities where AI augments rather than replaces human activity. In this position paper, we analyze how AI alters the conditions of governance via flooding government agencies with paralyzing volumes of input, concentrating control of infrastructure that threatens sovereignty, and flattening public debate into artificial agreement while reinforcing biases. We conclude with recommendations for evaluation methodology, institutional design, and procurement policy that treat sociopolitical resilience as a first-class objective alongside model-level safety.

paragraphs: This paper examines AI risks to a society’s ability to identify shared interests and act through its institutions. The authors argue that widespread deployment can change institutional operations in damaging ways by increasing their scale, speed, and opacity. These effects can arise with current systems that assist people, without requiring complete automation or a loss of control over AI.

The analysis considers three mechanisms: overwhelming government agencies with input, concentrating control over infrastructure in ways that threaten sovereignty, and producing artificial agreement in public debate while reinforcing biases. The shared concern is whether institutions can continue functioning effectively when AI changes the conditions under which they receive information, exercise authority, and support deliberation.

This perspective expands the unit of safety analysis beyond individual model outputs. A model’s behavior can satisfy output-level safeguards while its widespread use still undermines collective decision-making. The paper recommends changes to evaluation methods, institutional design, and procurement policy that explicitly prioritize sociopolitical resilience. Its central argument is that model safety and the functioning of society require complementary forms of assessment.
summary.tldr: AI safety assessments should examine how widespread deployment affects institutions and collective self-government alongside individual model behavior.

title: Position: Safe Models Do Not Guarantee Safe Societies

abstract: This position paper argues that the next generation of vision encoders should be image size agnostic and task driven. The source of our inspiration is a behavioral trait of biological vision – efficiency. We focus on a couple of ways in which vision in nature is efficient, but modern vision encoders not. Humans and animals deal with vast quantities of visual data, and need to be smart where they focus their limited energy. It is our belief that vision encoders should be dynamic and the computational complexity should depend on the task at hand rather than the size of the image. To realize this, we introduce SOVA (Sequential Observation with Visual Attention) – a proof-of-concept solution for image classification. Despite classification not being representative for what we are trying to achieve, it shows that our approach is feasible and promising. Code is available at: https://github.com/insait-institute/sova.

paragraphs: This paper argues that vision encoders should allocate computation according to the task they need to solve. The inspiration comes from biological vision: humans and animals encounter enormous amounts of visual information while having limited energy to spend on it. The authors want artificial vision systems to become similarly selective and dynamic in their processing.

Their proposed direction is image-size-agnostic encoding, where computational complexity depends on the demands of the task instead of the size of the input image. To explore its feasibility, they introduce SOVA, short for Sequential Observation with Visual Attention. SOVA is a proof-of-concept system applied to image classification, intended to make the broader architectural idea concrete.

The authors describe this demonstration as feasible and promising while explicitly acknowledging that classification does not represent the full ambition of the proposal. That qualification matters: the example supports further investigation of task-driven visual computation, without establishing the entire vision for future encoders. The paper combines a design argument about efficiency with an initial implementation that illustrates a possible direction.
summary.tldr: SOVA provides a classification proof of concept for vision encoders whose computation follows task demands rather than image size.

abstract: Boosting is a popular approach for building accurate classifiers. Despite the initial popular belief, boosting algorithms do exhibit overfitting and are sensitive to label noise. Part of the sensitivity of boosting algorithms to outliers and noise can be attributed to the unboundedness of the margin-based loss functions that they employ. In this paper we describe two leveraging algorithms that build on boosting techniques and employ a bounded loss function of the margin. The first algorithm interleaves the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm with boosting steps. The second algorithm decomposes a non-convex loss into a difference of two convex losses. We prove that both algorithms converge to a stationary point. We also analyze the generalization properties of the algorithms using the Rademacher complexity. We describe experiments with both synthetic data and natural data (OCR and text) that demonstrate the merits of our framework, in particular robustness to outliers.

paragraphs: This paper addresses boosting's sensitivity to noisy labels and outliers. The authors attribute part of that sensitivity to margin-based loss functions that are unbounded. They develop two algorithms that build on boosting while using a bounded loss of the margin, changing how the learning objective treats difficult observations.

The first algorithm alternates expectation-maximization with boosting steps. The second expresses a nonconvex loss as the difference of two convex losses. The authors prove that both algorithms converge to a stationary point. That is the stated convergence result; it does not establish that either procedure necessarily reaches a global optimum.

The paper also studies generalization through Rademacher complexity and evaluates the methods on synthetic data, optical character recognition, and text. The experiments demonstrate benefits of the framework, particularly robustness to outliers. Together, the optimization results, generalization analysis, and experiments support bounded margin losses as a way to address part of boosting's observed sensitivity to noise.
summary.tldr: Two boosting-based algorithms use bounded margin losses, converge to stationary points, and demonstrate robustness to outliers.

title: Leveraging the margin more carefully

abstract: How to assign appropriate weights to terms is one of the critical issues in information retrieval. Many term weighting schemes are unsupervised. They are either based on the empirical observation in information retrieval, or based on generative approaches for language modeling. As a result, the existing term weighting schemes are usually insufficient in distinguishing informative words from the uninformative ones, which is crucial to the performance of information retrieval. In this paper, we present supervised term weighting schemes that automatically learn term weights based on the correlation between word frequency and category information of documents. Empirical studies with the ImageCLEF dataset have indicated that the proposed methods perform substantially better than the state-of-the-art approaches for term weighting and other alternatives that exploit category information for information retrieval.

In this paper, we present supervised term weighting schemes that automatically learn term weights based on the correlation between word frequency and category information of documents. Empirical studies with the ImageCLEF dataset have indicated that the proposed methods perform substantially better than the state-of-the-art approaches for term weighting and other alternatives that exploit category information for information retrieval.

paragraphs: Information retrieval depends in part on deciding how much importance to give each word. The paper argues that existing unsupervised weighting schemes often struggle to separate informative words from less useful ones. It proposes using document categories as supervision for learning those weights, bringing information about document groupings into the weighting process.

The proposed schemes learn from correlations between word frequency and category information. This makes a term's weight depend on how its occurrence relates to labeled document categories. The approach uses that relationship to help identify words that carry useful information for retrieval, rather than relying only on an unsupervised weighting rule.

Experiments on the ImageCLEF dataset indicate substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art term-weighting approaches considered and over other alternatives that exploit category information. The finding supports learning how category information should influence individual term weights. Its empirical scope is the reported ImageCLEF study, where the learned weighting schemes performed better than those comparison methods.
summary.tldr: Learning term weights from word-frequency and document-category relationships substantially improves retrieval in the reported ImageCLEF experiments.

title: Learn to weight terms in information retrieval using category information

abstract: The current framework of reinforcement learning is based on maximizing the expected returns based on scalar rewards. But in many real world situations, tradeoffs must be made among multiple objectives. Moreover, the agent’s preferences between different objectives may vary with time. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning in the presence of time-varying preferences among multiple objectives, using numeric weights to represent their importance. We propose a method that allows us to store a finite number of policies, choose an appropriate policy for any weight vector and improve upon it. The idea is that although there are infinitely many weight vectors, they may be well-covered by a small number of optimal policies. We show this empirically in two domains: a version of the Buridan’s ass problem and network routing.

In this paper, we consider the problem of learning in the presence of time-varying preferences among multiple objectives, using numeric weights to represent their importance. We propose a method that allows us to store a finite number of policies, choose an appropriate policy for any weight vector and improve upon it. The idea is that although there are infinitely many weight vectors, they may be well-covered by a small number of optimal policies. paragraphs: Reinforcement learning usually expresses success through a single numerical reward. Many decisions instead involve several objectives, and the importance assigned to each objective can change over time. This paper studies learning under those changing preferences, representing the current importance of the objectives with numerical weights.

The proposed method stores a finite collection of policies. Given a weight vector, it selects an appropriate policy from that collection and can improve upon it. The motivation is that infinitely many possible preference settings may still be covered well by a small number of optimal policies. A separate stored policy for every possible weight vector may therefore be unnecessary.

The authors investigate this idea empirically in a version of the Buridan’s ass problem and in network routing. These examples support the possibility that a compact policy collection can serve a broad range of preferences. The result concerns adapting behavior as priorities change, with the empirical evidence supporting small collections in the studied domains rather than establishing that every multi-objective problem has such a compact representation.
summary.tldr: A finite collection of policies can support changing objective weights by providing a policy to select and improve for each preference setting.

title: Dynamic preferences in multi-criteria reinforcement learning

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-task learning, that is, learning multiple related functions. Our approach is based on a hierarchical Bayesian framework, that exploits the equivalence between parametric linear models and nonparametric Gaussian processes (GPs). The resulting models can be learned easily via an EM-algorithm. Empirical studies on multi-label text categorization suggest that the presented models allow accurate solutions of these multi-task problems.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of multi-task learning, that is, learning multiple related functions. Our approach is based on a hierarchical Bayesian framework, that exploits the equivalence between parametric linear models and nonparametric Gaussian processes (GPs). The resulting models can be learned easily via an EM-algorithm. paragraphs: The paper considers multi-task learning, where the goal is to learn several related functions. The relationship among tasks is central: a joint statistical framework provides a way to represent those functions together. The authors develop such a framework using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, placing the learning problems within a shared probabilistic construction.

Their approach exploits an equivalence between parametric linear models and nonparametric Gaussian processes. This connection provides the basis for the resulting multi-task models. It links two descriptions of function learning within the same framework and supports a practical estimation procedure. The authors state that the models can be learned readily with an expectation-maximization algorithm.

The empirical application is multi-label text categorization, where documents can receive multiple labels and the associated prediction functions form related tasks. The studies suggest that the proposed models can produce accurate solutions in this setting. The contribution combines a hierarchical treatment of task relationships, a connection between linear models and Gaussian processes, and a usable learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian framework connects linear models and Gaussian processes for multi-task learning, with encouraging text-categorization results.

abstract: We consider Gaussian multiresolution (MR) models in which coarser, hidden variables serve to capture statistical dependencies among the finest scale variables. Tree-structured MR models have limited modeling capabilities, as variables at one scale are forced to be independent of each other conditioned on other scales. We propose a new class of Gaussian MR models that capture the residual correlations within each scale using sparse covariance structure. Our goal is to learn a tree-structured graphical model connecting variables across different scales, while at the same time learning sparse structure for the conditional covariance within each scale conditioned on other scales. This model leads to an efficient, new inference algorithm that is similar to multipole methods in computational physics.

Tree-structured MR models have limited modeling capabilities, as variables at one scale are forced to be independent of each other conditioned on other scales. We propose a new class of Gaussian MR models that capture the residual correlations within each scale using sparse covariance structure. Our goal is to learn a tree-structured graphical model connecting variables across different scales, while at the same time learning sparse structure for the conditional covariance within each scale conditioned on other scales. This model leads to an efficient, new inference algorithm that is similar to multipole methods in computational physics.

paragraphs: Multiresolution models describe variables at several levels of detail. In the Gaussian models considered here, hidden variables at coarser scales capture dependencies among the finest-scale variables. A tree connecting the scales provides useful structure, but it imposes a restriction: variables within a scale become independent once the other scales are given.

The paper introduces a class of models that can represent correlations left over within each scale. It uses sparse conditional covariance structure to capture these residual relationships. The learning goal has two parts: discover a tree connecting variables across scales and learn the sparse within-scale covariance structure conditional on the other scales.

This combination expands what the model can express while retaining structure that supports efficient computation. The authors derive a new inference algorithm with similarities to multipole methods from computational physics. The contribution is a way to accommodate both broad dependencies across levels and remaining associations within a level, without forcing the cross-scale tree to account for every statistical relationship.
summary.tldr: The paper combines cross-scale trees with sparse within-scale covariances to make Gaussian multiresolution models more expressive while supporting efficient inference.

title: Exploiting sparse Markov and covariance structure in multiresolution models

abstract: The bootstrap provides a simple and powerful means of assessing the quality of estimators. However, in settings involving large datasets, the computation of bootstrap-based quantities can be prohibitively demanding. As an alternative, we present BLB, a new procedure which incorporates features of both the bootstrap and subsampling to obtain a robust, computationally efficient means of assessing the quality of estimators. BLB is well suited to modern parallel and distributed computing architectures and retains the generic applicability, statistical efficiency, and favorable theoretical properties of the bootstrap. We provide a theoretical analysis elucidating the properties of BLB, as well as an extensive empirical investigation, including a study of its statistical correctness, its large-scale implementation and performance, selection of hyperparameters, and performance on real data.

However, in settings involving large datasets, the computation of bootstrap-based quantities can be prohibitively demanding. BLB is well suited to modern parallel and distributed computing architectures and retains the generic applicability, statistical efficiency, and favorable theoretical properties of the bootstrap. We provide a theoretical analysis elucidating the properties of BLB, as well as an extensive empirical investigation, including a study of its statistical correctness, its large-scale implementation and performance, selection of hyperparameters, and performance on real data.

paragraphs: The bootstrap is a general method for assessing the quality of statistical estimates, but its computational demands can become prohibitive on large datasets. The paper introduces BLB to address this scaling problem. Its goal is to make estimator assessment computationally manageable while retaining the statistical strengths that make the bootstrap broadly useful.

BLB combines features of bootstrapping and subsampling. The resulting procedure is designed to work well with parallel and distributed computing architectures. The authors state that it preserves the bootstrap's generic applicability, statistical efficiency, and favorable theoretical properties while providing a robust and computationally efficient alternative for large-scale use.

The paper supports these claims with theoretical analysis and an extensive empirical investigation. The evaluation considers statistical correctness, implementation and performance at scale, hyperparameter selection, and real-data behavior. These topics connect the method's mathematical properties to the practical choices involved in deploying it. The main contribution is a way to assess estimator quality that treats computational scale and statistical reliability as joint design requirements.
summary.tldr: BLB combines bootstrap and subsampling ideas to assess estimator quality efficiently on large datasets while retaining favorable statistical properties.
